abstract: In this work we describe a new method that adjusts time-delays and the widths of time-windows in artificial neural networks automatically. The input of the units are weighted by a gaussian input-window over time which allows the learning rules for the delays and widths to be derived in the same way as it is used for the weights. Our results on a phoneme classification task compare well with results obtained with the TDNN by Waibel et al., which was manually optimized for the same task.

The input of the units are weighted by a gaussian input-window over time which allows the learning rules for the delays and widths to be derived in the same way as it is used for the weights. paragraphs: This paper introduces a method for learning the timing of information used by a neural network. Alongside connection weights, the method adjusts time delays and the widths of temporal windows. These parameters determine when a unit draws on input information and how broad an interval of that information contributes to its computation.

The mechanism uses a Gaussian window to weight inputs over time. This formulation lets learning rules for the delays and window widths be derived in the same manner as rules for the connection weights. Temporal selection becomes part of supervised learning, allowing training to adjust both the influence of an input and its timing.

The authors evaluate the method on phoneme classification and report results that compare well with a time-delay neural network manually optimized for the same task. The significance is that useful temporal settings can be learned automatically within the network. The comparison supports automatic adjustment as an effective way to configure the temporal processing required for the reported speech task.
summary.tldr: Tempo 2 learns time delays and temporal window widths automatically, with phoneme-classification results comparable to a manually optimized TDNN.

title: The Tempo 2 Algorithm: Adjusting Time-Delays By Supervised Learning

The action network is embedded in a sensory(cid:173) motoric system architecture that contains a separate world model. It is continuously fed with short-term predicted spatio-temporal obstacle trajectories, and receives robot state feedback. The ac(cid:173) tion net allows for external switching between alternative plan(cid:173) ning tasks. It generates goal-directed motor actions - subject to the robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints - such that colli(cid:173) sions with moving obstacles are avoided. Using supervised learn(cid:173) ing, we distribute examples of the optimal planner mapping over a structure-level adapted parsimonious higher order network. The training database is generated by a Dynamic Programming algo(cid:173) rithm. Extensive simulations reveal, that the local planner map(cid:173) ping is highly nonlinear, but can be effectively and sparsely repre(cid:173) sented by the chosen powerful net model. paragraphs: The paper studies short-term robot planning around moving obstacles in a simple test environment. A feedforward action network receives the robot's current state and predicted obstacle trajectories from a separate world model. Its job is to produce goal-directed motor actions while respecting the robot's movement constraints and avoiding collisions.

A dynamic-programming algorithm generates examples of the optimal planning mapping. Supervised learning transfers these examples into a compact higher-order network whose structure is adapted to the task. The architecture also permits external switching between alternative planning tasks. This arrangement separates prediction of the surrounding world from the network that chooses actions.

Extensive simulations indicate that the local planning mapping is highly nonlinear but can be represented effectively with the selected compact network. The authors report excellent generalization to obstacle configurations absent from training. They also discuss limitations as the planning horizon grows. The stated success therefore concerns learning a useful short-term controller from an optimization-based teacher, with longer-range planning identified as a separate challenge.
summary.tldr: A compact feedforward controller learns short-term moving-obstacle avoidance from dynamic-programming examples and generalizes to unseen configurations.

title: Learning Spatio-Temporal Planning from a Dynamic Programming Teacher: Feed-Forward Neurocontrol for Moving Obstacle Avoidance

abstract: We describe an analog VLSI implementation of a multi-dimensional gradient estimation and descent technique for minimizing an on(cid:173) chip scalar function fO. The implementation uses noise injec(cid:173) tion and multiplicative correlation to estimate derivatives, as in [Anderson, Kerns 92]. One intended application of this technique is setting circuit parameters on-chip automatically, rather than manually [Kirk 91]. Gradient descent optimization may be used to adjust synapse weights for a backpropagation or other on-chip learning implementation. The approach combines the features of continuous multi-dimensional gradient descent and the potential for an annealing style of optimization. We present data measured from our analog VLSI implementation.

The implementation uses noise injec(cid:173) tion and multiplicative correlation to estimate derivatives, as in [Anderson, Kerns 92]. One intended application of this technique is setting circuit parameters on-chip automatically, rather than manually [Kirk 91]. Gradient descent optimization may be used to adjust synapse weights for a backpropagation or other on-chip learning implementation. paragraphs: This paper implements a method for estimating gradients and performing gradient descent directly in analog VLSI hardware. The target is a scalar function computed on the chip, whose value depends on several adjustable parameters. Optimization requires estimating how changes in those parameters affect the function and then moving toward settings that reduce it.

The circuit estimates derivatives by injecting noise and using multiplicative correlation. The perturbations reveal how the measured function responds to parameter changes, providing the directional information needed for descent. This makes gradient estimation itself part of the on-chip computation and supports continuous adjustment across multiple dimensions.

One intended use is automatic circuit tuning, replacing manual parameter setting. Another is adjusting synaptic weights for an on-chip learning system, including a backpropagation implementation. The authors present measurements from the analog hardware and describe the possibility of annealing-style optimization alongside continuous gradient descent. The contribution is a physical implementation of an optimization mechanism that could serve both circuit calibration and learning.
summary.tldr: An analog chip uses injected noise and correlation to estimate gradients for automatic parameter tuning and potential on-chip learning.

title: Analog VLSI Implementation of Multi-dimensional Gradient Descent

abstract: Signal processing and classification algorithms often have limited applicability resulting from an inaccurate model of the signal's un(cid:173) derlying structure. We present here an efficient, Bayesian algo(cid:173) rithm for modeling a signal composed of the superposition of brief, Poisson-distributed functions. This methodology is applied to the specific problem of modeling and classifying extracellular neural waveforms which are composed of a superposition of an unknown number of action potentials CAPs). Previous approaches have had limited success due largely to the problems of determining the spike shapes, deciding how many are shapes distinct, and decomposing overlapping APs. A Bayesian solution to each of these problems is obtained by inferring a probabilistic model of the waveform. This approach quantifies the uncertainty of the form and number of the inferred AP shapes and is used to obtain an efficient method for decomposing complex overlaps. This algorithm can extract many times more information than previous methods and facilitates the extracellular investigation of neuronal classes and of interactions within neuronal circuits.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the problem of interpreting neural recordings in which several action potentials can overlap. A recorded waveform may combine an unknown number of spikes, and the characteristic shapes of those spikes are themselves unknown. The authors frame these difficulties as parts of one probabilistic modeling problem rather than treating each decision separately.

Their Bayesian method assumes that the signal is a superposition of brief functions whose occurrences follow a Poisson model. Applied to extracellular recordings, it infers spike shapes, the number of distinct shapes, and how overlapping action potentials contribute to the measured waveform. It also quantifies uncertainty about both the inferred shapes and their number.

That uncertainty matters because identifying a single plausible decomposition does not establish that it is the only explanation of a complex recording. The inferred model supports an efficient procedure for separating overlaps while retaining uncertainty about their ingredients. The authors report extracting many times more information than previous methods and connect this capability to studying neuronal classes and interactions within neural circuits.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian signal model jointly infers neural spike shapes, their number, and overlapping contributions while quantifying uncertainty.

title: Bayesian Modeling and Classification of Neural Signals

abstract: We investigate the optimization of neural networks governed by general objective functions. Practical formulations of such objec(cid:173) tives are notoriously difficult to solve; a common problem is the poor local extrema that result by any of the applied methods. In this paper, a novel framework is introduced for the solution oflarge(cid:173) scale optimization problems. It assumes little about the objective function and can be applied to general nonlinear, non-convex func(cid:173) tions; objectives in thousand of variables are thus efficiently min(cid:173) imized by a combination of techniques - deterministic annealing, multiscale optimization, attention mechanisms and trust region op(cid:173) timization methods.

Practical formulations of such objec(cid:173) tives are notoriously difficult to solve; a common problem is the poor local extrema that result by any of the applied methods. In this paper, a novel framework is introduced for the solution oflarge(cid:173) scale optimization problems. It assumes little about the objective function and can be applied to general nonlinear, non-convex func(cid:173) tions; objectives in thousand of variables are thus efficiently min(cid:173) imized by a combination of techniques - deterministic annealing, multiscale optimization, attention mechanisms and trust region op(cid:173) timization methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of optimizing neural networks whose behavior is governed by a general objective function. Practical objectives can have poor local extrema: solutions that look favorable nearby but are unsatisfactory overall. This makes the path taken by an optimization procedure important, particularly when the problem contains many variables.

The proposed framework combines deterministic annealing, multiscale optimization, attention mechanisms, and trust region methods. These bring together ways of changing the optimization landscape, working at different scales, directing computational effort, and controlling local optimization steps. The contribution is their combination into a framework intended for large optimization problems.

The abstract reports efficient minimization of objectives with thousands of variables. It also emphasizes that the framework assumes little about the objective and accommodates nonlinear, nonconvex functions. That scope matters because these functions need not have a single convenient minimum. The stated result supports combining complementary optimization techniques to handle difficult objectives, without implying that every resulting solution is globally optimal.
summary.tldr: A framework combining annealing, multiple scales, attention, and trust regions efficiently minimizes difficult objectives with thousands of variables.

title: A Multiscale Attentional Framework for Relaxation Neural Networks

abstract: This paper presents probabilistic modeling methods to solve the problem of dis(cid:173) criminating between five facial orientations with very little labeled data. Three models are explored. The first model maintains no inter-pixel dependencies, the second model is capable of modeling a set of arbitrary pair-wise dependencies, and the last model allows dependencies only between neighboring pixels. We show that for all three of these models, the accuracy of the learned models can be greatly improved by augmenting a small number of labeled training images with a large set of unlabeled images using Expectation-Maximization. This is important because it is often difficult to obtain image labels, while many unla(cid:173) beled images are readily available. Through a large set of empirical tests, we examine the benefits of unlabeled data for each of the models. By using only two randomly selected labeled examples per class, we can discriminate between the five facial orientations with an accuracy of 94%; with six labeled examples, we achieve an accuracy of 98%.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification of faces into five orientations when labeled images are scarce. It compares three probabilistic models with different treatments of pixel relationships. One treats pixels independently, another permits a set of arbitrary pairwise dependencies, and the third restricts dependencies to neighboring pixels. This makes the use of unlabeled data testable across different model structures.

The authors use expectation-maximization to combine a small labeled training set with a much larger unlabeled set. The motivation is practical: assigning image labels can be difficult, while unlabeled images are readily available. The experiments show that adding unlabeled images can substantially improve accuracy for all three model types.

The abstract reports 94% accuracy with two randomly selected labeled examples per class and 98% in a setting described as using six labeled examples. These findings demonstrate that useful orientation classification can be learned with very little labeling in the reported task. The broader contribution is evidence that unlabeled images can benefit models with several different assumptions about pixel dependencies.
summary.tldr: Using EM to add unlabeled images greatly improves five-way face-orientation classification when labeled examples are scarce.

title: Probabilistic Modeling for Face Orientation Discrimination: Learning from Labeled and Unlabeled Data

abstract: We use graphical models to explore the question of how people learn sim(cid:173) ple causal relationships from data. The two leading psychological theo(cid:173) ries can both be seen as estimating the parameters of a fixed graph. We argue that a complete account of causal induction should also consider how people learn the underlying causal graph structure, and we propose to model this inductive process as a Bayesian inference. Our argument is supported through the discussion of three data sets.
originalAbstract: We use graphical models to explore the question of how people learn sim(cid:173) ple causal relationships from data. The two leading psychological theo(cid:173) ries can both be seen as estimating the parameters of a fixed graph. We argue that a complete account of causal induction should also consider how people learn the underlying causal graph structure, and we propose to model this inductive process as a Bayesian inference. Our argument is supported through the discussion of three data sets.

paragraphs: The paper asks how people learn simple causal relationships from observed data. It uses graphical models to separate two aspects of this learning problem: estimating the properties of relationships within a given causal structure and determining what the structure itself should be. That distinction frames the authors' account of causal induction.

The authors interpret two leading psychological theories as estimating parameters within a fixed graph. In such an account, learning adjusts a model whose pattern of connections is already specified. They argue that a complete explanation must also address how people learn the underlying causal graph, including which relationships belong in it.

They propose treating this structural learning as Bayesian inference, so that data inform beliefs about possible causal structures. Discussion of three datasets supports their argument. The contribution is a broader account of what causal learning involves: the learner may need to infer the organization of causal relationships as well as their parameters. The paper presents Bayesian structure inference as a model of that additional inductive process.
summary.tldr: The paper models human causal induction as Bayesian learning of graph structure as well as estimation of relationships within a graph.

title: Structure Learning in Human Causal Induction

abstract: We consider noisy Euclidean traveling salesman problems in the plane, which are random combinatorial problems with underlying structure. Gibbs sampling is used to compute average trajectories, which estimate the underlying structure common to all instances. This procedure requires identifying the exact relationship between permutations and tours. In a learning setting, the average trajec(cid:173) tory is used as a model to construct solutions to new instances sampled from the same source. Experimental results show that the average trajectory can in fact estimate the underlying structure and that overfitting effects occur if the trajectory adapts too closely to a single instance.
originalAbstract: We consider noisy Euclidean traveling salesman problems in the plane, which are random combinatorial problems with underlying structure. Gibbs sampling is used to compute average trajectories, which estimate the underlying structure common to all instances. This procedure requires identifying the exact relationship between permutations and tours. In a learning setting, the average trajec(cid:173) tory is used as a model to construct solutions to new instances sampled from the same source. Experimental results show that the average trajectory can in fact estimate the underlying structure and that overfitting effects occur if the trajectory adapts too closely to a single instance.

paragraphs: The paper studies noisy traveling-salesman problems in the plane whose random instances share an underlying structure. Its learning objective is to capture that common structure and use it when constructing solutions for new instances drawn from the same source. This makes a collection of related routing problems the basis for learning.

The authors use Gibbs sampling to compute average trajectories that estimate the shared structure. Doing this requires identifying the exact relationship between permutations and tours, so the representation of a route is part of the method. The resulting average trajectory serves as the model used on subsequent instances.

Experiments show that an average trajectory can estimate the underlying structure. They also reveal overfitting when the trajectory adapts too closely to one particular instance. The finding highlights the distinction between representing what related problems have in common and matching the noise in an individual problem. Generalization here is explicitly tied to new instances sampled from the same source.
summary.tldr: Gibbs-sampled average tours can learn shared structure across noisy routing problems, but fitting one instance too closely causes overfitting.

title: The Noisy Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem and Learning

abstract: A model of auditory grouping is described in which auditory attention plays a key role. The model is based upon an oscillatory correlation framework, in which neural oscillators representing a single perceptual stream are synchronised, and are desynchronised from oscillators representing other streams. The model suggests a mechanism by which attention can be directed to the high or low tones in a repeating sequence of tones with alternating frequencies. In addition, it simulates the perceptual segregation of a mistuned harmonic from a complex tone.
originalAbstract: A model of auditory grouping is described in which auditory attention plays a key role. The model is based upon an oscillatory correlation framework, in which neural oscillators representing a single perceptual stream are synchronised, and are desynchronised from oscillators representing other streams. The model suggests a mechanism by which attention can be directed to the high or low tones in a repeating sequence of tones with alternating frequencies. In addition, it simulates the perceptual segregation of a mistuned harmonic from a complex tone.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a model of how sounds are grouped into perceptual streams, with attention playing an active role. The central question is how parts of an auditory sequence can belong together perceptually while remaining separate from other parts. The model expresses those relationships through the timing of neural oscillators.

Oscillators representing the same perceptual stream synchronize with one another. Oscillators representing different streams remain desynchronized. Shared timing therefore represents grouping, while differing timing represents separation. Within this framework, the model suggests a mechanism for directing attention toward either the higher or the lower tones in a repeating sequence that alternates between frequencies.

The model also simulates hearing a mistuned harmonic as separate from a complex tone. This extends its application from selecting among alternating tones to separating one component of a combined sound. Together, the examples show how oscillatory relationships can represent auditory grouping while incorporating selective attention. The proposed mechanism is a modeling account of these perceptual effects.
summary.tldr: A neural oscillator model uses synchronization and attention to explain the grouping and separation of auditory streams.

title: A Neural Oscillator Model of Auditory Selective Attention

abstract: This paper gives distribution-free concentration inequalities for the miss- ing mass and the error rate of histogram rules. Negative association meth- ods can be used to reduce these concentration problems to concentration questions about independent sums. Although the sums are independent, they are highly heterogeneous. Such highly heterogeneous independent sums cannot be analyzed using standard concentration inequalities such as Hoeffding’s inequality, the Angluin-Valiant bound, Bernstein’s in- equality, Bennett’s inequality, or McDiarmid’s theorem.
originalAbstract: This paper gives distribution-free concentration inequalities for the miss- ing mass and the error rate of histogram rules. Negative association meth- ods can be used to reduce these concentration problems to concentration questions about independent sums. Although the sums are independent, they are highly heterogeneous. Such highly heterogeneous independent sums cannot be analyzed using standard concentration inequalities such as Hoeffding’s inequality, the Angluin-Valiant bound, Bernstein’s in- equality, Bennett’s inequality, or McDiarmid’s theorem.

paragraphs: The paper derives probability bounds for the missing mass and the error rate of histogram rules. Missing mass concerns probability assigned to outcomes that a sample has not revealed. Concentration inequalities describe how strongly such random quantities stay near their typical values. The bounds are distribution-free, so they do not require choosing a particular underlying distribution.

The analysis uses negative association to reduce the original concentration questions to questions about sums of independent random variables. This reduction is useful because it changes the dependence structure of the problem into a form that can be studied through independent contributions.

Independence does not resolve the entire difficulty. The resulting contributions are highly heterogeneous, and the abstract states that standard concentration tools, including Hoeffding's and Bernstein's inequalities, cannot analyze the sums at issue. The contribution is therefore both the distribution-free bounds and an approach that addresses the remaining heterogeneity after dependence has been handled. It shows why a reduction to independent variables can still require specialized probability analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes distribution-free concentration bounds for missing mass and histogram-rule error by addressing highly heterogeneous independent sums.

title: Concentration Inequalities for the Missing Mass and for Histogram Rule Error

abstract: We describe the application of probabilistic model-based learning to the problem of automatically identifying classes of galaxies, based on both morphological and pixel intensity characteristics. The EM algorithm can be used to learn how to spatially orient a set of galaxies so that they are geometrically aligned. We augment this “ordering-model” with a mixture model on objects, and demonstrate how classes of galaxies can be learned in an unsupervised manner using a two-level EM algorithm. The resulting models provide highly accurate classi£cation of galaxies in cross-validation experiments.
originalAbstract: We describe the application of probabilistic model-based learning to the problem of automatically identifying classes of galaxies, based on both morphological and pixel intensity characteristics. The EM algorithm can be used to learn how to spatially orient a set of galaxies so that they are geometrically aligned. We augment this “ordering-model” with a mixture model on objects, and demonstrate how classes of galaxies can be learned in an unsupervised manner using a two-level EM algorithm. The resulting models provide highly accurate classi£cation of galaxies in cross-validation experiments.

paragraphs: The paper applies probabilistic learning to automatically identify classes of galaxies using their shapes and pixel intensities. A key part of the problem is spatial orientation: the method learns how to align a collection of galaxies geometrically. This makes alignment an inferred component of the analysis rather than requiring the images to arrive already oriented consistently.

Expectation-maximization is used to learn this alignment through an ordering model. The authors augment that model with a mixture model over objects, allowing different galaxy classes to be represented. A two-level EM procedure then learns the classes without supervision, bringing geometric alignment and the discovery of groups into a combined probabilistic framework.

The resulting models provide highly accurate galaxy classification in the reported cross-validation experiments. The finding supports the usefulness of combining orientation learning with class learning for this image task. Both shape and intensity contribute to the model, while the alignment mechanism gives those characteristics a consistent geometric context. The empirical claim concerns the evaluated models and experiments, with no numerical accuracy specified in the abstract.
summary.tldr: A two-level EM model jointly learns galaxy alignment and unsupervised classes, yielding highly accurate classification in reported cross-validation experiments.

title: Learning to Classify Galaxy Shapes Using the EM Algorithm

abstract: We study a method of optimal data-driven aggregation of classifiers in a convex combination and establish tight upper bounds on its excess risk with respect to a convex loss function under the assumption that the so- lution of optimal aggregation problem is sparse. We use a boosting type algorithm of optimal aggregation to develop aggregate classifiers of ac- tivation patterns in fMRI based on locally trained SVM classifiers. The aggregation coefficients are then used to design a "boosting map" of the brain needed to identify the regions with most significant impact on clas- sification.
originalAbstract: We study a method of optimal data-driven aggregation of classifiers in a convex combination and establish tight upper bounds on its excess risk with respect to a convex loss function under the assumption that the so- lution of optimal aggregation problem is sparse. We use a boosting type algorithm of optimal aggregation to develop aggregate classifiers of ac- tivation patterns in fMRI based on locally trained SVM classifiers. The aggregation coefficients are then used to design a "boosting map" of the brain needed to identify the regions with most significant impact on clas- sification.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to combine classifiers using weights learned from data. The combination is convex, so the aggregate draws on component classifiers through nonnegative weights that sum to one. The theoretical question is how much excess risk the learned aggregate incurs when performance is measured with a convex loss.

The authors establish tight upper bounds under the assumption that the optimal aggregation solution is sparse. Sparsity means that the optimal combination uses only a limited subset of the available classifiers. This is a condition supporting the bounds, connecting the structure of the best aggregate with the theoretical account of learning performance.

For fMRI, a boosting-type aggregation algorithm combines support vector machines trained locally on brain activation patterns. The learned coefficients also define a boosting map that identifies regions with the strongest impact on classification. The approach therefore uses the same aggregation weights both to build a classifier and to describe which local contributions matter most to its decisions.
summary.tldr: Sparse aggregation theory supports combining local fMRI classifiers and mapping their contributions through learned boosting weights.

title: Optimal Aggregation of Classifiers and Boosting Maps in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging

abstract: Integrate-and-Fire-type models are usually criticized because of their simplicity. On the other hand, the Integrate-and-Fire model is the basis of most of the theoretical studies on spiking neuron models. Here, we develop a sequential procedure to quantitatively evaluate an equivalent Integrate-and-Fire-type model based on intracellular recordings of cortical pyramidal neurons. We find that the resulting effective model is sufficient to predict the spike train of the real pyramidal neuron with high accuracy. In in vivo-like regimes, predicted and recorded traces are almost indistinguishable and a significant part of the spikes can be predicted at the correct timing. Slow processes like spike-frequency adaptation are shown to be a key feature in this context since they are necessary for the model to connect between different driving regimes.
originalAbstract: Integrate-and-Fire-type models are usually criticized because of their simplicity. On the other hand, the Integrate-and-Fire model is the basis of most of the theoretical studies on spiking neuron models. Here, we develop a sequential procedure to quantitatively evaluate an equivalent Integrate-and-Fire-type model based on intracellular recordings of cortical pyramidal neurons. We find that the resulting effective model is sufficient to predict the spike train of the real pyramidal neuron with high accuracy. In in vivo-like regimes, predicted and recorded traces are almost indistinguishable and a significant part of the spikes can be predicted at the correct timing. Slow processes like spike-frequency adaptation are shown to be a key feature in this context since they are necessary for the model to connect between different driving regimes.

paragraphs: Integrate-and-fire models are widely used to study spiking neurons, yet their simplicity raises questions about how faithfully they can reproduce real neuronal activity. This paper evaluates that issue using intracellular recordings from cortical pyramidal neurons. The authors develop a sequential procedure for quantitatively evaluating an effective integrate-and-fire-type model against those recordings.

The resulting model predicts the real neuron's spike train with high accuracy. In regimes resembling conditions in vivo, the predicted and recorded traces are almost indistinguishable, and a significant portion of spikes occur at the correctly predicted times. These findings demonstrate substantial predictive ability for the effective model in the conditions examined.

Slow processes, especially spike-frequency adaptation, are central to this result. The authors find them necessary for connecting model behavior across different driving regimes. The paper's claim of adequacy therefore concerns a model that incorporates adaptation: retaining this slow behavior allows a comparatively simple neuronal description to reproduce important aspects of the recorded activity.
summary.tldr: An integrate-and-fire-type model predicts recorded neuronal activity accurately, with adaptation needed to connect behavior across driving regimes.

title: Integrate-and-Fire models with adaptation are good enough

abstract: In this paper, we investigate how similar images sharing the same global description can help with unsupervised scene segmentation in an image. In contrast to recent work in semantic alignment of scenes, we allow an input image to be explained by partial matches of similar scenes. This allows for a better explanation of the input scenes. We perform MRF-based segmentation that optimizes over matches, while respecting boundary information. The recovered segments are then used to re-query a large database of images to retrieve better matches for the target region. We show improved performance in detecting occluding boundaries over previous methods on data gathered from the LabelMe database.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we investigate how similar images sharing the same global description can help with unsupervised scene segmentation in an image. In contrast to recent work in semantic alignment of scenes, we allow an input image to be explained by partial matches of similar scenes. This allows for a better explanation of the input scenes. We perform MRF-based segmentation that optimizes over matches, while respecting boundary information. The recovered segments are then used to re-query a large database of images to retrieve better matches for the target region. We show improved performance in detecting occluding boundaries over previous methods on data gathered from the LabelMe database.

paragraphs: This paper explores how other images with a similar overall description can help divide a scene into regions without supervised segmentation. Its central idea is that an input image can be explained using partial matches from multiple similar scenes. Different parts of the input can therefore draw support from different reference images.

The method uses a Markov random field formulation to optimize the segmentation over those matches while taking image boundaries into account. Matching and segmentation are connected: the selected correspondences help explain regions, while boundary information helps determine where regions should separate. This gives the method a way to combine evidence from similar scenes with evidence inside the input itself.

The resulting segments are then used to search a large image database again for better matches to individual target regions. Region discovery thus guides a more focused retrieval step. On data gathered from LabelMe, the authors report improved detection of occluding boundaries over previous methods. The stated finding supports the usefulness of partial scene matches and region-specific retrieval for locating those boundaries.
summary.tldr: Combining partial matches from similar images with boundary-aware segmentation improves occluding-boundary detection on LabelMe data.

title: Segmenting Scenes by Matching Image Composites

abstract: Consider a convex relaxation $\hat f$ of a pseudo-boolean function $f$. We say that the relaxation is {\em totally half-integral} if $\hat f(\bx)$ is a polyhedral function with half-integral extreme points $\bx$, and this property is preserved after adding an arbitrary combination of constraints of the form $x_i=x_j$, $x_i=1-x_j$, and $x_i=\gamma$ where $\gamma\in\{0,1,\frac{1}{2}\}$ is a constant. A well-known example is the {\em roof duality} relaxation for quadratic pseudo-boolean functions $f$. We argue that total half-integrality is a natural requirement for generalizations of roof duality to arbitrary pseudo-boolean functions. Our contributions are as follows. First, we provide a complete characterization of totally half-integral relaxations $\hat f$ by establishing a one-to-one correspondence with {\em bisubmodular functions}. Second, we give a new characterization of bisubmodular functions. Finally, we show some relationships between general totally half-integral relaxations and relaxations based on the roof duality.

paragraphs: A pseudo-Boolean function takes binary inputs, while a convex relaxation allows a broader set of values to make optimization more manageable. Roof duality provides a familiar relaxation for quadratic functions of this kind. This paper asks what mathematical property should guide extensions of roof duality to functions beyond the quadratic case.

The proposed requirement is total half-integrality. The relaxation is polyhedral, and its extreme points use only zero, one-half, and one. Crucially, that structure must survive constraints that equate variables, make them complements, or fix them to one of those three values. This preservation requirement makes the property stronger than simply observing half-integral extreme points in the original relaxation.

The authors completely characterize these relaxations through a one-to-one correspondence with bisubmodular functions. They also give a new characterization of bisubmodularity and establish relationships with relaxations based on roof duality. These results provide a structural foundation for generalizing the method: they identify exactly which functions correspond to the proposed class of relaxations.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes totally half-integral convex relaxations through an exact correspondence with bisubmodular functions.

title: Generalized roof duality and bisubmodular functions

abstract: Distributing labeling tasks among hundreds or thousands of annotators is an increasingly important method for annotating large datasets. We present a method for estimating the underlying value (e.g. the class) of each image from (noisy) annotations provided by multiple annotators. Our method is based on a model of the image formation and annotation process. Each image has different characteristics that are represented in an abstract Euclidean space. Each annotator is modeled as a multidimensional entity with variables representing competence, expertise and bias. This allows the model to discover and represent groups of annotators that have different sets of skills and knowledge, as well as groups of images that differ qualitatively. We find that our model predicts ground truth labels on both synthetic and real data more accurately than state of the art methods. Experiments also show that our model, starting from a set of binary labels, may discover rich information, such as different "schools of thought" amongst the annotators, and can group together images belonging to separate categories.

paragraphs: When many people label images, their judgments can be noisy and their abilities can differ across kinds of images. This paper develops a method for estimating underlying image labels while representing those differences explicitly. Its model describes both the image-formation process and how annotators produce their responses.

Images have characteristics represented in an abstract Euclidean space. Annotators have multidimensional descriptions of competence, expertise, and bias. This allows the model to discover groups of people with different skills or knowledge, together with groups of images that differ qualitatively. The approach can therefore account for variation that would be obscured by treating annotator ability as a single uniform property.

On synthetic and real data, the model predicts ground-truth labels more accurately than the compared state-of-the-art methods. Experiments also show that binary annotations may contain enough information to reveal different schools of thought among annotators and group images from separate categories. The model thus uses disagreement both to improve label estimation and to uncover structure in the annotation process.
summary.tldr: Modeling annotators' multidimensional expertise and bias improves label aggregation and can reveal groups of annotators and images.

title: The Multidimensional Wisdom of Crowds

abstract: Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) is a popular, iterative algorithm for computing strategies in extensive-form games. The Monte Carlo CFR (MCCFR) variants reduce the per iteration time cost of CFR by traversing a sampled portion of the tree. The previous most effective instances of MCCFR can still be very slow in games with many player actions since they sample every action for a given player. In this paper, we present a new MCCFR algorithm, Average Strategy Sampling (AS), that samples a subset of the player's actions according to the player's average strategy. Our new algorithm is inspired by a new, tighter bound on the number of iterations required by CFR to converge to a given solution quality. In addition, we prove a similar, tighter bound for AS and other popular MCCFR variants. Finally, we validate our work by demonstrating that AS converges faster than previous MCCFR algorithms in both no-limit poker and Bluff.

paragraphs: Counterfactual Regret Minimization computes strategies in extensive-form games through repeated updates. Monte Carlo variants reduce the work per iteration by exploring only sampled portions of the game tree. Yet previously effective variants still examine every action for a given player, leaving a substantial computational burden when that player has many possible actions.

The proposed Average Strategy Sampling algorithm samples only a subset of those actions, using the player's average strategy to guide selection. This makes action sampling itself part of the efficiency improvement. The method is motivated by a new, tighter bound on how many iterations ordinary CFR needs to reach a specified solution quality.

The authors also prove similarly tighter iteration bounds for Average Strategy Sampling and other popular Monte Carlo CFR variants. Experiments in no-limit poker and Bluff show faster convergence than previous Monte Carlo CFR algorithms. The contribution therefore combines a revised theoretical understanding of convergence with an action-sampling method that demonstrates practical benefits in the evaluated games.
summary.tldr: Average Strategy Sampling reduces action exploration in Monte Carlo CFR and achieves faster convergence in no-limit poker and Bluff.

title: Efficient Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret Minimization in Games with Many Player Actions

abstract: Multiple-output regression models require estimating multiple functions, one for each output. To improve parameter estimation in such models, methods based on structural regularization of the model parameters are usually needed. In this paper, we present a multiple-output regression model that leverages the covariance structure of the functions (i.e., how the multiple functions are related with each other) as well as the conditional covariance structure of the outputs. This is in contrast with existing methods that usually take into account only one of these structures. More importantly, unlike most of the other existing methods, none of these structures need be known a priori in our model, and are learned from the data. Several previously proposed structural regularization based multiple-output regression models turn out to be special cases of our model. Moreover, in addition to being a rich model for multiple-output regression, our model can also be used in estimating the graphical model structure of a set of variables (multivariate outputs) conditioned on another set of variables (inputs). Experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Multiple-output regression can improve by sharing structure across its predictive functions, but outputs may also remain dependent after conditioning on the inputs. This paper models both relationships together. It distinguishes similarity among the functions from residual conditional covariance among the output variables.

Neither structure must be supplied in advance; both are learned from data. The model encompasses several earlier structural-regularization methods as special cases. It can also estimate a conditional graphical model among outputs, giving the learned dependencies an interpretation beyond their role in improving prediction.

Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution is a unified view of two sources of statistical sharing that are often treated separately. Learning which predictors should resemble one another and which outputs remain conditionally linked can reveal complementary information, enabling a richer regression model than imposing only one type of covariance structure.
summary.tldr: A multiple-output regression model jointly learns relationships among predictive functions and conditional dependencies among outputs.

title: Simultaneously Leveraging Output and Task Structures for Multiple-Output Regression

abstract: Large Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are usually solved using Approximate Dynamic Programming (ADP) methods such as Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) or Approximate Policy Iteration (API). The main contribution of this paper is to show that, alternatively, the optimal state-action value function can be estimated using Difference of Convex functions (DC) Programming. To do so, we study the minimization of a norm of the Optimal Bellman Residual (OBR) $T^*Q-Q$, where $T^*$ is the so-called optimal Bellman operator. Controlling this residual allows controlling the distance to the optimal action-value function, and we show that minimizing an empirical norm of the OBR is consistant in the Vapnik sense. Finally, we frame this optimization problem as a DC program. That allows envisioning using the large related literature on DC Programming to address the Reinforcement Leaning (RL) problem.

paragraphs: Large reinforcement learning problems often estimate value functions through approximate value iteration or policy iteration. This paper develops an alternative optimization formulation for estimating the optimal state-action value function, which describes the value of taking an action in a state and then behaving optimally.

The proposed objective measures the optimal Bellman residual: the difference between a candidate value function and the result of applying the optimal Bellman operator to it. This residual captures how far the candidate is from satisfying the optimality equation. The authors establish that controlling the residual also controls distance to the optimal action-value function, giving the optimization target a direct connection to the desired estimate.

They further show consistency, in the Vapnik sense, for minimizing an empirical norm of this residual. Finally, they express the optimization as a difference-of-convex-functions program. This formulation connects reinforcement learning to an existing optimization literature and opens the possibility of applying its methods. The stated contribution is this theoretically supported route to value estimation, rather than a reported experimental comparison of solvers.
summary.tldr: Optimal Bellman residual minimization can be formulated as difference-of-convex programming, providing a theoretically supported alternative for estimating action values.

title: Difference of Convex Functions Programming for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Machine learning offers a fantastically powerful toolkit for building useful complexprediction systems quickly. This paper argues it is dangerous to think ofthese quick wins as coming for free. Using the software engineering frameworkof technical debt, we find it is common to incur massive ongoing maintenancecosts in real-world ML systems. We explore several ML-specific risk factors toaccount for in system design. These include boundary erosion, entanglement,hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, data dependencies, configurationissues, changes in the external world, and a variety of system-level anti-patterns.

paragraphs: This paper examines the ongoing cost of maintaining machine-learning systems after their initial predictive capability has been built. It uses technical debt as its organizing idea: rapid development can create obligations that become expensive to manage later. The authors argue that substantial maintenance burdens are common in real-world ML systems despite the speed of early progress.

Their analysis identifies risks involving system boundaries, tightly entangled components, hidden feedback loops, and consumers whose dependencies have not been declared. These categories draw attention to how a predictive system connects to the rest of its environment. The maintenance concern extends beyond the model to relationships among data, software, and the systems that use its outputs.

Other risk factors include data dependencies, configuration problems, external-world changes, and recurring system-level anti-patterns. The paper's contribution is a design-oriented account of these ML-specific sources of debt. Its message is that judging a system by how quickly it becomes useful leaves out the continuing work required to maintain that usefulness as its surrounding dependencies and conditions evolve.
summary.tldr: Machine-learning systems can accumulate substantial maintenance debt through data dependencies, entanglement, feedback loops, configuration, and changes around them.

title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems

abstract: We develop an efficient alternating framework for learning a generalized version of Factorization Machine (gFM) on steaming data with provable guarantees. When the instances are sampled from $d$ dimensional random Gaussian vectors and the target second order coefficient matrix in gFM is of rank $k$, our algorithm converges linearly, achieves $O(\epsilon)$ recovery error after retrieving $O(k^{3}d\log(1/\epsilon))$ training instances, consumes $O(kd)$ memory in one-pass of dataset and only requires matrix-vector product operations in each iteration. The key ingredient of our framework is a construction of an estimation sequence endowed with a so-called Conditionally Independent RIP condition (CI-RIP). As special cases of gFM, our framework can be applied to symmetric or asymmetric rank-one matrix sensing problems, such as inductive matrix completion and phase retrieval.

paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for learning a generalized factorization machine from streaming data. The model includes a matrix of second-order coefficients, which describes interactions between input features. The approach alternates between estimation steps while processing the dataset once, making its storage requirements especially relevant when examples arrive continuously.

The recovery guarantees depend on explicit assumptions: inputs are random Gaussian vectors in d dimensions, and the target coefficient matrix has rank k. Under these conditions, the algorithm converges linearly and reaches O(ε) recovery error using O(k³d log(1/ε)) training examples. It needs O(kd) memory, and each iteration uses matrix-vector products.

The theoretical construction is an estimation sequence satisfying a condition called conditionally independent RIP. This condition supports the analysis of the alternating procedure. The framework also covers symmetric and asymmetric rank-one matrix sensing as special cases, connecting the result to inductive matrix completion and phase retrieval. Its contribution combines a streaming implementation with recovery guarantees for the stated data model.
summary.tldr: A one-pass alternating algorithm learns generalized factorization machines with efficient memory use and provable recovery under Gaussian-input and low-rank assumptions.

title: A Non-convex One-Pass Framework for Generalized Factorization Machine and Rank-One Matrix Sensing

abstract: We consider a seller with an unlimited supply of a single good, who is faced with a stream of $T$ buyers. Each buyer has a window of time in which she would like to purchase, and would buy at the lowest price in that window, provided that this price is lower than her private value (and otherwise, would not buy at all). In this setting, we give an algorithm that attains $O(T^{2/3})$ regret over any sequence of $T$ buyers with respect to the best fixed price in hindsight, and prove that no algorithm can perform better in the worst case.

Each buyer has a window of time in which she would like to purchase, and would buy at the lowest price in that window, provided that this price is lower than her private value (and otherwise, would not buy at all). In this setting, we give an algorithm that attains $O(T^{2/3})$ regret over any sequence of $T$ buyers with respect to the best fixed price in hindsight, and prove that no algorithm can perform better in the worst case.

paragraphs: This paper studies a seller who has an unlimited supply of one good and encounters a sequence of buyers. Buyers are patient in a precise sense: each has a purchase window and chooses the lowest price offered during that window. A purchase occurs only if that lowest price is below the buyer’s private value.

This behavior makes pricing across time matter, because a buyer’s decision depends on multiple offered prices rather than only the price at arrival. The paper evaluates the seller against the best single fixed price that could have been chosen after seeing the entire buyer sequence. Regret measures the revenue shortfall relative to that hindsight benchmark.

The authors give an algorithm with O(T^(2/3)) regret for any sequence of T buyers and prove a matching worst-case limit. Because this growth is sublinear, the guaranteed regret per buyer decreases as the sequence grows. The optimality statement is specific to the worst case and the fixed-price benchmark; it does not compare the algorithm with an unrestricted hindsight schedule of changing prices.
summary.tldr: Online pricing for patient buyers admits O(T^(2/3)) regret against the best fixed price, and this rate is worst-case optimal.

title: Online Pricing with Strategic and Patient Buyers

abstract: Fast algorithms for nearest neighbor (NN) search have in large part focused on L2 distance. Here we develop an approach for L1 distance that begins with an explicit and exact embedding of the points into L2. We show how this embedding can efficiently be combined with random projection methods for L2 NN search, such as locality-sensitive hashing or random projection trees. We rigorously establish the correctness of the methodology and show by experimentation that it is competitive in practice with available alternatives.

We rigorously establish the correctness of the methodology and show by experimentation that it is competitive in practice with available alternatives.

paragraphs: Nearest neighbor search finds stored points that are closest to a query, but the meaning of closeness depends on the distance used. This paper targets L1 distance, while much of the existing fast search machinery focuses on L2 distance. Its central idea is to connect these settings so that methods developed for L2 search can help solve L1 search.

The approach begins with an explicit, exact embedding of the original points into an L2 setting. The embedding supplies the mathematical bridge between the original search problem and the transformed one. The authors then show how to combine it efficiently with random projection approaches, including locality-sensitive hashing and random projection trees.

The contribution has both a theoretical and a practical component. A rigorous correctness argument supports the transformation and search methodology, while experiments show competitive performance against available alternatives. The practical finding is competitiveness, rather than universal superiority. More broadly, the work demonstrates how an appropriate representation change can make existing search techniques useful for a different distance measure.
summary.tldr: An exact embedding connects L1 nearest neighbor search to efficient L2 search methods, with correctness guarantees and competitive experimental results.

title: An algorithm for L1 nearest neighbor search via monotonic embedding

abstract: Reconstruction of neuroanatomy is a fundamental problem in neuroscience. Stochastic expression of colors in individual cells is a promising tool, although its use in the nervous system has been limited due to various sources of variability in expression. Moreover, the intermingled anatomy of neuronal trees is challenging for existing segmentation algorithms. Here, we propose a method to automate the segmentation of neurons in such (potentially pseudo-colored) images. The method uses spatio-color relations between the voxels, generates supervoxels to reduce the problem size by four orders of magnitude before the final segmentation, and is parallelizable over the supervoxels. To quantify performance and gain insight, we generate simulated images, where the noise level and characteristics, the density of expression, and the number of fluorophore types are variable. We also present segmentations of real Brainbow images of the mouse hippocampus, which reveal many of the dendritic segments.

paragraphs: Coloring individual neurons can help reveal their anatomy, but turning those images into separate neuronal structures remains difficult. Color expression varies, and branching neurons intertwine. The paper develops an automated segmentation method for multispectral images, including images whose displayed colors may be assigned rather than directly recorded.

The method uses both spatial relationships and color relationships between voxels, the three-dimensional counterparts of pixels. It first groups voxels into supervoxels, reducing the problem size by four orders of magnitude before the final segmentation. Computation can also be parallelized across those groups. These design choices address the scale of the image-processing problem while retaining spatial and color information.

To study performance, the authors generate simulated images with controllable noise, expression density, and numbers of fluorescent marker types. They also apply the method to real Brainbow images of the mouse hippocampus, recovering many dendritic segments. Those results demonstrate useful anatomical segmentation without claiming that every neuron or complete branching structure is reconstructed.
summary.tldr: An automated neuron-segmentation method combines spatial and color information with supervoxels to reduce computation and recover dendritic segments.

title: Automated scalable segmentation of neurons from multispectral images

abstract: This paper considers a number of related inverse filtering problems for hidden Markov models (HMMs). In particular, given a sequence of state posteriors and the system dynamics; i) estimate the corresponding sequence of observations, ii) estimate the observation likelihoods, and iii) jointly estimate the observation likelihoods and the observation sequence. We show how to avoid a computationally expensive mixed integer linear program (MILP) by exploiting the algebraic structure of the HMM filter using simple linear algebra operations, and provide conditions for when the quantities can be uniquely reconstructed. We also propose a solution to the more general case where the posteriors are noisily observed. Finally, the proposed inverse filtering algorithms are evaluated on real-world polysomnographic data used for automatic sleep segmentation.

We show how to avoid a computationally expensive mixed integer linear program (MILP) by exploiting the algebraic structure of the HMM filter using simple linear algebra operations, and provide conditions for when the quantities can be uniquely reconstructed. paragraphs: This paper studies how to work backward through a hidden Markov model’s filtering process. Given a sequence of posterior beliefs about hidden states and the system’s dynamics, the goal is to reconstruct information behind those beliefs. The authors consider recovering the observation sequence, recovering observation likelihoods, and estimating both together.

Their approach exploits the algebraic structure of the HMM filter. This allows them to replace a computationally expensive mixed integer linear program with simple linear algebra operations. They also provide conditions under which the desired quantities can be reconstructed uniquely. Those conditions distinguish cases where the posterior sequence identifies one answer from cases where uniqueness is not established.

The authors extend the approach to a more general setting in which the posterior beliefs themselves are observed with noise. They evaluate the inverse-filtering algorithms on real polysomnographic data used for automatic sleep segmentation. The contribution combines a more direct computational route to reconstruction with an analysis of when reconstruction is identifiable and a treatment of noisy posterior inputs.
summary.tldr: Inverse HMM filtering uses linear algebra to reconstruct observations or observation likelihoods from state posteriors, with conditions for uniqueness and an extension to noisy inputs.

title: Inverse Filtering for Hidden Markov Models

abstract: Bandit learning is characterized by the tension between long-term exploration and short-term exploitation. However, as has recently been noted, in settings in which the choices of the learning algorithm correspond to important decisions about individual people (such as criminal recidivism prediction, lending, and sequential drug trials), exploration corresponds to explicitly sacrificing the well-being of one individual for the potential future benefit of others. In such settings, one might like to run a ``greedy'' algorithm, which always makes the optimal decision for the individuals at hand --- but doing this can result in a catastrophic failure to learn. In this paper, we consider the linear contextual bandit problem and revisit the performance of the greedy algorithm. We give a smoothed analysis, showing that even when contexts may be chosen by an adversary, small perturbations of the adversary's choices suffice for the algorithm to achieve ``no regret'', perhaps (depending on the specifics of the setting) with a constant amount of initial training data. This suggests that in slightly perturbed environments, exploration and exploitation need not be in conflict in the linear setting.

paragraphs: Bandit learning usually balances choosing what currently looks best with trying alternatives to learn more. When decisions affect people, deliberate exploration can impose a cost on one person for the possible benefit of others. A greedy algorithm avoids that deliberate sacrifice by always taking the action judged best from its current information, but it can also fail badly at learning.

The paper studies this tension for linear contextual bandits using smoothed analysis. It allows an adversary to choose the contexts that describe decision situations, then considers small perturbations to those choices. The central result is that these perturbations suffice for the greedy algorithm to achieve no regret. Depending on the setting, a constant amount of initial training data may also be needed.

No regret means that the algorithm's average performance shortfall vanishes over time relative to the relevant benchmark. The result suggests that environmental variation can supply enough learning opportunities without deliberate exploration in this linear setting. Its force is conditional on the perturbed environment; it does not establish that greedy decisions always learn successfully.
summary.tldr: Small context perturbations can let greedy linear contextual bandit learning achieve no regret, sometimes with a constant amount of initial training data.

title: A Smoothed Analysis of the Greedy Algorithm for the Linear Contextual Bandit Problem

abstract: Many real-world vision problems suffer from inherent ambiguities. In clinical applications for example, it might not be clear from a CT scan alone which particular region is cancer tissue. Therefore a group of graders typically produces a set of diverse but plausible segmentations. We consider the task of learning a distribution over segmentations given an input. To this end we propose a generative segmentation model based on a combination of a U-Net with a conditional variational autoencoder that is capable of efficiently producing an unlimited number of plausible hypotheses. We show on a lung abnormalities segmentation task and on a Cityscapes segmentation task that our model reproduces the possible segmentation variants as well as the frequencies with which they occur, doing so significantly better than published approaches. These models could have a high impact in real-world applications, such as being used as clinical decision-making algorithms accounting for multiple plausible semantic segmentation hypotheses to provide possible diagnoses and recommend further actions to resolve the present ambiguities.

We show on a lung abnormalities segmentation task and on a Cityscapes segmentation task that our model reproduces the possible segmentation variants as well as the frequencies with which they occur, doing so significantly better than published approaches. paragraphs: Some images support several reasonable segmentations, even when carefully examined. A medical scan, for example, may not uniquely determine which region contains abnormal tissue. This paper treats that ambiguity as something a model should represent. Its goal is to learn a distribution over possible segmentations for an image, including how frequently different plausible interpretations occur.

The proposed Probabilistic U-Net combines a U-Net with a conditional variational autoencoder. This generative design can efficiently produce an unlimited number of segmentation hypotheses for a given input. The resulting output is a collection of possible interpretations rather than a single fixed segmentation, making alternative readings of the same visual evidence available.

On lung abnormality segmentation and a Cityscapes segmentation task, the model reproduces both segmentation variants and their occurrence frequencies significantly better than published approaches. The authors suggest that such distributions could support clinical decisions by preserving multiple plausible hypotheses and informing actions to resolve ambiguity. That clinical role is presented as a potential application of the approach.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic U-Net learns multiple plausible segmentations and their frequencies, improving ambiguity modeling on two segmentation tasks.

title: A Probabilistic U-Net for Segmentation of Ambiguous Images

abstract: While domain adaptation has been actively researched, most algorithms focus on the single-source-single-target adaptation setting. In this paper we propose new generalization bounds and algorithms under both classification and regression settings for unsupervised multiple source domain adaptation. Our theoretical analysis naturally leads to an efficient learning strategy using adversarial neural networks: we show how to interpret it as learning feature representations that are invariant to the multiple domain shifts while still being discriminative for the learning task. To this end, we propose multisource domain adversarial networks (MDAN) that approach domain adaptation by optimizing task-adaptive generalization bounds. To demonstrate the effectiveness of MDAN, we conduct extensive experiments showing superior adaptation performance on both classification and regression problems: sentiment analysis, digit classification, and vehicle counting.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation asks how knowledge learned in one setting can remain useful in another. This paper addresses the case where several source domains contribute information to an unsupervised target-domain adaptation problem. Multiple sources introduce multiple shifts in the data, so a representation must account for more than a single source-to-target mismatch.

The authors derive generalization bounds for both classification and regression. These bounds motivate multisource domain adversarial networks, or MDAN. The networks learn features that resist differences among domains while retaining information needed for the prediction task. Their training objective is tied to task-adaptive generalization bounds, giving the adversarial learning strategy a theoretical basis.

Experiments cover sentiment analysis, digit classification, and vehicle counting, with reported superior adaptation performance across classification and regression tasks. These results support the usefulness of treating multiple domain shifts together. The central contribution is the connection between a theoretical account of transfer and a practical neural-network method for learning representations that remain predictive across those shifts.
summary.tldr: MDAN uses generalization bounds to guide adversarial learning from multiple source domains for classification and regression.

title: Adversarial Multiple Source Domain Adaptation

abstract: Model-free reinforcement learning aims to offer off-the-shelf solutions for controlling dynamical systems without requiring models of the system dynamics. We introduce a model-free random search algorithm for training static, linear policies for continuous control problems. Common evaluation methodology shows that our method matches state-of-the-art sample efficiency on the benchmark MuJoCo locomotion tasks. Nonetheless, more rigorous evaluation reveals that the assessment of performance on these benchmarks is optimistic. We evaluate the performance of our method over hundreds of random seeds and many different hyperparameter configurations for each benchmark task. This extensive evaluation is possible because of the small computational footprint of our method. Our simulations highlight a high variability in performance in these benchmark tasks, indicating that commonly used estimations of sample efficiency do not adequately evaluate the performance of RL algorithms. Our results stress the need for new baselines, benchmarks and evaluation methodology for RL algorithms.

Under commonly used evaluation practices, the method matches state-of-the-art sample efficiency on MuJoCo locomotion benchmarks, making it a useful point of comparison for more elaborate approaches.

Its small computational cost also permits a much broader evaluation. The authors test hundreds of random seeds and many hyperparameter configurations for each benchmark task. These experiments reveal substantial variability, showing that conclusions drawn from narrower evaluations can give an overly optimistic impression of performance.

The contribution therefore includes both a competitive control method and evidence about how control methods should be assessed. The apparent sample-efficiency result is explicitly qualified by the more rigorous evaluation. The findings suggest that commonly reported estimates do not adequately characterize reinforcement learning performance on these tasks, and motivate new baselines, benchmarks, and evaluation methods that better account for variation across runs and configurations.
summary.tldr: Simple random search appears highly competitive on locomotion benchmarks, while extensive testing exposes variability that makes common evaluations optimistic.

title: Simple random search of static linear policies is competitive for reinforcement learning

abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) attempts to infer human rewards or preferences from observed behavior. Since human planning systematically deviates from rationality, several approaches have been tried to account for specific human shortcomings. However, the general problem of inferring the reward function of an agent of unknown rationality has received little attention. Unlike the well-known ambiguity problems in IRL, this one is practically relevant but cannot be resolved by observing the agent's policy in enough environments. This paper shows (1) that a No Free Lunch result implies it is impossible to uniquely decompose a policy into a planning algorithm and reward function, and (2) that even with a reasonable simplicity prior/Occam's razor on the set of decompositions, we cannot distinguish between the true decomposition and others that lead to high regret. To address this, we need simple `normative' assumptions, which cannot be deduced exclusively from observations.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer preferences from behavior, but behavior reflects both what an agent wants and how it plans. When the agent's degree of rationality is unknown, those two contributions become difficult to separate. This paper studies that general ambiguity rather than assuming a particular, already specified form of human planning error.

The authors show that a No Free Lunch result rules out uniquely decomposing an observed policy into a planning algorithm and a reward function. Observing the policy in additional environments does not resolve this ambiguity. They further show that a reasonable preference for simpler explanations cannot reliably distinguish the true decomposition from alternative decompositions that lead to high regret.

The implication is that simplicity and behavioral observations alone do not supply everything needed for preference inference in this setting. The authors argue that simple normative assumptions are required: assumptions about how behavior should be interpreted that cannot be derived exclusively from observations. The result identifies a foundational obstacle to learning human preferences when planning behavior itself remains unrestricted or unknown.
summary.tldr: Behavior and a reasonable simplicity prior cannot uniquely identify an agent's preferences when its planning process is unknown.

title: Occam's razor is insufficient to infer the preferences of irrational agents

abstract: We propose SWA-Gaussian (SWAG), a simple, scalable, and general purpose approach for uncertainty representation and calibration in deep learning. Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA), which computes the first moment of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) iterates with a modified learning rate schedule, has recently been shown to improve generalization in deep learning. With SWAG, we fit a Gaussian using the SWA solution as the first moment and a low rank plus diagonal covariance also derived from the SGD iterates, forming an approximate posterior distribution over neural network weights; we then sample from this Gaussian distribution to perform Bayesian model averaging. We empirically find that SWAG approximates the shape of the true posterior, in accordance with results describing the stationary distribution of SGD iterates. Moreover, we demonstrate that SWAG performs well on a wide variety of tasks, including out of sample detection, calibration, and transfer learning, in comparison to many popular alternatives including variational inference, MC dropout, KFAC Laplace, and temperature scaling.

paragraphs: SWAG addresses how a neural network can represent uncertainty about its predictions. It builds on Stochastic Weight Averaging, which averages the weights visited during training with a modified learning-rate schedule. Instead of using that average as a single final model, SWAG makes it the center of a probability distribution over possible network weights.

The method fits a Gaussian distribution whose covariance also comes from the training trajectory. Its low-rank component represents coordinated variation among weights, while its diagonal component provides additional per-weight variation. Sampling weights from this distribution and combining their predictions implements an approximate form of Bayesian model averaging. The construction therefore extracts uncertainty information from the same sequence of weights used to form the average.

The authors empirically find that this Gaussian approximates the shape of the true posterior. They also report good performance across calibration, out-of-sample detection, and transfer learning compared with several popular alternatives. These findings support SWAG as a simple, scalable uncertainty method, while retaining its status as a posterior approximation.
summary.tldr: SWAG estimates uncertainty by fitting a Gaussian to training-time network weights and averaging predictions from sampled models.

title: A Simple Baseline for Bayesian Uncertainty in Deep Learning

abstract: Despite some exciting progress on high-quality image generation from structured (scene graphs) or free-form (sentences) descriptions, most of them only guarantee the image-level semantical consistency, i.e. the generated image matching the semantic meaning of the description. They still lack the investigations on synthesizing the images in a more controllable way, like finely manipulating the visual appearance of every object. Therefore, to generate the images with preferred objects and rich interactions, we propose a semi-parametric method, PasteGAN, for generating the image from the scene graph and the image crops, where spatial arrangements of the objects and their pair-wise relationships are defined by the scene graph and the object appearances are determined by the given object crops. To enhance the interactions of the objects in the output, we design a Crop Refining Network and an Object-Image Fuser to embed the objects as well as their relationships into one map. Multiple losses work collaboratively to guarantee the generated images highly respecting the crops and complying with the scene graphs while maintaining excellent image quality. A crop selector is also proposed to pick the most-compatible crops from our external object tank by encoding the interactions around the objects in the scene graph if the crops are not provided. Evaluated on Visual Genome and COCO-Stuff dataset, our proposed method significantly outperforms the SOTA methods on Inception Score, Diversity Score and Fréchet Inception Distance. Extensive experiments also demonstrate our method’s ability to generate complex and diverse images with given objects. The code is available at https://github.com/yikang-li/PasteGAN.
