A scene graph specifies object arrangements and pairwise relationships, while supplied image crops determine how the objects should look. This gives the generator more detailed guidance than a description that only specifies the overall scene meaning.

A Crop Refining Network and an Object-Image Fuser combine objects and their relationships into a shared map. Multiple training losses encourage the generated image to respect the crops, follow the scene graph, and maintain visual quality. If crops are absent, a selector chooses compatible examples from an external object collection using information about the surrounding relationships in the graph.

On Visual Genome and COCO-Stuff, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in Inception Score, Diversity Score, and Fréchet Inception Distance. Further experiments demonstrate the ability to generate complex, varied images containing given objects. The contribution links explicit appearance choices with relational scene generation, supporting control over what objects look like as well as how they interact.
summary.tldr: PasteGAN combines scene graphs with object image crops to generate images with controllable object appearances and relationships.

title: PasteGAN: A Semi-Parametric Method to Generate Image from Scene Graph

abstract: A recent body of exciting work seeks to shed light on the behavior of accelerated methods in optimization via high-resolution differential equations. These differential equations are continuous counterparts of the discrete-time optimization algorithms, and their convergence properties can be characterized using the powerful tools provided by classical Lyapunov stability analysis. An outstanding question of pivotal importance is how to discretize these continuous flows while maintaining their convergence rates. This paper provides a novel approach through the idea of opportunistic state-triggered control. We take advantage of the Lyapunov functions employed to characterize the rate of convergence of high-resolution differential equations to design variable-stepsize forward-Euler discretizations that preserve the Lyapunov decay of the original dynamics. The philosophy of our approach is not limited to forward-Euler discretizations and may be combined with other integration schemes.

paragraphs: Accelerated optimization algorithms can be studied through differential equations that describe related continuous-time dynamics. These equations make it possible to analyze convergence using Lyapunov functions, which track progress toward a solution. The practical challenge is converting a continuous flow into discrete computational steps while preserving the convergence behavior established for that flow.

This paper uses opportunistic state-triggered control to choose variable step sizes for forward-Euler discretization. The step-size design draws directly on the Lyapunov functions used to analyze the original differential equations. In this way, the same mathematical description of progress guides how the continuous dynamics are turned into an algorithm.

The resulting discretizations preserve the Lyapunov decay of the original dynamics, connecting the continuous convergence analysis to discrete updates. This matters because a useful continuous-time rate must survive discretization to inform an implementable method. The authors also suggest that the design philosophy may work with integration schemes other than forward Euler, presenting that broader applicability as a possibility rather than an established result for every scheme.
summary.tldr: Lyapunov-guided variable step sizes turn accelerated continuous optimization flows into discrete updates that preserve their Lyapunov decay.

title: Convergence-Rate-Matching Discretization of Accelerated Optimization Flows Through Opportunistic State-Triggered Control

abstract: Discovery of causal relations from observational data is essential for many disciplines of science and real-world applications. However, unlike other machine learning algorithms, whose development has been greatly fostered by a large amount of available benchmark datasets, causal discovery algorithms are notoriously difficult to be systematically evaluated because few datasets with known ground-truth causal relations are available. In this work, we handle the problem of evaluating causal discovery algorithms by building a flexible simulator in the medical setting. We develop a neuropathic pain diagnosis simulator, inspired by the fact that the biological processes of neuropathic pathophysiology are well studied with well-understood causal influences. Our simulator exploits the causal graph of the neuropathic pain pathology and its parameters in the generator are estimated from real-life patient cases. We show that the data generated from our simulator have similar statistics as real-world data. As a clear advantage, the simulator can produce infinite samples without jeopardizing the privacy of real-world patients. Our simulator provides a natural tool for evaluating various types of causal discovery algorithms, including those to deal with practical issues in causal discovery, such as unknown confounders, selection bias, and missing data. Using our simulator, we have evaluated extensively causal discovery algorithms under various settings.

paragraphs: Evaluating causal discovery is difficult because real datasets rarely come with known causal relationships. Without that reference, it is hard to determine whether an algorithm recovered the correct structure. This paper builds a medical simulator intended to provide data whose generating causal relationships are available for evaluation.

The simulator draws on the causal graph of neuropathic pain pathology, a domain with well-studied biological influences. Its generating parameters are estimated from real patient cases. The authors show that simulated data have statistics similar to real-world data, connecting a known generating structure with empirical characteristics of actual observations.

The simulator can generate unlimited samples without compromising real patients' privacy, according to the abstract. It also supports evaluation under practical complications such as unknown confounders, selection bias, and missing data. The authors use it to evaluate causal discovery algorithms extensively across different settings. Its central value is as a controlled testing resource: algorithms can be examined against a known causal structure while facing complications relevant to observational research.
summary.tldr: A neuropathic pain simulator generates realistic synthetic data with known causal structure for evaluating causal discovery under practical complications.

title: Neuropathic Pain Diagnosis Simulator for Causal Discovery Algorithm Evaluation

abstract: The paper introduces a new algorithm for planning in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDP) based on the idea of aggregate simulation. The algorithm uses product distributions to approximate the belief state and shows how to build a representation graph of an approximate action-value function over belief space. The graph captures the result of simulating the model in aggregate under independence assumptions, giving a symbolic representation of the value function. The algorithm supports large observation spaces using sampling networks, a representation of the process of sampling values of observations, which is integrated into the graph representation. Following previous work in MDPs this approach enables action selection in POMDPs through gradient optimization over the graph representation. This approach complements recent algorithms for POMDPs which are based on particle representations of belief states and an explicit search for action selection. Our approach enables scaling to large factored action spaces in addition to large state spaces and observation spaces. An experimental evaluation demonstrates that the algorithm provides excellent performance relative to state of the art in large POMDP problems.

paragraphs: Planning in a partially observable Markov decision process requires decisions based on uncertainty about the current state. This paper proposes an online planning algorithm built around aggregate simulation. It approximates the belief state with product distributions and represents an approximate action-value function as a graph over the space of beliefs.

The graph symbolically captures simulations of the model under independence assumptions. Sampling networks, which represent the process of sampling observations, are integrated into that graph to handle large observation spaces. The resulting representation supports action selection through gradient optimization, connecting the simulation structure directly to the search for a useful action.

The approach complements methods that represent beliefs with particles and select actions through explicit search. It is designed to scale across large state and observation spaces as well as large factored action spaces. Experiments report strong performance relative to state-of-the-art algorithms on large POMDP problems. The product-distribution approximation and independence assumptions are central to how the aggregate representation is constructed.
summary.tldr: Aggregate simulation and sampling networks enable gradient-based POMDP planning with large state, observation, and factored action spaces.

title: Sampling Networks and Aggregate Simulation for Online POMDP Planning

abstract: Nonlinear embedding manifold learning methods provide invaluable visual insights into a structure of high-dimensional data. However, due to a complicated nonconvex objective function, these methods can easily get stuck in local minima and their embedding quality can be poor. We propose a natural extension to several manifold learning methods aimed at identifying pressured points, i.e. points stuck in the poor local minima and have poor embedding quality. We show that the objective function can be decreased by temporarily allowing these points to make use of an extra dimension in the embedding space. Our method is able to improve the objective function value of existing methods even after they get stuck in a poor local minimum.

paragraphs: Nonlinear manifold learning methods place high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space to reveal structure visually. Their objectives are nonconvex, so optimization can settle into a poor local minimum. Once there, ordinary updates may stop improving the arrangement even though the resulting embedding does not represent the data well.

This paper proposes an extension to several such methods that identifies pressured points: points caught in poor local minima with low embedding quality. It temporarily gives those points access to one additional embedding dimension. The extra freedom changes the space in which they can move, allowing the method to improve an arrangement that was stuck in the original space.

The authors show that this temporary dimensional expansion can decrease the objective function, including after an existing method has reached a poor local minimum. The contribution therefore offers a way to continue improving embeddings beyond the stopping point of the original optimization. The stated result is an improvement in objective value, rather than a guarantee that every local minimum is escaped or that a global optimum is found.
summary.tldr: Temporarily giving poorly embedded points an extra dimension can improve manifold-learning objectives after optimization becomes stuck.

title: No Pressure! Addressing the Problem of Local Minima in Manifold Learning Algorithms

abstract: Causal inference in randomized experiments typically assumes that the units of randomization and the units of analysis are one and the same. In some applications, however, these two roles are played by distinct entities linked by a bipartite graph. The key challenge in such bipartite settings is how to avoid interference bias, which would typically arise if we simply randomized the treatment at the level of analysis units. One effective way of minimizing interference bias in standard experiments is through cluster randomization, but this design has not been studied in the bipartite setting where conventional clustering schemes can lead to poorly powered experiments. This paper introduces a novel clustering objective and a corresponding algorithm that partitions a bipartite graph so as to maximize the statistical power of a bipartite experiment on that graph. Whereas previous work relied on balanced partitioning, our formulation suggests the use of a correlation clustering objective. We use a publicly-available graph of Amazon user-item reviews to validate our solution and illustrate how it substantially increases the statistical power in bipartite experiments.

paragraphs: Randomized experiments commonly treat the entities receiving treatment and those being analyzed as the same units. In bipartite experiments, these are different kinds of entities connected by a graph. Randomizing directly at the analysis-unit level can introduce interference bias, so the relationship between the two sides must inform the experimental design.

Cluster randomization helps reduce interference in standard settings, but conventional clustering can leave bipartite experiments with low statistical power. This paper proposes a clustering objective and algorithm specifically for the bipartite structure. The objective is designed to maximize the experiment's power, connecting the partition directly to the statistical goal of the study.

Where previous work used balanced partitions, the new formulation points to correlation clustering. The authors validate their approach using a publicly available graph of Amazon users and item reviews, reporting a substantial increase in statistical power. The contribution is an experiment-specific way to form clusters, recognizing that a partition suitable for ordinary graph balancing may be poorly suited to detecting effects in a bipartite experiment.
summary.tldr: A correlation-clustering objective improves statistical power in experiments whose treatment and analysis units occupy different sides of a bipartite graph.

title: Variance Reduction in Bipartite Experiments through Correlation Clustering

abstract: Graph matching plays a central role in such fields as computer vision, pattern recognition, and bioinformatics. Graph matching problems can be cast as two types of quadratic assignment problems (QAPs): Koopmans-Beckmann's QAP or Lawler's QAP. In our paper, we provide a unifying view for these two problems by introducing new rules for array operations in Hilbert spaces. Consequently, Lawler's QAP can be considered as the Koopmans-Beckmann's alignment between two arrays in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), making it possible to efficiently solve the problem without computing a huge affinity matrix. Furthermore, we develop the entropy-regularized Frank-Wolfe (EnFW) algorithm for optimizing QAPs, which has the same convergence rate as the original FW algorithm while dramatically reducing the computational burden for each outer iteration. We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate our approach, and show that our algorithm significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art in both matching accuracy and scalability.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks correspondences between graphs and is used in fields including computer vision, pattern recognition, and bioinformatics. Two standard mathematical formulations describe it as different quadratic assignment problems. This paper develops a common view of those formulations, creating a route to solving matching problems with less computational overhead.

The authors introduce rules for array operations in Hilbert spaces. Under this formulation, Lawler’s quadratic assignment problem becomes an alignment between two arrays in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, in the style of the Koopmans-Beckmann formulation. The practical benefit is that the method can avoid explicitly computing a huge affinity matrix.

The paper also introduces an entropy-regularized Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm. It preserves the convergence rate of the original Frank-Wolfe method while greatly reducing computation per outer iteration. Extensive experiments show significant improvements over the state of the art in both matching accuracy and scalability. The contribution therefore combines a more economical representation of the matching problem with a less expensive optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: KerGM unifies two graph-matching formulations and uses entropy-regularized optimization to improve reported accuracy and scalability.

title: KerGM: Kernelized Graph Matching

abstract: Continuous-time Bayesian Networks (CTBNs) represent a compact yet powerful framework for understanding multivariate time-series data. Given complete data, parameters and structure can be estimated efficiently in closed-form. However, if data is incomplete, the latent states of the CTBN have to be estimated by laboriously simulating the intractable dynamics of the assumed CTBN. This is a problem, especially for structure learning tasks, where this has to be done for each element of a super-exponentially growing set of possible structures. In order to circumvent this notorious bottleneck, we develop a novel gradient-based approach to structure learning. Instead of sampling and scoring all possible structures individually, we assume the generator of the CTBN to be composed as a mixture of generators stemming from different structures. In this framework, structure learning can be performed via a gradient-based optimization of mixture weights. We combine this approach with a new variational method that allows for a closed-form calculation of this mixture marginal likelihood. We show the scalability of our method by learning structures of previously inaccessible sizes from synthetic and real-world data.

We combine this approach with a new variational method that allows for a closed-form calculation of this mixture marginal likelihood. We show the scalability of our method by learning structures of previously inaccessible sizes from synthetic and real-world data.

It assumes that the network’s generator is a mixture of generators associated with different structures. Structure learning then becomes optimization of the mixture weights. title: Scalable Structure Learning of Continuous-Time Bayesian Networks from Incomplete Data

abstract: Linear systems are the bedrock of virtually all numerical computation. Machine learning poses specific challenges for the solution of such systems due to their scale, characteristic structure, stochasticity and the central role of uncertainty in the field. Unifying earlier work we propose a class of probabilistic linear solvers which jointly infer the matrix, its inverse and the solution from matrix-vector product observations. This class emerges from a fundamental set of desiderata which constrains the space of possible algorithms and recovers the method of conjugate gradients under certain conditions. We demonstrate how to incorporate prior spectral information in order to calibrate uncertainty and experimentally showcase the potential of such solvers for machine learning.

This paper develops probabilistic solvers that treat the computation as an inference problem. The aim includes representing uncertainty about the quantities involved as information is gathered.

The proposed class jointly infers the system matrix, its inverse, and the solution using observations of matrix-vector products. The authors derive the class from a fundamental collection of requirements that restrict which algorithms are possible. Under certain conditions, the resulting framework recovers conjugate gradients, linking the probabilistic approach to an established solver.

The paper also shows how prior spectral information can be incorporated to calibrate uncertainty. This connects knowledge about the matrix to the confidence expressed by the solver. The contribution is a unified framework that combines linear-system computation with uncertainty inference, while retaining a conditional connection to a familiar numerical method.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic linear solvers jointly infer a matrix, its inverse, and its solution while using prior information to calibrate uncertainty.

title: Probabilistic Linear Solvers for Machine Learning

abstract: Novelty detection, i.e., identifying whether a given sample is drawn from outside the training distribution, is essential for reliable machine learning. To this end, there have been many attempts at learning a representation well-suited for novelty detection and designing a score based on such representation. In this paper, we propose a simple, yet effective method named contrasting shifted instances (CSI), inspired by the recent success on contrastive learning of visual representations. Specifically, in addition to contrasting a given sample with other instances as in conventional contrastive learning methods, our training scheme contrasts the sample with distributionally-shifted augmentations of itself. Based on this, we propose a new detection score that is specific to the proposed training scheme. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of our method under various novelty detection scenarios, including unlabeled one-class, unlabeled multi-class and labeled multi-class settings, with various image benchmark datasets. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/alinlab/CSI.

CSI addresses this problem by learning an image representation specifically suited to distinguishing familiar data from unfamiliar data. It combines a modified contrastive training scheme with a detection score designed for that scheme.

Conventional contrastive learning compares a sample with other instances. CSI adds comparisons between the sample and augmented versions of itself that have undergone distributional shifts. This makes the relationship between an original example and its shifted variants part of the training signal. The accompanying detection score uses the representation produced by this particular learning setup.

The authors report superior performance across several image benchmarks and three novelty-detection settings: unlabeled data from one class, unlabeled data from multiple classes, and labeled data from multiple classes. This breadth matters because the available labels and the diversity of familiar examples change the detection problem. The findings support jointly designing representation learning and novelty scoring around distributional shifts.
summary.tldr: CSI improves image novelty detection by contrasting samples with distributionally shifted versions of themselves and using a matching detection score.

title: CSI: Novelty Detection via Contrastive Learning on Distributionally Shifted Instances

abstract: Limitations in acquiring training data restrict potential applications of deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods to the training of real-world robots. Here we train an RL agent to align a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, which is an essential part of many optical experiments, based on images of interference fringes acquired by a monocular camera. The agent is trained in a simulated environment, without any hand-coded features or a priori information about the physics, and subsequently transferred to a physical interferometer. Thanks to a set of domain randomizations simulating uncertainties in physical measurements, the agent successfully aligns this interferometer without any fine-tuning, achieving a performance level of a human expert.

paragraphs: Training reinforcement learning systems directly on physical equipment can be constrained by the difficulty of collecting enough experience. This paper tackles that problem for aligning a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, an optical instrument used in experiments. The agent receives camera images of interference fringes and learns to use that visual information for alignment.

Training takes place in a simulated environment. The agent is not supplied with hand-designed image features or prior information about the underlying physics. To prepare it for physical measurements, the simulation includes domain randomizations that represent measurement uncertainties. These variations expose the learner to differences it may encounter when moving from simulated images to the actual apparatus.

The trained agent is then transferred to a physical interferometer and successfully aligns it without additional fine-tuning. The authors report performance at the level of a human expert. The result demonstrates that, for this alignment task, simulation training with suitable uncertainty variation can produce a usable visual control policy without requiring a further learning stage on the real instrument.
summary.tldr: An agent trained on randomized simulations aligns a physical interferometer from camera images without fine-tuning, reaching reported human-expert performance.

title: Interferobot: aligning an optical interferometer by a reinforcement learning agent

abstract: Recent works (e.g., (Li \& Arora, 2020)) suggest that the use of popular normalization schemes (including Batch Normalization) in today's deep learning can move it far from a traditional optimization viewpoint, e.g., use of exponentially increasing learning rates. The current paper highlights other ways in which behavior of normalized nets departs from traditional viewpoints, and then initiates a formal framework for studying their mathematics via suitable adaptation of the conventional framework namely, modeling SGD-induced training trajectory via a suitable stochastic differential equation (SDE) with a noise term that captures gradient noise. This yields: (a) A new \textquotedblleft intrinsic learning rate\textquotedblright\ parameter that is the product of the normal learning rate $\eta$ and weight decay factor $\lambda$. Analysis of the SDE shows how the effective speed of learning varies and equilibrates over time under the control of intrinsic LR. (b) A challenge---via theory and experiments---to popular belief that good generalization requires large learning rates at the start of training. (c) New experiments, backed by mathematical intuition, suggesting the number of steps to equilibrium (in function space) scales as the inverse of the intrinsic learning rate, as opposed to the exponential time convergence bound implied by SDE analysis. We name it the \emph{Fast Equilibrium Conjecture} and suggest it holds the key to why Batch Normalization is effective.

paragraphs: Normalization changes neural-network training in ways that conventional optimization intuitions may not capture. This paper begins a mathematical framework for studying those differences by modeling stochastic gradient descent trajectories with a stochastic differential equation. The equation includes a noise term representing randomness in the gradients.

The analysis introduces an intrinsic learning rate equal to the ordinary learning rate multiplied by the weight-decay factor. This parameter governs how the effective speed of learning changes and reaches equilibrium in the model. The authors also use theory and experiments to challenge the belief that good generalization requires a large learning rate at the start of training.

This is faster than the exponential-time convergence bound implied by the SDE analysis. The authors call this the Fast Equilibrium Conjecture and suggest it may explain Batch Normalization’s effectiveness. That scaling remains a conjecture, distinct from the formal analysis.
summary.tldr: An SDE framework identifies learning rate times weight decay as an intrinsic training parameter and motivates a conjecture about fast equilibrium in normalized networks.

title: Reconciling Modern Deep Learning with Traditional Optimization Analyses: The Intrinsic Learning Rate

abstract: Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DWI) is the only non-invasive method for quantifying microstructure and reconstructing white-matter pathways in the living human brain. Fluctuations from multiple sources create significant noise in DWI data which must be suppressed before subsequent microstructure analysis. We introduce a self-supervised learning method for denoising DWI data, Patch2Self, which uses the entire volume to learn a full-rank locally linear denoiser for that volume. By taking advantage of the oversampled q-space of DWI data, Patch2Self can separate structure from noise without requiring an explicit model for either. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Patch2Self via quantitative and qualitative improvements in microstructure modeling, tracking (via fiber bundle coherency) and model estimation relative to other unsupervised methods on real and simulated data.

Patch2Self introduces a self-supervised method for suppressing that noise. It learns from the volume being processed, using the entire volume to construct a denoiser tailored to that data.

The method takes advantage of the oversampled measurement space of diffusion MRI, called q-space. This supplies information for separating structure from noise without specifying an explicit model for either one. The learned denoiser is locally linear and full-rank, giving the approach a particular mathematical form while retaining its data-driven training procedure.

The authors evaluate Patch2Self on both real and simulated data, comparing it with other unsupervised methods. They report quantitative and qualitative improvements in microstructure modeling, fiber tracking through bundle coherency, and model estimation. These results connect denoising to the quality of subsequent analysis: the claimed benefit extends beyond cleaner-looking images to improvements in the uses of the diffusion measurements.
summary.tldr: Patch2Self learns a diffusion-MRI denoiser from each volume and improves downstream analysis without explicit signal or noise models.

title: Patch2Self: Denoising Diffusion MRI with Self-Supervised Learning​

abstract: This paper introduces novel results for the score-function gradient estimator of the importance-weighted variational bound (IWAE). We prove that in the limit of large $K$ (number of importance samples) one can choose the control variate such that the Signal-to-Noise ratio (SNR) of the estimator grows as $\sqrt{K}$. This is in contrast to the standard pathwise gradient estimator where the SNR decreases as $1/\sqrt{K}$. Based on our theoretical findings we develop a novel control variate that extends on VIMCO. Empirically, for the training of both continuous and discrete generative models, the proposed method yields superior variance reduction, resulting in an SNR for IWAE that increases with $K$ without relying on the reparameterization trick. The novel estimator is competitive with state-of-the-art reparameterization-free gradient estimators such as Reweighted Wake-Sleep (RWS) and the thermodynamic variational objective (TVO) when training generative models.

paragraphs: Training with an importance-weighted variational bound requires estimating gradients from samples. Increasing the number of samples can change how much useful signal those estimates contain relative to noise. This paper studies that relationship for score-function estimators and develops a way to reduce their variance.

The authors prove that, as the number of importance samples K becomes large, a suitable control variate can make the signal-to-noise ratio grow as the square root of K. For the standard pathwise gradient estimator, the corresponding ratio instead decreases as the inverse square root of K. The favorable result depends on choosing the control variate appropriately and is an asymptotic statement.

Guided by the theory, the paper develops a control variate extending VIMCO. In experiments with continuous and discrete generative models, it provides superior variance reduction and a signal-to-noise ratio that increases with K without reparameterization. The estimator is also competitive with Reweighted Wake-Sleep and the thermodynamic variational objective. The findings show how variance control can make additional importance samples useful for reparameterization-free gradient estimation.
summary.tldr: An appropriately chosen control variate can make score-function gradient signal-to-noise improve with more importance samples.

title: Optimal Variance Control of the Score-Function Gradient Estimator for Importance-Weighted Bounds

abstract: Checklists are simple decision aids that are often used to promote safety and reliability in clinical applications. In this paper, we present a method to learn checklists for clinical decision support. We represent predictive checklists as discrete linear classifiers with binary features and unit weights. We then learn globally optimal predictive checklists from data by solving an integer programming problem. Our method allows users to customize checklists to obey complex constraints, including constraints to enforce group fairness and to binarize real-valued features at training time. In addition, it pairs models with an optimality gap that can inform model development and determine the feasibility of learning sufficiently accurate checklists on a given dataset. We pair our method with specialized techniques that speed up its ability to train a predictive checklist that performs well and has a small optimality gap. We benchmark the performance of our method on seven clinical classification problems, and demonstrate its practical benefits by training a short-form checklist for PTSD screening. Our results show that our method can fit simple predictive checklists that perform well and that can easily be customized to obey a rich class of custom constraints.

This paper represents such checklists as discrete linear classifiers and learns them from data through integer programming. The formulation supports a search for globally optimal checklists within the chosen objective and constraints.

Users can impose complex requirements, including group-fairness constraints, and the method can turn real-valued measurements into binary features during training. It also associates learned models with an optimality gap. That gap indicates how much room for improvement remains relative to the optimization bound, helping guide model development and assess whether sufficiently accurate checklists are feasible.

Specialized techniques accelerate the search for checklists that perform well and have small optimality gaps. The authors evaluate the method on seven clinical classification problems and demonstrate a short checklist for PTSD screening. Their findings support the possibility of learning useful, simple decision aids while enforcing a rich set of application-specific requirements directly during training.
summary.tldr: Integer programming learns simple predictive checklists with customizable constraints and optimality gaps that quantify remaining optimization uncertainty.

title: Learning Optimal Predictive Checklists

abstract: We introduce a new general identifiable framework for principled disentanglement referred to as Structured Nonlinear Independent Component Analysis (SNICA). Our contribution is to extend the identifiability theory of deep generative models for a very broad class of structured models. While previous works have shown identifiability for specific classes of time-series models, our theorems extend this to more general temporal structures as well as to models with more complex structures such as spatial dependencies. In particular, we establish the major result that identifiability for this framework holds even in the presence of noise of unknown distribution. Finally, as an example of our framework's flexibility, we introduce the first nonlinear ICA model for time-series that combines the following very useful properties: it accounts for both nonstationarity and autocorrelation in a fully unsupervised setting; performs dimensionality reduction; models hidden states; and enables principled estimation and inference by variational maximum-likelihood.

paragraphs: Learning hidden factors from observations is more useful when the model can identify those factors in a principled way. This paper introduces Structured Nonlinear Independent Component Analysis, or SNICA, as a framework for such disentanglement. Its contribution centers on extending identifiability theory for deep generative models to a broad class of structured data models.

Earlier results covered particular kinds of time-series models. SNICA's theorems extend the treatment to more general temporal structure and to richer dependencies, including spatial ones. A central result establishes identifiability within the framework even when observations contain noise whose distribution is unknown. This expands the theoretical setting in which hidden structure can be recovered without specifying the noise distribution beforehand.

To illustrate the framework, the authors introduce a nonlinear ICA time-series model that combines several capabilities. It handles both changing statistical behavior over time and temporal correlation in a fully unsupervised setting, reduces dimensionality, and models hidden states. Variational maximum-likelihood methods provide estimation and inference. This example shows how the broader identifiability framework can support multiple modeling requirements within one construction.
summary.tldr: SNICA extends identifiable nonlinear latent-variable modeling to richer temporal and spatial structures, including noise with an unknown distribution.

title: Disentangling Identifiable Features from Noisy Data with Structured Nonlinear ICA

abstract: Graph neural networks, a popular class of models effective in a wide range of graph-based learning tasks, have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. While the majority of the literature focuses on such vulnerability in node-level classification tasks, little effort has been dedicated to analysing adversarial attacks on graph-level classification, an important problem with numerous real-life applications such as biochemistry and social network analysis. The few existing methods often require unrealistic setups, such as access to internal information of the victim models, or an impractically-large number of queries. We present a novel Bayesian optimisation-based attack method for graph classification models. Our method is black-box, query-efficient and parsimonious with respect to the perturbation applied. We empirically validate the effectiveness and flexibility of the proposed method on a wide range of graph classification tasks involving varying graph properties, constraints and modes of attack. Finally, we analyse common interpretable patterns behind the adversarial samples produced, which may shed further light on the adversarial robustness of graph classification models.

paragraphs: This paper studies attacks on models that assign a label to an entire graph. That differs from attacking the classification of individual nodes, which has received more attention. Whole-graph classification matters in applications such as biochemistry and social network analysis, so understanding its vulnerabilities is a distinct problem with practical relevance.

The authors propose an attack based on Bayesian optimization. It works through black-box access, without requiring the internal model information assumed by some earlier methods. The method is designed to use relatively few queries and restrained graph perturbations. These properties address two practical obstacles to evaluating attacks: expensive repeated model access and the need to keep modifications limited.

Experiments examine graph classification tasks with different graph properties, constraints, and attack modes. The reported results support the method's effectiveness and flexibility across those evaluated settings. The authors also analyze recurring, interpretable patterns in the adversarial graphs they produce. Those patterns may help explain vulnerabilities in graph classifiers, although the abstract presents that explanatory role as a possibility rather than a complete account of robustness.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian optimization attack exposes graph-classifier vulnerabilities using black-box access, relatively few queries, and limited graph changes.

title: Adversarial Attacks on Graph Classifiers via Bayesian Optimisation

abstract: The advancement of deep neural networks over the last decade has enabled progress in scientific knowledge discovery in the form of learning Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) directly from experiment data. Nevertheless, forward simulation and backward learning of large-scale dynamic systems require handling billions of mutually interacting elements, the scale of which overwhelms current computing architectures. We propose Locality Sensitive Hashing Accelerated Simulation and Learning (LSH-SMILE), a unified framework to scale up both forward simulation and backward learning of physics systems. LSH-SMILE takes advantage of (i) the locality of PDE updates, (ii) similar temporal dynamics shared by multiple elements. LSH-SMILE hashes elements with similar dynamics into a single hash bucket and handles their updates at once. This allows LSH-SMILE to scale with respect to the number of non-empty hash buckets, a drastic improvement over conventional approaches. Theoretically, we prove a novel bound on the errors introduced by LSH-SMILE. Experimentally, we demonstrate that LSH-SMILE simulates physics systems at comparable quality with exact approaches, but with way less time and space complexity. Such savings also translate to better learning performance due to LSH-SMILE's ability to propagate gradients over a long duration.

LSH-SMILE provides a shared framework for accelerating these two operations. It exploits the locality of partial differential equation updates and the fact that multiple elements can exhibit similar behavior over time.

The method uses locality-sensitive hashing to group elements with similar dynamics into buckets and process their updates together. Its computation scales with the number of occupied buckets rather than treating every element's update separately. The potential saving comes from repeated dynamics: elements that behave similarly can share update work within the framework.

The authors prove a bound on the approximation errors introduced by this grouping. In experiments, simulations achieve quality comparable to exact approaches while requiring substantially less time and space. Those savings also improve learning performance by allowing gradients to propagate over longer durations. The contribution therefore links efficient simulation to better learning of dynamics, with both a theoretical error analysis and empirical evidence for the benefits of grouped computation.
summary.tldr: LSH-SMILE groups elements with similar dynamics to accelerate physical simulation and learning, with an error bound and comparable simulation quality in experiments.

title: LSH-SMILE: Locality Sensitive Hashing Accelerated Simulation and Learning

abstract: Various approaches have been developed to upper bound the generalization error of a supervised learning algorithm. However, existing bounds are often loose and lack of guarantees. As a result, they may fail to characterize the exact generalization ability of a learning algorithm.Our main contribution is an exact characterization of the expected generalization error of the well-known Gibbs algorithm (a.k.a. Gibbs posterior) using symmetrized KL information between the input training samples and the output hypothesis. Our result can be applied to tighten existing expected generalization error and PAC-Bayesian bounds. Our approach is versatile, as it also characterizes the generalization error of the Gibbs algorithm with data-dependent regularizer and that of the Gibbs algorithm in the asymptotic regime, where it converges to the empirical risk minimization algorithm. Of particular relevance, our results highlight the role the symmetrized KL information plays in controlling the generalization error of the Gibbs algorithm.

Our approach is versatile, as it also characterizes the generalization error of the Gibbs algorithm with data-dependent regularizer and that of the Gibbs algorithm in the asymptotic regime, where it converges to the empirical risk minimization algorithm. Of particular relevance, our results highlight the role the symmetrized KL information plays in controlling the generalization error of the Gibbs algorithm.

paragraphs: Generalization analysis asks how a learning algorithm’s performance on its training data relates to its performance beyond those data. Many analyses provide upper bounds, which can leave substantial uncertainty about the actual gap. This paper obtains an exact characterization of the expected generalization error for the Gibbs learning algorithm, also known as the Gibbs posterior.

The characterization uses symmetrized KL information between the training samples and the hypothesis produced by the algorithm. This quantity describes their statistical dependence through a symmetric combination of KL information. The result identifies that dependence as an exact ingredient in expected generalization error for this algorithm, giving it a stronger role than merely appearing in a potentially loose bound.

The authors show that their result can tighten existing expected-error and PAC-Bayesian bounds. They also extend the analysis to Gibbs learning with a data-dependent regularizer and to an asymptotic regime in which the algorithm approaches empirical risk minimization. These extensions make the characterization useful across several versions of Gibbs learning while retaining its focus on expected generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper exactly characterizes the Gibbs algorithm’s expected generalization error using symmetrized KL information.

title: An Exact Characterization of the Generalization Error for the Gibbs Algorithm

abstract: Noisy labels are inevitable in large real-world datasets. In this work, we explore an area understudied by previous works --- how the network's architecture impacts its robustness to noisy labels. We provide a formal framework connecting the robustness of a network to the alignments between its architecture and target/noise functions. Our framework measures a network's robustness via the predictive power in its representations --- the test performance of a linear model trained on the learned representations using a small set of clean labels. We hypothesize that a network is more robust to noisy labels if its architecture is more aligned with the target function than the noise. To support our hypothesis, we provide both theoretical and empirical evidence across various neural network architectures and different domains. We also find that when the network is well-aligned with the target function, its predictive power in representations could improve upon state-of-the-art (SOTA) noisy-label-training methods in terms of test accuracy and even outperform sophisticated methods that use clean labels.

This paper investigates that relationship through a formal framework connecting architecture to both the intended target function and the function describing label noise.

Specifically, it measures the test performance of a linear model trained on those representations using a small set of clean labels. The authors hypothesize that robustness improves when the architecture is better aligned with the target function than with the noise, and provide theoretical and empirical evidence across architectures and domains.

These are qualified findings tied to alignment, making architecture an important part of understanding noisy-label learning alongside the training method and the availability of reliable labels.
summary.tldr: The paper links noisy-label robustness to how well an architecture aligns with the target function relative to label noise.

title: How does a Neural Network's Architecture Impact its Robustness to Noisy Labels?

abstract: In this manuscript we consider Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) under the Gaussian design. Exponents for the decay of the excess generalization error of KRR have been reported in various works under the assumption of power-law decay of eigenvalues of the features co-variance. These decays were, however, provided for sizeably different setups, namely in the noiseless case with constant regularization and in the noisy optimally regularized case. Intermediary settings have been left substantially uncharted. In this work, we unify and extend this line of work, providing characterization of all regimes and excess error decay rates that can be observed in terms of the interplay of noise and regularization. In particular, we show the existence of a transition in the noisy setting between the noiseless exponents to its noisy values as the sample complexity is increased. Finally, we illustrate how this crossover can also be observed on real data sets.

paragraphs: This paper asks how quickly kernel ridge regression's excess prediction error decreases as more samples become available. Earlier results gave different decay exponents for substantially different conditions, including noiseless learning with constant regularization and noisy learning with optimally chosen regularization. Those results left much of the territory between these settings unexplained.

The authors analyze kernel ridge regression under Gaussian design, in the line of work assuming power-law decay of feature covariance eigenvalues. They characterize the regimes and error decay rates arising from the interaction between noise and regularization. This creates a common account of behaviors that had previously been studied under separate choices of conditions.

A central finding is that even noisy data can exhibit a crossover: as the sample count grows, the error decay changes from noiseless-style exponents to noisy ones. The authors also illustrate this behavior on real datasets. The result explains why the apparent learning rate can depend on how much data is available, as well as on noise and regularization.
summary.tldr: The analysis unifies kernel regression error rates and shows how noisy learning can cross from noiseless-style to noisy decay as sample size grows.

title: Generalization Error Rates in Kernel Regression: The Crossover from the Noiseless to Noisy Regime

abstract: Augmenting pre-trained language models with knowledge graphs (KGs) has achieved success on various commonsense reasoning tasks. However, for a given task instance, the KG, or certain parts of the KG, may not be useful. Although KG-augmented models often use attention to focus on specific KG components, the KG is still always used, and the attention mechanism is never explicitly taught which KG components should be used. Meanwhile, saliency methods can measure how much a KG feature (e.g., graph, node, path) influences the model to make the correct prediction, thus explaining which KG features are useful. This paper explores how saliency explanations can be used to improve KG-augmented models' performance. First, we propose to create coarse (Is the KG useful?) and fine (Which nodes/paths in the KG are useful?) saliency explanations. Second, to motivate saliency-based supervision, we analyze oracle KG-augmented models which directly use saliency explanations as extra inputs for guiding their attention. Third, we propose SalKG, a framework for KG-augmented models to learn from coarse and/or fine saliency explanations. Given saliency explanations created from a task's training set, SalKG jointly trains the model to predict the explanations, then solve the task by attending to KG features highlighted by the predicted explanations. On three popular commonsense QA benchmarks (CSQA, OBQA, CODAH) and a range of KG-augmented models, we show that SalKG can yield considerable performance gains --- up to 2.76% absolute improvement on CSQA.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs can help language models answer commonsense questions, but their usefulness varies from question to question. A graph may add little, or only some of its nodes and paths may help. Ordinary attention mechanisms select graph components without explicit instruction about which components actually support a correct prediction.

SalKG uses saliency explanations to provide that instruction. Coarse explanations indicate whether the graph is useful at all, while fine explanations identify useful nodes or paths. The authors first examine oracle models given these explanations directly. They then train models jointly to predict explanations from training-set supervision and solve the task by attending to the graph features highlighted by those predictions.

This makes explanations part of the learning process, providing a target for how the model should use external knowledge. Evaluations cover CSQA, OBQA, and CODAH, along with several graph-augmented model designs. SalKG yields considerable gains in these experiments, including up to 2.76 percentage points of absolute improvement on CSQA. The findings support supervising both whether knowledge is needed and which parts deserve attention.
summary.tldr: SalKG improves commonsense question answering by teaching models to predict explanations of whether and which knowledge-graph information is useful.

title: SalKG: Learning From Knowledge Graph Explanations for Commonsense Reasoning

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are ubiquitous in computer vision, with a myriad of effective and efficient variations. Recently, Transformers -- originally introduced in natural language processing -- have been increasingly adopted in computer vision. While early adopters continued to employ CNN backbones, the latest networks are end-to-end CNN-free Transformer solutions. A recent surprising finding now shows that a simple MLP based solution without any traditional convolutional or Transformer components can produce effective visual representations. While CNNs, Transformers and MLP-Mixers may be considered as completely disparate architectures, we provide a unified view showing that they are in fact special cases of a more general method to aggregate spatial context in a neural network stack. We present the \model (CONText AggregatIon NEtwoRk), a general-purpose building block for multi-head context aggregation that can exploit long-range interactions \emph{a la} Transformers while still exploiting the inductive bias of the local convolution operation leading to faster convergence speeds, often seen in CNNs. Our \model architecture achieves 82.7 \% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet using 22M parameters, +2.8 improvement compared with DeiT-Small, and can converge to 79.9 \% Top-1 accuracy in just 200 epochs. In contrast to Transformer-based methods that do not scale well to downstream tasks that rely on larger input image resolutions, our efficient network, named \modellight, can be employed in object detection and instance segmentation networks such as DETR, RetinaNet and Mask-RCNN to obtain an impressive detection mAP of 38.9, 43.8, 45.1 and mask mAP of 41.3, providing large improvements of 6.6, 7.3, 6.9 and 6.6 pts respectively, compared to a ResNet-50 backbone with a comparable compute and parameter size. Our method also achieves promising results on self-supervised learning compared to DeiT on the DINO framework. Code is released at https://github.com/allenai/container.

This paper gives them a shared interpretation as methods for aggregating spatial context. That perspective provides a common framework for understanding how a network combines information from different image locations and motivates a more general building block.

The aim is to retain broad spatial communication while benefiting from the faster convergence often associated with convolutional networks. These findings connect the unifying architectural view to practical gains across several visual learning tasks.
summary.tldr: Container unifies spatial context aggregation and combines local convolutional structure with long-range interactions to improve visual learning performance.

title: Container: Context Aggregation Networks

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a challenging setting for optimization due to the heterogeneity of the data across different clients which gives rise to the client drift phenomenon. In fact, obtaining an algorithm for FL which is uniformly better than simple centralized training has been a major open problem thus far. In this work, we propose a general algorithmic framework, Mime, which i) mitigates client drift and ii) adapts arbitrary centralized optimization algorithms such as momentum and Adam to the cross-device federated learning setting. Mime uses a combination of control-variates and server-level statistics (e.g. momentum) at every client-update step to ensure that each local update mimics that of the centralized method run on iid data. We prove a reduction result showing that Mime can translate the convergence of a generic algorithm in the centralized setting into convergence in the federated setting. Further, we show that when combined with momentum based variance reduction, Mime is provably faster than any centralized method--the first such result. We also perform a thorough experimental exploration of Mime's performance on real world datasets.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across clients whose data can differ substantially. Those differences cause client drift: local optimization steps can pull training in inconsistent directions. This paper introduces Mime, a framework designed to reduce that drift while adapting centralized optimizers, including momentum and Adam, to learning across devices.

Mime combines control variates with statistics maintained at the server, such as momentum, at every local update. These corrections make client updates mimic those of the corresponding centralized method operating on independent, identically distributed data. The important design choice is to bring shared optimization information into individual client steps, rather than relying only on local data.

The authors prove a reduction that carries convergence results for a generic centralized algorithm into the federated setting. When Mime is combined with momentum-based variance reduction, they further prove faster convergence than any centralized method in the analyzed setting, describing this as the first such result. They also investigate performance experimentally on real-world datasets. The framework links familiar optimizer behavior to federated training through both an algorithmic construction and a convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: Mime adapts centralized optimizers to federated learning and, with momentum-based variance reduction, establishes a provable convergence advantage over centralized methods.

title: Breaking the centralized barrier for cross-device federated learning

abstract: While programming is one of the most broadly applicable skills in modern society, it is unclear how well state-of-the-art machine learning models can write code. Despite its importance, there has been surprisingly little work on evaluating code generation, and it can be difficult to assess code generation performance in an accurate and rigorous manner. To meet this challenge, we introduce APPS, a benchmark for code generation. Unlike prior work in more restricted settings, our benchmark measures the ability of models to take an arbitrary natural language specification and generate satisfactory Python code. Similar to how companies assess candidate software developers, we evaluate models by checking their generated code on test cases. Our benchmark includes 10,000 problems, which range from having simple one-line solutions to being substantial algorithmic challenges. We fine-tune large language models on both GitHub and our training set, and we find that the prevalence of syntax errors is decreasing exponentially as models improve. Recent models such as GPT-Neo can pass approximately 20% of the test cases of introductory problems, so we find that machine learning models are now beginning to learn how to code. As the social significance of automatic code generation increases over the coming years, our benchmark can provide an objective measure for tracking advancements.

paragraphs: APPS evaluates whether a model can turn a natural-language programming specification into satisfactory Python code. The benchmark contains 10,000 problems, ranging from exercises with one-line solutions to substantial algorithmic challenges. This variety is intended to assess coding ability across a broader range of difficulty than more restricted code-generation settings.

Generated programs are evaluated using test cases, connecting the assessment to what the code actually does. The authors fine-tune large language models using GitHub data and the benchmark's training set. They report that syntax errors become exponentially less prevalent as models improve, suggesting progress in producing code that follows the language's formal rules.

Functional success remains more limited in the reported experiments: models such as GPT-Neo pass approximately 20% of test cases on introductory problems. This is a test-case result, rather than a claim that 20% of complete problems are solved. The findings indicate emerging coding ability while leaving substantial scope for improvement. APPS provides a common behavioral measure for tracking such progress across programming challenges.
summary.tldr: APPS tests generated Python programs on 10,000 coding problems, finding emerging functional ability alongside substantial remaining difficulty.

title: Measuring Coding Challenge Competence With APPS

abstract: Meta-learning provides a popular and effective family of methods for data-efficient learning of new tasks. However, several important issues in meta-learning have proven hard to study thus far. For example, performance degrades in real-world settings where meta-learners must learn from a wide and potentially multi-modal distribution of training tasks; and when distribution shift exists between meta-train and meta-test task distributions. These issues are typically hard to study since the shape of task distributions, and shift between them are not straightforward to measure or control in standard benchmarks. We propose the channel coding problem as a benchmark for meta-learning. Channel coding is an important practical application where task distributions naturally arise, and fast adaptation to new tasks is practically valuable. We use this benchmark to study several aspects of meta-learning, including the impact of task distribution breadth and shift on meta-learner performance, which can be controlled in the coding problem. Going forward, this benchmark provides a tool for the community to study the capabilities and limitations of meta-learning, and to drive research on practically robust and effective meta-learners.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to make learning a new task possible with little task-specific data. Evaluating that ability becomes harder when training tasks are very diverse or when new tasks differ from those encountered during training. Standard benchmarks often make these conditions difficult to isolate because researchers cannot easily measure or adjust the distributions from which tasks come.

This paper proposes channel coding as a setting where those distributions can be controlled. It is also a practical application in which quickly adapting to new tasks is valuable. The benchmark lets researchers vary both how broadly training tasks differ and how much the test tasks depart from the training distribution, making these factors explicit parts of evaluation.

The authors use the benchmark to study how task diversity and distribution shift affect meta-learning performance. Its contribution is a way to investigate these challenges systematically within an application that motivates adaptation. This creates a basis for assessing where meta-learning works reliably and for developing methods that remain effective under broader or changing task conditions.
summary.tldr: A channel coding benchmark makes task diversity and distribution shift controllable for studying meta-learning.

title: A Channel Coding Benchmark for Meta-Learning

abstract: We present Theseus, an efficient application-agnostic open source library for differentiable nonlinear least squares (DNLS) optimization built on PyTorch, providing a common framework for end-to-end structured learning in robotics and vision. Existing DNLS implementations are application specific and do not always incorporate many ingredients important for efficiency. Theseus is application-agnostic, as we illustrate with several example applications that are built using the same underlying differentiable components, such as second-order optimizers, standard costs functions, and Lie groups. For efficiency, Theseus incorporates support for sparse solvers, automatic vectorization, batching, GPU acceleration, and gradient computation with implicit differentiation and direct loss minimization. We do extensive performance evaluation in a set of applications, demonstrating significant efficiency gains and better scalability when these features are incorporated. Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/theseus-ai/

paragraphs: Theseus is an open-source PyTorch library for differentiable nonlinear least-squares optimization. It provides reusable optimization components for end-to-end structured learning in robotics and vision. The paper addresses a practical problem: existing implementations are often tied to particular applications and do not consistently include features needed for efficient computation.

Several example applications use the same underlying components, including second-order optimizers, standard cost functions, and Lie groups. This shared foundation illustrates the library's application-independent design. Differentiability makes the optimization procedure part of the learning system, and Theseus supports gradient computation through implicit differentiation and direct loss minimization.

For computational efficiency, the library includes sparse solvers, automatic vectorization, batching, and GPU acceleration. Extensive evaluations across a set of applications demonstrate significant efficiency gains and improved scalability when these features are incorporated. The contribution is therefore both a common implementation framework and evidence that integrating these computational capabilities helps structured learning applications run more efficiently.
summary.tldr: Theseus provides reusable differentiable nonlinear optimization in PyTorch, with efficiency features that improve performance and scalability in evaluated applications.

title: Theseus: A Library for Differentiable Nonlinear Optimization

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) improves model generalization by leveraging massive unlabeled data to augment limited labeled samples. However, currently, popular SSL evaluation protocols are often constrained to computer vision (CV) tasks. In addition, previous work typically trains deep neural networks from scratch, which is time-consuming and environmentally unfriendly. To address the above issues, we construct a Unified SSL Benchmark (USB) for classification by selecting 15 diverse, challenging, and comprehensive tasks from CV, natural language processing (NLP), and audio processing (Audio), on which we systematically evaluate the dominant SSL methods, and also open-source a modular and extensible codebase for fair evaluation of these SSL methods. We further provide the pre-trained versions of the state-of-the-art neural models for CV tasks to make the cost affordable for further tuning. USB enables the evaluation of a single SSL algorithm on more tasks from multiple domains but with less cost. Specifically, on a single NVIDIA V100, only 39 GPU days are required to evaluate FixMatch on 15 tasks in USB while 335 GPU days (279 GPU days on 4 CV datasets except for ImageNet) are needed on 5 CV tasks with TorchSSL.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled data alongside a limited labeled set to improve generalization. Its common evaluation protocols have concentrated on computer vision and often trained networks from scratch. USB addresses both the narrow task coverage and the computational expense by providing a unified classification benchmark spanning several kinds of data.

The benchmark includes 15 tasks from computer vision, natural-language processing, and audio. The authors systematically evaluate leading semi-supervised methods and release a modular, extensible codebase for fair comparisons. They also provide pretrained versions of state-of-the-art vision models, making further tuning more affordable and reducing reliance on expensive training from scratch.

The reported FixMatch evaluation takes 39 GPU days across USB's 15 tasks on a single NVIDIA V100. The comparison with TorchSSL requires 335 GPU days across five vision tasks, including 279 days for the four datasets other than ImageNet. This illustrates broader evaluation coverage at lower reported cost, making cross-domain assessment of a single algorithm more practical.
summary.tldr: USB evaluates semi-supervised classification across vision, language, and audio while reducing the reported computational cost of broad benchmarking.

title: USB: A Unified Semi-supervised Learning Benchmark for Classification

abstract: The phenomenon that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) favors flat minima has played a critical role in understanding the implicit regularization of SGD. In this paper, we provide an explanation of this striking phenomenon by relating the particular noise structure of SGD to its \emph{linear stability} (Wu et al., 2018). Specifically, we consider training over-parameterized models with square loss. We prove that if a global minimum $\theta^*$ is linearly stable for SGD, then it must satisfy $\|H(\theta^*)\|_F\leq O(\sqrt{B}/\eta)$, where $\|H(\theta^*)\|_F, B,\eta$ denote the Frobenius norm of Hessian at $\theta^*$, batch size, and learning rate, respectively. Otherwise, SGD will escape from that minimum \emph{exponentially} fast. Hence, for minima accessible to SGD, the sharpness---as measured by the Frobenius norm of the Hessian---is bounded \emph{independently} of the model size and sample size. The key to obtaining these results is exploiting the particular structure of SGD noise: The noise concentrates in sharp directions of local landscape and the magnitude is proportional to loss value. This alignment property of SGD noise provably holds for linear networks and random feature models (RFMs), and is empirically verified for nonlinear networks. Moreover, the validity and practical relevance of our theoretical findings are also justified by extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 dataset.

We prove that if a global minimum $\theta^*$ is linearly stable for SGD, then it must satisfy $\|H(\theta^*)\|_F\leq O(\sqrt{B}/\eta)$, where $\|H(\theta^*)\|_F, B,\eta$ denote the Frobenius norm of Hessian at $\theta^*$, batch size, and learning rate, respectively. Hence, for minima accessible to SGD, the sharpness---as measured by the Frobenius norm of the Hessian---is bounded \emph{independently} of the model size and sample size. The key to obtaining these results is exploiting the particular structure of SGD noise: The noise concentrates in sharp directions of local landscape and the magnitude is proportional to loss value. This alignment property of SGD noise provably holds for linear networks and random feature models (RFMs), and is empirically verified for nonlinear networks. Moreover, the validity and practical relevance of our theoretical findings are also justified by extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 dataset.

paragraphs: The paper explains a preference of stochastic gradient descent for flat minima through linear stability. It studies overparameterized models trained with square loss and measures sharpness using the Frobenius norm of the Hessian. This asks whether the local behavior of the optimization process permits it to remain near a particular global minimum.

The authors prove that a linearly stable global minimum must have sharpness bounded on the order of the square root of batch size divided by learning rate. Otherwise, SGD escapes exponentially fast. The bound does not depend on model size or sample size. It supplies a necessary condition for linear stability in the analyzed setting.

The explanation relies on SGD noise concentrating in sharp directions, with magnitude proportional to the loss. The authors prove this alignment property for linear networks and random feature models and verify it empirically for nonlinear networks. CIFAR-10 experiments further support the theory's practical relevance. The distinction between these theoretical and empirical findings matters: the paper provides a specific noise-based mechanism connecting stability with the selection of flatter minima.
summary.tldr: A stability analysis links SGD's preference for flat minima to noise aligned with sharp directions and derives a sharpness bound for stable global minima.

title: The alignment property of SGD noise and how it helps select flat minima: A stability analysis

abstract: The adaptation of a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) aims to transfer a pre-trained GAN to a target domain with limited training data. In this paper, we focus on the one-shot case, which is more challenging and rarely explored in previous works. We consider that the adaptation from a source domain to a target domain can be decoupled into two parts: the transfer of global style like texture and color, and the emergence of new entities that do not belong to the source domain. While previous works mainly focus on style transfer, we propose a novel and concise framework to address the \textit{generalized one-shot adaptation} task for both style and entity transfer, in which a reference image and its binary entity mask are provided. Our core idea is to constrain the gap between the internal distributions of the reference and syntheses by sliced Wasserstein distance. To better achieve it, style fixation is used at first to roughly obtain the exemplary style, and an auxiliary network is introduced to the generator to disentangle entity and style transfer. Besides, to realize cross-domain correspondence, we propose the variational Laplacian regularization to constrain the smoothness of the adapted generator. Both quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in various scenarios. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhangzc21/Generalized-One-shot-GAN-adaptation}.

A reference can introduce both textures or colors and entities absent from the source domain. This paper addresses both kinds of change using a reference image and a binary mask identifying its entity.

The method constrains differences between internal distributions of the reference image and generated images using sliced Wasserstein distance. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate effectiveness in several scenarios. Its one-shot setting still includes the supplied entity mask, which is part of the information used to guide the transfer.
summary.tldr: The method adapts a GAN's style and entities from one reference image and its binary entity mask.

title: Generalized One-shot Domain Adaptation of Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: This paper presents a systematic study on gap-dependent sample complexity in offline reinforcement learning. Prior works showed when the density ratio between an optimal policy and the behavior policy is upper bounded (single policy coverage), then the agent can achieve an $O\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2}\right)$ rate, which is also minimax optimal. We show under the same single policy coverage assumption, the rate can be improved to $O\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$ when there is a gap in the optimal $Q$-function. Furthermore, we show under a stronger uniform single policy coverage assumption, the sample complexity can be further improved to $O(1)$. Lastly, we also present nearly-matching lower bounds to complement our gap-dependent upper bounds.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from data collected by a behavior policy. This paper studies how much data are needed to reach a target accuracy, epsilon, when the available data sufficiently cover an optimal policy. The coverage assumption is expressed through an upper bound on the density ratio between the optimal and behavior policies.

Previous results give a sample-complexity rate proportional to 1/epsilon squared under this single-policy coverage assumption, with matching worst-case optimality. The authors show that an additional gap in the optimal Q-function allows a faster 1/epsilon rate under the same coverage assumption. The gap supplies extra problem structure beyond what the general worst-case analysis assumes.

With a stronger uniform single-policy coverage assumption, the paper further improves the dependence on epsilon to a constant. This is a statement about accuracy dependence under the stated assumptions, not a claim that data are unnecessary. Nearly matching lower bounds accompany the upper bounds. Together, the results show how value gaps and the strength of coverage can substantially change the statistical difficulty of offline learning.
summary.tldr: A gap in the optimal Q-function improves offline reinforcement-learning sample-complexity rates under coverage assumptions, with stronger coverage enabling constant dependence on target accuracy.

title: On Gap-dependent Bounds for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the problem of online learning in competitive settings in the context of two-sided matching markets. In particular, one side of the market, the agents, must learn about their preferences over the other side, the firms, through repeated interaction while competing with other agents for successful matches. We propose a class of decentralized, communication- and coordination-free algorithms that agents can use to reach to their stable match in structured matching markets. In contrast to prior works, the proposed algorithms make decisions based solely on an agent's own history of play and requires no foreknowledge of the firms' preferences. Our algorithms are constructed by splitting up the statistical problem of learning one's preferences, from noisy observations, from the problem of competing for firms. We show that under realistic structural assumptions on the underlying preferences of the agents and firms, the proposed algorithms incur a regret which grows at most logarithmically in the time horizon. However, we note that in the worst case, it may grow exponentially in the size of the market.
