paragraphs: In a two-sided matching market, agents must discover which firms they prefer while competing with other agents for matches. Feedback is noisy, and an agent's ability to interact with a firm depends on that competition. The paper develops decentralized algorithms for reaching stable matches in markets with structured preferences.

Each agent makes decisions using only its own history of play. The algorithms require neither communication and coordination among agents nor advance knowledge of firms' preferences. Their design separates two difficulties: statistically learning preferences from noisy observations and managing competition for firms. This separation allows learning to proceed using locally available information.

Under structural assumptions on agent and firm preferences, the authors prove that regret grows at most logarithmically with the time horizon. This establishes favorable long-run learning behavior for the markets covered by those assumptions. However, the same regret can grow exponentially with market size in the worst case. The result therefore distinguishes efficiency over time from scalability across increasingly large markets, rather than treating them as interchangeable guarantees.
summary.tldr: Agents can learn stable matches from their own histories with logarithmic time-dependent regret under structural assumptions, although worst-case market-size dependence can be exponential.

title: Decentralized, Communication- and Coordination-free Learning in Structured Matching Markets

abstract: We prove identifiability of a broad class of deep latent variable models that (a) have universal approximation capabilities and (b) are the decoders of variational autoencoders that are commonly used in practice. Unlike existing work, our analysis does not require weak supervision, auxiliary information, or conditioning in the latent space. Specifically, we show that for a broad class of generative (i.e. unsupervised) models with universal approximation capabilities, the side information $u$ is not necessary: We prove identifiability of the entire generative model where we do not observe $u$ and only observe the data $x$. The models we consider match autoencoder architectures used in practice that leverage mixture priors in the latent space and ReLU/leaky-ReLU activations in the encoder, such as VaDE and MFC-VAE. Our main result is an identifiability hierarchy that significantly generalizes previous work and exposes how different assumptions lead to different ``strengths'' of identifiability, and includes certain ``vanilla'' VAEs with isotropic Gaussian priors as a special case. For example, our weakest result establishes (unsupervised) identifiability up to an affine transformation, and thus partially resolves an open problem regarding model identifiability raised in prior work. These theoretical results are augmented with experiments on both simulated and real data.

paragraphs: Identifiability asks how uniquely observed data determine the underlying generative model. This paper proves identification results for a broad class of deep latent-variable models with universal approximation capabilities, including models associated with variational autoencoders used in practice. The analysis uses the observed data alone, without requiring weak supervision or auxiliary information about the latent variables.

The considered models connect to practical architectures using mixture priors and ReLU or leaky-ReLU activations, including VaDE and MFC-VAE. The central result is a hierarchy: different assumptions yield different degrees of identifiability. Certain conventional VAEs with isotropic Gaussian priors also fall within the framework as special cases.

The weakest result identifies the model only up to an affine transformation, so identification does not always mean recovering one uniquely fixed latent coordinate system. Even this qualified result partially resolves a previously raised open problem. Experiments on simulated and real data accompany the theory, supporting an investigation of when unsupervised recovery is possible without the side information required by earlier analyses.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a hierarchy of identifiability guarantees for broad classes of deep generative models using observed data without auxiliary information.

title: Identifiability of deep generative models without auxiliary information

abstract: Generalization in image-based reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a robust policy that could be applied directly on unseen visual environments, which is a challenging task since agents usually tend to overfit to their training environment. To handle this problem, a natural approach is to increase the data diversity by image based augmentations. However, different with most vision tasks such as classification and detection, RL tasks are not always invariant to spatial based augmentations due to the entanglement of environment dynamics and visual appearance. In this paper, we argue with two principles for augmentations in RL: First, the augmented observations should facilitate learning a universal policy, which is robust to various distribution shifts. Second, the augmented data should be invariant to the learning signals such as action and reward. Following these rules, we revisit image-based RL tasks from the view of frequency domain and propose a novel augmentation method, namely Spectrum Random Masking (SRM),which is able to help agents to learn the whole frequency spectrum of observation for coping with various distributions and compatible with the pre-collected action and reward corresponding to original observation. Extensive experiments conducted on DMControl Generalization Benchmark demonstrate the proposed SRM achieves the state-of-the-art performance with strong generalization potentials.

paragraphs: Agents trained from images often overfit to the appearance of their training environment. Image augmentation can increase visual diversity, but reinforcement learning adds a complication: a spatial change to an observation may alter its relationship to the recorded action or reward. Transformations useful in ordinary vision tasks therefore need additional care in this setting.

The paper proposes two guiding requirements: augmentations should encourage policies robust to distribution shifts and preserve compatibility with learning signals such as actions and rewards. Spectrum Random Masking approaches augmentation in the frequency domain. It is designed to encourage learning across the observation's full frequency spectrum while remaining compatible with the action and reward attached to the original observation.

Experiments on the DMControl Generalization Benchmark show state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization potential. These results support frequency-based augmentation as a way to increase useful visual variation for policy learning. The central contribution is connecting the augmentation design to both visual robustness and the meaning of the reinforcement-learning signals.
summary.tldr: Spectrum Random Masking augments observations in the frequency domain to improve visual reinforcement-learning generalization while preserving action and reward compatibility.

title: Spectrum Random Masking for Generalization in Image-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recording the dynamics of unscripted human interactions in the wild is challenging due to the delicate trade-offs between several factors: participant privacy, ecological validity, data fidelity, and logistical overheads. To address these, following a 'datasets for the community by the community' ethos, we propose the Conference Living Lab (ConfLab): a new concept for multimodal multisensor data collection of in-the-wild free-standing social conversations. For the first instantiation of ConfLab described here, we organized a real-life professional networking event at a major international conference. Involving 48 conference attendees, the dataset captures a diverse mix of status, acquaintance, and networking motivations. Our capture setup improves upon the data fidelity of prior in-the-wild datasets while retaining privacy sensitivity: 8 videos (1920x1080, 60 fps) from a non-invasive overhead view, and custom wearable sensors with onboard recording of body motion (full 9-axis IMU), privacy-preserving low-frequency audio (1250 Hz), and Bluetooth-based proximity. Additionally, we developed custom solutions for distributed hardware synchronization at acquisition, and time-efficient continuous annotation of body keypoints and actions at high sampling rates. Our benchmarks showcase some of the open research tasks related to in-the-wild privacy-preserving social data analysis: keypoints detection from overhead camera views, skeleton-based no-audio speaker detection, and F-formation detection.

paragraphs: ConfLab is a framework and dataset for studying unscripted social conversations among people standing and moving freely. Its first collection took place at a real professional networking event with 48 conference attendees. This setting captures interactions involving different levels of acquaintance, professional status, and networking motivation while addressing the competing demands of realistic behavior, recording quality, privacy, and practical logistics.

Together, these tasks make the dataset useful for investigating several visible aspects of social interaction. The contribution includes both recorded evidence and a collection methodology designed to improve data fidelity while retaining sensitivity to participant privacy.
summary.tldr: ConfLab combines overhead video and wearable sensing to support privacy-sensitive research on natural social interactions.

title: ConfLab: A Data Collection Concept, Dataset, and Benchmark for Machine Analysis of Free-Standing Social Interactions in the Wild

abstract: To overcome the quadratic cost of self-attention, recent works have proposed various sparse attention modules, most of which fall under one of two groups: 1) sparse attention under a hand-crafted patterns and 2) full attention followed by a sparse variant of softmax such as $\alpha$-entmax. Unfortunately, the first group lacks adaptability to data while the second still requires quadratic cost in training. In this work, we propose SBM-Transformer, a model that resolves both problems by endowing each attention head with a mixed-membership Stochastic Block Model (SBM). Then, each attention head data-adaptively samples a bipartite graph, the adjacency of which is used as an attention mask for each input. During backpropagation, a straight-through estimator is used to flow gradients beyond the discrete sampling step and adjust the probabilities of sampled edges based on the predictive loss. The forward and backward cost are thus linear to the number of edges, which each attention head can also choose flexibly based on the input. By assessing the distribution of graphs, we theoretically show that SBM-Transformer is a universal approximator for arbitrary sequence-to-sequence functions in expectation. Empirical evaluations under the LRA and GLUE benchmarks demonstrate that our model outperforms previous efficient variants as well as the original Transformer with full attention. Our implementation can be found in https://github.com/sc782/SBM-Transformer.

SBM-Transformer addresses both concerns by letting each attention head choose an input-dependent pattern of connections. The method equips each head with a mixed-membership stochastic block model.

For each input, a head samples a bipartite graph whose edges determine the attention mask. A straight-through estimator allows predictive-loss gradients to pass through the discrete sampling operation and update edge probabilities. Both forward and backward costs scale linearly with the number of edges, and the head can vary that number according to the input. This makes the chosen connectivity relevant to both information flow and computational cost.

Experiments on LRA and GLUE show better performance than the compared efficient attention variants and the original full-attention Transformer. The paper combines a learned sparse computation structure with theoretical expressiveness and reported benchmark gains.
summary.tldr: SBM-Transformer learns input-dependent attention graphs whose training and inference costs scale with their selected edges.

title: Transformers meet Stochastic Block Models: Attention with Data-Adaptive Sparsity and Cost

abstract: We argue that the theory and practice of diffusion-based generative models are currently unnecessarily convoluted and seek to remedy the situation by presenting a design space that clearly separates the concrete design choices. This lets us identify several changes to both the sampling and training processes, as well as preconditioning of the score networks. Together, our improvements yield new state-of-the-art FID of 1.79 for CIFAR-10 in a class-conditional setting and 1.97 in an unconditional setting, with much faster sampling (35 network evaluations per image) than prior designs. To further demonstrate their modular nature, we show that our design changes dramatically improve both the efficiency and quality obtainable with pre-trained score networks from previous work, including improving the FID of a previously trained ImageNet-64 model from 2.07 to near-SOTA 1.55, and after re-training with our proposed improvements to a new SOTA of 1.36.

paragraphs: The paper argues that diffusion-model theory and implementation obscure choices that can be considered separately. It organizes these choices into a clearer design space, making it easier to identify which parts of training and image generation can be improved independently.

Using this organization, the authors introduce changes to sampling, training, and score-network preconditioning. Together, these produce reported state-of-the-art CIFAR-10 FID scores of 1.79 with class conditioning and 1.97 without it. Sampling requires 35 network evaluations per image, which the abstract reports as much faster than earlier designs. The results therefore address both image quality and the computational work required to generate an image.

The authors also apply their design changes to previously trained score networks, demonstrating that some benefits carry over without retraining. For an existing ImageNet-64 model, FID improves from 2.07 to 1.55; retraining with the proposed improvements brings it to 1.36. These findings support the modular nature of the design space by separating improvements available from an existing network from those obtained through changed training.
summary.tldr: Separating diffusion-model design choices yields improvements in sampling speed and image quality, including benefits for already-trained networks.

title: Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models

abstract: The susceptibility of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to adversarial attacks indicates the necessity to evaluate the robustness of the learned representations along with the generation performance. The vulnerability of VAEs has been attributed to the limitations associated with their variational formulation. Deterministic autoencoders could overcome the practical limitations associated with VAEs and offer a promising alternative for image generation applications. In this work, we propose an adversarially robust deterministic autoencoder with superior performance in terms of both generation and robustness of the learned representations. We introduce a regularization scheme to incorporate adversarially perturbed data points to the training pipeline without increasing the computational complexity or compromising the generation fidelity by leveraging a loss based on the two-point Kolmogorov–Smirnov test between representations. We conduct extensive experimental studies on popular image benchmark datasets to quantify the robustness of the proposed approach based on the adversarial attacks targeted at VAEs. Our empirical findings show that the proposed method achieves significant performance in both robustness and fidelity when compared to the robust VAE models.

paragraphs: Image-generating autoencoders need to produce convincing images and learn representations that withstand adversarial perturbations. The paper explores deterministic autoencoders as an alternative to variational autoencoders, whose vulnerability has been associated with their variational formulation. Its goal is to improve robustness without sacrificing generated-image quality.

The proposed method adds a regularization scheme that incorporates adversarially perturbed examples during training. Its loss compares representations using a two-point Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. According to the abstract, this scheme does not increase computational complexity or compromise generation fidelity, making the representation-level comparison central to the proposed combination of robustness and quality.

The authors evaluate the approach on popular image benchmarks using attacks targeted at variational autoencoders. Their empirical findings show strong performance in both robustness and fidelity compared with robust VAE models. The significance is that the evaluated deterministic approach improves both goals together. The evidence supports this result for the reported comparisons, rather than establishing resistance to every possible attack.
summary.tldr: A representation-based regularizer gives deterministic autoencoders improved adversarial robustness and image fidelity in comparisons with robust VAEs.

title: Trading off Image Quality for Robustness is not Necessary with Regularized Deterministic Autoencoders

abstract: Distributional assumptions have been shown to be necessary for the robust learnability of concept classes when considering the exact-in-the-ball robust risk and access to random examples by Gourdeau et al. (2019). In this paper, we study learning models where the learner is given more power through the use of local queries, and give the first distribution-free algorithms that perform robust empirical risk minimization (ERM) for this notion of robustness. The first learning model we consider uses local membership queries (LMQ), where the learner can query the label of points near the training sample. We show that, under the uniform distribution, LMQs do not increase the robustness threshold of conjunctions and any superclass, e.g., decision lists and halfspaces. Faced with this negative result, we introduce the local equivalence query (LEQ) oracle, which returns whether the hypothesis and target concept agree in the perturbation region around a point in the training sample, as well as a counterexample if it exists. We show a separation result: on one hand, if the query radius $\lambda$ is strictly smaller than the adversary's perturbation budget $\rho$, then distribution-free robust learning is impossible for a wide variety of concept classes; on the other hand, the setting $\lambda=\rho$ allows us to develop robust ERM algorithms. We then bound the query complexity of these algorithms based on online learning guarantees and further improve these bounds for the special case of conjunctions. We finish by giving robust learning algorithms for halfspaces with margins on both $\{0,1\}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$.

In this paper, we study learning models where the learner is given more power through the use of local queries, and give the first distribution-free algorithms that perform robust empirical risk minimization (ERM) for this notion of robustness. The first learning model we consider uses local membership queries (LMQ), where the learner can query the label of points near the training sample. We show that, under the uniform distribution, LMQs do not increase the robustness threshold of conjunctions and any superclass, e.g., decision lists and halfspaces. Faced with this negative result, we introduce the local equivalence query (LEQ) oracle, which returns whether the hypothesis and target concept agree in the perturbation region around a point in the training sample, as well as a counterexample if it exists. We show a separation result: on one hand, if the query radius $\lambda$ is strictly smaller than the adversary's perturbation budget $\rho$, then distribution-free robust learning is impossible for a wide variety of concept classes; on the other hand, the setting $\lambda=\rho$ allows us to develop robust ERM algorithms. We then bound the query complexity of these algorithms based on online learning guarantees and further improve these bounds for the special case of conjunctions. We finish by giving robust learning algorithms for halfspaces with margins on both $\{0,1\}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether additional questions about points near training examples can enable robust learning without assumptions on the data distribution. Its robustness notion requires agreement throughout a perturbation region. The first query type supplies labels of nearby points, but under the uniform distribution these local membership queries do not increase the robustness threshold for conjunctions or their superclasses.

The authors then introduce local equivalence queries. This oracle checks whether a proposed hypothesis agrees with the target concept throughout a local perturbation region and returns a counterexample when agreement fails. It provides information about an entire region through a query, giving the learner a different form of access to errors.

The query radius is decisive. If it is strictly smaller than the adversary's perturbation budget, distribution-free robust learning remains impossible for many concept classes. When the radii match, the authors construct robust empirical risk minimization algorithms and bound their query requirements using online learning guarantees. They sharpen bounds for conjunctions and provide robust algorithms for halfspaces with margins.
summary.tldr: Local equivalence queries enable distribution-free robust ERM when their radius matches the adversary's budget, while smaller radii leave broad impossibility results.

title: When are Local Queries Useful for Robust Learning?

abstract: Explaining artificial intelligence (AI) predictions is increasingly important and even imperative in many high-stake applications where humans are the ultimate decision-makers. In this work, we propose two novel architectures of explainable image classifiers that first explain, and then predict (as opposed to post-hoc explanation methods). Our models first rank the training-set images by their distance with the query in an image-level deep feature space. And then, we re-rank the top-50 shortlisted candidates using patch-wise similarity of 5 highest-similarity pairs of patches between the query and every candidate. On ImageNet, our models improve (by 1-4 points) the out-of-distribution accuracy on several datasets including Adversarial Patch and ImageNet-R while performing marginally worse (by 1-2 points) on ImageNet to the baselines (ResNet-50 pre-trained ImageNet). A consistent trend is observed on CUB. Via a large-scale, human study (~60 users per method per dataset) on ImageNet and CUB, we find our proposed correspondence-based explanations led to human-alone image classification accuracy and human-AI team accuracy that are consistently better than those of k-NN. Our correspondence-based explanations help users better correctly reject AI's wrong decisions than all other tested methods.Interestingly, for the first time, we show that it is possible to achieve complementary human-AI team accuracy (i.e. that is higher than either AI-alone or human-alone), in both image classification tasks.

They also help users correctly reject wrong AI decisions more often than all other tested methods. In both classification tasks, team accuracy can exceed either participant alone. summary.tldr: Classifiers that explain predictions through matching image patches improve reported robustness and help human-AI teams outperform either participant alone.

title: Visual correspondence-based explanations improve AI robustness and human-AI team accuracy

abstract: We study the problem of change-point detection and localisation for functional data sequentially observed on a general $d$-dimensional space, where we allow the functional curves to be either sparsely or densely sampled. Data of this form naturally arise in a wide range of applications such as biology, neuroscience, climatology and finance. To achieve such a task, we propose a kernel-based algorithm named functional seeded binary segmentation (FSBS). FSBS is computationally efficient, can handle discretely observed functional data, and is theoretically sound for heavy-tailed and temporally-dependent observations. Moreover, FSBS works for a general $d$-dimensional domain, which is the first in the literature of change-point estimation for functional data. We show the consistency of FSBS for multiple change-point estimation and further provide a sharp localisation error rate, which reveals an interesting phase transition phenomenon depending on the number of functional curves observed and the sampling frequency for each curve. Extensive numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of FSBS and its advantage over existing methods in the literature under various settings. A real data application is further conducted, where FSBS localises change-points of sea surface temperature patterns in the south Pacific attributed to El Ni\~{n}o.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify when a sequence of observed functions changes. Each observation can describe a pattern across a spatial domain, and that pattern may be measured at only a few locations or sampled densely. The goal is both to detect multiple changes and to locate where they occur in the sequence.

The proposed method, functional seeded binary segmentation, uses kernels to handle discretely observed functional data. It works over general multidimensional domains, extending the scope of functional change-point estimation. Its theoretical analysis accommodates heavy-tailed observations and dependence over time, rather than requiring the observations to be temporally independent.

The authors establish consistency for estimating multiple change points and derive a sharp localization error rate. That rate exhibits a phase transition governed by both the number of observed functions and the sampling frequency within each function. Experiments demonstrate advantages over existing methods across several settings. An application to South Pacific sea surface temperatures identifies changes in spatial temperature patterns attributed to El Niño.
summary.tldr: FSBS detects changes in sparsely or densely sampled functional data, with guarantees covering multidimensional domains and temporal dependence.

title: Change-point Detection for Sparse and Dense Functional Data in General Dimensions

abstract: Through a deeper understanding of predictions of neural networks, Influence Function (IF) has been applied to various tasks such as detecting and relabeling mislabeled samples, dataset pruning, and separation of data sources in practice. However, we found standard approximations of IF suffer from performance degradation due to oversimplified influence distributions caused by their bilinear approximation, suppressing the expressive power of samples with a relatively strong influence. To address this issue, we propose a new interpretation of existing IF approximations as an average relationship between two linearized losses over parameters sampled from the Laplace approximation (LA). In doing so, we highlight two significant limitations of current IF approximations: the linearity of gradients and the singularity of Hessian. Accordingly, by improving each point, we introduce a new IF approximation method with the following features: i) the removal of linearization to alleviate the bilinear constraint and ii) the utilization of Geometric Ensemble (GE) tailored for non-linear losses. Empirically, our approach outperforms existing IF approximations for downstream tasks with lighter computation, thereby providing new feasibility of low-complexity/nonlinear-based IF design.

paragraphs: Influence functions help connect neural-network predictions to training examples, supporting tasks such as finding mislabeled data and deciding which examples to remove. This paper argues that standard approximations can flatten the distribution of influence too aggressively. Their bilinear form limits how strongly influential examples can be represented, degrading performance on downstream tasks.

The authors reinterpret existing approximations as an average relationship between two linearized losses, with model parameters sampled from a Laplace approximation. This perspective exposes two issues: the linear treatment of gradients and singularity of the Hessian, a matrix describing loss curvature. The reinterpretation provides a route to changing the approximation itself.

Their method, GEX, removes loss linearization and uses a geometric ensemble suited to nonlinear losses. Empirically, it performs better than existing influence approximations on downstream tasks while requiring less computation. The results support the feasibility of influence estimators that retain nonlinear behavior without necessarily incurring greater computational expense, particularly when simplified influence distributions lose useful information.
summary.tldr: GEX uses a geometric ensemble and nonlinear losses to approximate training-data influence more effectively and with lighter computation in the reported experiments.

title: GEX: A flexible method for approximating influence via Geometric Ensemble

abstract: We introduce a new type of query mechanism for collecting human feedback, called the perceptual adjustment query (PAQ). Being both informative and cognitively lightweight, the PAQ adopts an inverted measurement scheme, and combines advantages from both cardinal and ordinal queries. We showcase the PAQ in the metric learning problem, where we collect PAQ measurements to learn an unknown Mahalanobis distance. This gives rise to a high-dimensional, low-rank matrix estimation problem to which standard matrix estimators cannot be applied. Consequently, we develop a two-stage estimator for metric learning from PAQs, and provide sample complexity guarantees for this estimator. We present numerical simulations demonstrating the performance of the estimator and its notable properties.

We showcase the PAQ in the metric learning problem, where we collect PAQ measurements to learn an unknown Mahalanobis distance. This gives rise to a high-dimensional, low-rank matrix estimation problem to which standard matrix estimators cannot be applied. Consequently, we develop a two-stage estimator for metric learning from PAQs, and provide sample complexity guarantees for this estimator. We present numerical simulations demonstrating the performance of the estimator and its notable properties.

paragraphs: Human feedback can be useful for learning a distance function, but the way feedback is requested affects both its informativeness and the effort involved. This paper introduces perceptual adjustment queries, or PAQs, as a cognitively lightweight mechanism. The authors describe the mechanism as combining advantages of numerical judgments and ordering-based judgments through an inverted measurement scheme.

They study PAQs in the task of learning an unknown Mahalanobis distance. In this setting, the feedback produces a high-dimensional matrix-estimation problem with a low-rank structure. The resulting measurements cannot be handled by standard matrix estimators, so collecting feedback through the new query mechanism also requires a corresponding change in how the distance is estimated.

The authors develop a two-stage estimator tailored to PAQ measurements and establish sample-complexity guarantees describing its data requirements. Numerical simulations demonstrate its performance and properties. The contribution therefore couples a human-feedback interface with estimation theory: the proposed query is backed by a method for turning its responses into a learned metric and by analysis of that method.
summary.tldr: Perceptual adjustment queries provide a new feedback mechanism for metric learning, supported by a tailored estimator and sample-complexity guarantees.

title: Perceptual adjustment queries and an inverted measurement paradigm for low-rank metric learning

abstract: Drawbacks of ignoring the causal mechanisms when performing imitation learning have recently been acknowledged. Several approaches both to assess the feasibility of imitation and to circumvent causal confounding and causal misspecifications have been proposed in the literature.However, the potential benefits of the incorporation of additional information about the underlying causal structure are left unexplored.An example of such overlooked information is context-specific independence (CSI), i.e., independence that holds only in certain contexts.We consider the problem of causal imitation learning when CSI relations are known.We prove that the decision problem pertaining to the feasibility of imitation in this setting is NP-hard.Further, we provide a necessary graphical criterion for imitation learning under CSI and show that under a structural assumption, this criterion is also sufficient.Finally, we propose a sound algorithmic approach for causal imitation learning which takes both CSI relations and data into account.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can fail when it ignores the causal mechanisms behind observed behavior. This paper investigates what becomes possible when the learner also knows context-specific independence relations. These are relationships in which variables are independent only under particular circumstances, providing causal information that a description without those contexts would overlook.

The authors first show that deciding whether imitation is feasible with this information is NP-hard. They then derive a necessary graphical criterion: successful imitation requires the causal structure to satisfy this condition. Under an additional structural assumption, they prove that the same criterion is sufficient. The assumption matters because the unrestricted necessity result alone does not establish feasibility.

Finally, the paper proposes a sound algorithmic approach that uses both the known independence relations and observed data. Its contribution connects additional causal knowledge to concrete feasibility tests and a learning procedure. The results also expose a computational challenge: more detailed causal information can help formulate imitation, while deciding feasibility remains difficult in the general setting studied.
summary.tldr: Known context-specific independences enable new causal imitation criteria and a sound algorithm, although deciding feasibility is NP-hard in general.

title: Causal Imitability Under Context-Specific Independence Relations

abstract: Text-guided image editing is widely needed in daily life, ranging from personal use to professional applications such as Photoshop.However, existing methods are either zero-shot or trained on an automatically synthesized dataset, which contains a high volume of noise.Thus, they still require lots of manual tuning to produce desirable outcomes in practice.To address this issue, we introduce MagicBrush, the first large-scale, manually annotated dataset for instruction-guided real image editing that covers diverse scenarios: single-turn, multi-turn, mask-provided, and mask-free editing.MagicBrush comprises over 10K manually annotated triplets (source image, instruction, target image), which supports trainining large-scale text-guided image editing models.We fine-tune InstructPix2Pix on MagicBrush and show that the new model can produce much better images according to human evaluation.We further conduct extensive experiments to evaluate current image editing baselines from multiple dimensions including quantitative, qualitative, and human evaluations.The results reveal the challenging nature of our dataset and the gap between current baselines and real-world editing needs.

paragraphs: Instruction-guided image editing aims to turn a written request into the corresponding visual change. The paper argues that existing systems still need substantial manual adjustment, partly because training on automatically synthesized examples introduces considerable noise. MagicBrush addresses the training-data problem with manually annotated examples of edits to real images.

The dataset contains more than 10,000 triplets, each pairing an original image and an instruction with the intended edited image. It covers individual edits and sequences of edits, along with settings where a mask identifying the edit region is either provided or absent. This range makes the dataset relevant to several ways people might interact with editing software.

Fine-tuning InstructPix2Pix on MagicBrush produces much better images according to human evaluation. The authors also assess existing editing baselines through quantitative measurements, qualitative inspection, and human judgments. Those evaluations show that the dataset remains challenging and that current methods fall short of real-world editing needs. MagicBrush therefore contributes both training examples and a demanding basis for evaluating instruction-following edits.
summary.tldr: MagicBrush supplies manually annotated image-editing examples that improve InstructPix2Pix and expose remaining gaps in instruction-guided editing.

title: MagicBrush: A Manually Annotated Dataset for Instruction-Guided Image Editing

abstract: Finding tight linear bounds for activation functions in neural networksis an essential part of several state of the art neural network robustness certification tools. An activation function is an arbitrary, nonlinear,scalar function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. In the existing work on robustness certification, such bounds have been computed using human ingenuity for a handful of the most popular activation functions. While a number of heuristics have been proposed for bounding arbitrary functions,no analysis of the tightness optimality for general scalar functions has been offered yet, to the best of our knowledge. We fill this gap by formulating a concise optimality criterion for tightness of the approximation which allows us tobuild optimal bounds for any function convex in the region of interest $R$. Fora more general class of functions Lipshitz-continuous in $R$ we propose a sampling-based approach (SOL) which, given an instance of the bounding problem, efficiently computes the tightest linear bounds within a given $\varepsilon > 0$ threshold. We leverage an adaptive sampling technique to iteratively build a setof sample points suitable for representing the target activation function. While the theoretical worst case time complexity of our approach is$O(\varepsilon^{-2d})$,it typically only takes $O(\log^{\beta} \frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ time for some $\beta \ge 1$ and isthus sufficiently fast in practice. We provide empirical evidence of SOL's practicalityby incorporating it into a robustness certifier and observing that itproduces similar or higher certification rates while taking as low as quarter of the time compared to the other methods.

paragraphs: Neural-network robustness certifiers often need linear bounds on nonlinear activation functions. Tight bounds help these tools reason about network behavior, but existing constructions have relied heavily on manually designed solutions for familiar functions. This paper introduces a criterion for measuring bound tightness and a more general procedure for constructing bounds.

For functions convex within the region of interest, the criterion supports optimal bounds. For the broader class of functions that are Lipschitz-continuous in that region, SOL adaptively selects sample points and computes linear bounds within a chosen epsilon tolerance of optimal tightness. Adaptive sampling builds a representation suited to the particular function being bounded.

The theoretical worst-case runtime scales as epsilon to the power minus 2d, where d is the input dimension. The authors report substantially milder typical behavior, described by a power of log(1/epsilon). After incorporating SOL into a robustness certifier, they observe similar or higher certification rates and runtimes as low as one quarter of those of other methods. This provides empirical support for practicality despite the demanding worst-case bound.
summary.tldr: SOL adaptively samples Lipschitz-continuous functions to construct nearly optimal linear bounds, with practical gains demonstrated in robustness certification.

title: SOL: Sampling-based Optimal Linear bounding of arbitrary scalar functions

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) algorithms can produce useful image representations by learning to associate different parts of natural images with one another. However, when taken to the extreme, SSL models can unintendedly memorize specific parts in individual training samples rather than learning semantically meaningful associations. In this work, we perform a systematic study of the unintended memorization of image-specific information in SSL models -- which we refer to as déjà vu memorization. Concretely, we show that given the trained model and a crop of a training image containing only the background (e.g., water, sky, grass), it is possible to infer the foreground object with high accuracy or even visually reconstruct it. Furthermore, we show that déjà vu memorization is common to different SSL algorithms, is exacerbated by certain design choices, and cannot be detected by conventional techniques for evaluating representation quality. Our study of déjà vu memorization reveals previously unknown privacy risks in SSL models, as well as suggests potential practical mitigation strategies.

paragraphs: Self-supervised image learning often builds useful representations by associating different parts of an image. This paper investigates what happens when those associations become specific to individual training examples. The authors call this déjà vu memorisation: a model retains image-specific information instead of learning only broadly meaningful relationships between visual content.

Their central demonstration starts with a trained model and a background-only crop from one of its training images. Even though the crop contains material such as sky, grass, or water, the model can make it possible to infer the missing foreground object with high accuracy, or even reconstruct it visually. This reveals information about the training image beyond the content directly visible in the crop.

The study finds this behaviour across different self-supervised algorithms and shows that some design choices make it worse. Conventional representation-quality evaluations fail to detect it. The findings therefore identify a privacy risk that useful downstream representations can conceal, while also suggesting potential practical mitigation strategies rather than establishing that the risk has been eliminated.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised image models can memorise training-specific associations that reveal foreground objects from background crops, escaping conventional representation-quality checks.

title: Do SSL Models Have Déjà Vu? A Case of Unintended Memorization in Self-supervised Learning

abstract: Mixup is an efficient data augmentation approach that improves the generalization of neural networks by smoothing the decision boundary with mixed data. Recently, dynamic mixup methods have improved previous \textit{static} policies effectively (e.g., linear interpolation) by maximizing target-related salient regions in mixed samples, but excessive additional time costs are not acceptable. These additional computational overheads mainly come from optimizing the mixed samples according to the mixed labels. However, we found that the extra optimizing step may be redundant because label-mismatched mixed samples are informative hard mixed samples for deep models to localize discriminative features. In this paper, we thus are not trying to propose a more complicated dynamic mixup policy but rather an efficient mixup objective function with decoupled regularizer, named decoupled mixup (DM). The primary effect is that DM can adaptively utilize those hard mixed samples to mine discriminative features without losing the original smoothness of mixup. As a result, DM enables static mixup methods to achieve comparable or even exceed the performance of dynamic methods without any extra computation. This also leads to an interesting objective design problem for mixup training that we need to focus on both smoothing the decision boundaries and identifying discriminative features. Extensive experiments on supervised and semi-supervised learning benchmarks across seven datasets validate the effectiveness of DM.

paragraphs: Mixup trains neural networks on combinations of examples to encourage smoother decision boundaries. Dynamic mixup methods improve these combinations by emphasizing relevant image regions, but optimizing mixed examples against their labels adds computation. This paper questions whether that extra optimization is always useful: a mismatch between a mixed example and its label can itself provide an informative training challenge.

The authors introduce decoupled mixup, or DM, which changes the training objective through a decoupled regularizer. Its purpose is to use difficult mixed examples adaptively to identify discriminative features while retaining mixup’s smoothing effect. The method therefore addresses two aspects of learning together: keeping boundaries smooth and recognizing the features that distinguish classes.

Experiments cover supervised and semi-supervised learning across seven datasets. The reported results show that DM lets static mixup methods match or sometimes exceed dynamic methods without additional computation. The broader implication is that improving how a model learns from mixed examples can be effective without making the process for constructing those examples more complicated.
summary.tldr: Decoupled mixup uses difficult mixed examples to learn discriminative features while preserving smooth decision boundaries and avoiding extra computation.

title: Harnessing Hard Mixed Samples with Decoupled Regularizer

abstract: This paper introduces the novel concept of few-shot weakly supervised learning for pathology Whole Slide Image (WSI) classification, denoted as FSWC. A solution is proposed based on prompt learning and the utilization of a large language model, GPT-4. Since a WSI is too large and needs to be divided into patches for processing, WSI classification is commonly approached as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem. In this context, each WSI is considered a bag, and the obtained patches are treated as instances. The objective of FSWC is to classify both bags and instances with only a limited number of labeled bags. Unlike conventional few-shot learning problems, FSWC poses additional challenges due to its weak bag labels within the MIL framework. Drawing inspiration from the recent achievements of vision-language models (V-L models) in downstream few-shot classification tasks, we propose a two-level prompt learning MIL framework tailored for pathology, incorporating language prior knowledge. Specifically, we leverage CLIP to extract instance features for each patch, and introduce a prompt-guided pooling strategy to aggregate these instance features into a bag feature. Subsequently, we employ a small number of labeled bags to facilitate few-shot prompt learning based on the bag features. Our approach incorporates the utilization of GPT-4 in a question-and-answer mode to obtain language prior knowledge at both the instance and bag levels, which are then integrated into the instance and bag level language prompts. Additionally, a learnable component of the language prompts is trained using the available few-shot labeled data. We conduct extensive experiments on three real WSI datasets encompassing breast cancer, lung cancer, and cervical cancer, demonstrating the notable performance of the proposed method in bag and instance classification. All codes will be made publicly accessible.

Specifically, we leverage CLIP to extract instance features for each patch, and introduce a prompt-guided pooling strategy to aggregate these instance features into a bag feature. Subsequently, we employ a small number of labeled bags to facilitate few-shot prompt learning based on the bag features. Our approach incorporates the utilization of GPT-4 in a question-and-answer mode to obtain language prior knowledge at both the instance and bag levels, which are then integrated into the instance and bag level language prompts. Additionally, a learnable component of the language prompts is trained using the available few-shot labeled data. We conduct extensive experiments on three real WSI datasets encompassing breast cancer, lung cancer, and cervical cancer, demonstrating the notable performance of the proposed method in bag and instance classification. All codes will be made publicly accessible.

paragraphs: Pathology whole-slide images are too large to process as single inputs, so they are divided into patches. This paper studies classifying both entire slides and individual patches when only a small number of slides have labels. In its multiple-instance learning formulation, each slide is a bag containing patch instances.

The proposed framework uses CLIP to extract patch features, then prompt-guided pooling combines them into a slide representation. GPT-4 supplies language knowledge through questions and answers at both patch and slide levels. That knowledge is incorporated into corresponding language prompts. Learnable prompt components are trained using the small set of labeled slides, connecting language guidance with the available supervision.

The framework addresses the difficulty of learning patch-level predictions from sparse labels attached only to whole slides. Experiments on three real datasets covering breast, lung, and cervical cancer demonstrate notable performance for both slide and patch classification. The contribution brings two levels of language guidance into the same learning process, supporting predictions at both scales from limited slide-level labels.
summary.tldr: Two-level language prompts help classify pathology slides and patches using only a few labeled whole-slide images.

title: The Rise of AI Language Pathologists: Exploring Two-level Prompt Learning for Few-shot Weakly-supervised Whole Slide Image Classification

abstract: We study the problem of optimizing biological sequences, e.g., proteins, DNA, and RNA, to maximize a black-box score function that is only evaluated in an offline dataset. We propose a novel solution, bootstrapped training of score-conditioned generator (BootGen) algorithm. Our algorithm repeats a two-stage process. In the first stage, our algorithm trains the biological sequence generator with rank-based weights to enhance the accuracy of sequence generation based on high scores. The subsequent stage involves bootstrapping, which augments the training dataset with self-generated data labeled by a proxy score function. Our key idea is to align the score-based generation with a proxy score function, which distills the knowledge of the proxy score function to the generator. After training, we aggregate samples from multiple bootstrapped generators and proxies to produce a diverse design. Extensive experiments show that our method outperforms competitive baselines on biological sequential design tasks. We provide reproducible source code: https://github.com/kaist-silab/bootgen.

paragraphs: BootGen addresses biological sequence design when the desired scoring function has been evaluated only on an existing offline dataset. The goal is to generate sequences, such as proteins, DNA, or RNA, with high scores. Learning must therefore draw on the available evaluations and a proxy scoring function.

Training repeatedly alternates between two stages. First, a score-conditioned generator learns with rank-based weights that emphasize accurate generation for high scores. Next, it produces new sequences, which a proxy function scores and adds to the training dataset. This bootstrapping process aligns the generator's score-conditioned behavior with the proxy, transferring knowledge from the scoring model into the generation process.

After training, BootGen combines samples from multiple bootstrapped generators and proxies to produce a diverse set of designs. Experiments show it outperforming competitive baselines on biological sequence design tasks. The approach matters because it brings the proxy's scoring knowledge into how sequences are generated, then uses multiple trained generators and proxies when assembling the final designs.
summary.tldr: BootGen improves offline biological sequence design by repeatedly training a score-conditioned generator on proxy-scored, self-generated sequences.

title: Bootstrapped Training of Score-Conditioned Generator for Offline Design of Biological Sequences

abstract: Audio editing is applicable for various purposes, such as adding background sound effects, replacing a musical instrument, and repairing damaged audio. Recently, some diffusion-based methods achieved zero-shot audio editing by using a diffusion and denoising process conditioned on the text description of the output audio. However, these methods still have some problems: 1) they have not been trained on editing tasks and cannot ensure good editing effects; 2) they can erroneously modify audio segments that do not require editing; 3) they need a complete description of the output audio, which is not always available or necessary in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose AUDIT, an instruction-guided audio editing model based on latent diffusion models. Specifically, \textbf{AUDIT} has three main design features: 1) we construct triplet training data (instruction, input audio, output audio) for different audio editing tasks and train a diffusion model using instruction and input (to be edited) audio as conditions and generating output (edited) audio; 2) it can automatically learn to only modify segments that need to be edited by comparing the difference between the input and output audio; 3) it only needs edit instructions instead of full target audio descriptions as text input. AUDIT achieves state-of-the-art results in both objective and subjective metrics for several audio editing tasks (e.g., adding, dropping, replacement, inpainting, super-resolution). Demo samples are available at https://audit-demopage.github.io/.

paragraphs: AUDIT addresses audio editing through instructions that describe a requested change. Earlier diffusion approaches condition editing on a description of the complete desired recording, even when a user only needs a local modification. The paper also identifies unwanted changes to unaffected audio and a lack of editing-specific training as problems with those approaches.

The authors construct training examples containing an instruction, an input recording, and its edited output. A latent diffusion model learns to generate the output while conditioned on both the instruction and the original audio. Comparing input and output recordings lets it learn which segments require modification, supporting edits that preserve portions outside the requested change.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on objective and subjective measures across several editing tasks, including adding, removing, and replacing sounds, inpainting, and super-resolution. These findings support training directly for editing rather than relying solely on output descriptions. The practical benefit is an interface centered on what should change, with the existing recording providing the remaining context.
summary.tldr: AUDIT trains a latent diffusion model on audio-editing examples so users can request changes without describing the entire desired recording.

title: AUDIT: Audio Editing by Following Instructions with Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Intrinsic images, in the original sense, are image-like maps of scene properties like depth, normal, albedo, or shading. This paper demonstrates that StyleGAN can easily be induced to produce intrinsic images. The procedure is straightforward. We show that if StyleGAN produces $G({\bf w})$ from latent ${\bf w}$, then for each type of intrinsic image, there is a fixed offset ${\bf d}_c$ so that $G({\bf w}+{\bf d}_c)$ is that type of intrinsic image for $G({\bf w})$. Here ${\bf d}_c$ is {\em independent of ${\bf w}$}. The StyleGAN we used was pretrained by others, so this property is not some accident of our training regime. We show that there are image transformations StyleGAN will {\em not} produce in this fashion, so StyleGAN is not a generic image regression engine. It is conceptually exciting that an image generator should ``know'' and represent intrinsic images. There may also be practical advantages to using a generative model to produce intrinsic images. The intrinsic images obtained from StyleGAN compare well both qualitatively and quantitatively with those obtained by using SOTA image regression techniques; but StyleGAN's intrinsic images are robust to relighting effects, unlike SOTA methods.

paragraphs: Intrinsic images describe scene properties such as depth, surface orientation, albedo, or shading. This paper shows that a pretrained StyleGAN can be induced to generate these property maps for its own images. The finding suggests that a model trained to generate images also represents information about properties underlying their appearance.

The mechanism is a fixed shift in the generator's latent input. For each type of intrinsic image, the authors identify an offset that turns the output associated with a latent code into the corresponding property map. Crucially, that offset does not depend on the original code. The generator was pretrained by others, so this behavior was not created by a special training regime devised for the study.

The resulting maps compare well qualitatively and quantitatively with state-of-the-art image-regression methods and show robustness to relighting effects. The authors also identify transformations that cannot be produced through this offset mechanism. That distinction makes the discovery specific: the generator exposes useful intrinsic-image structure without functioning as a general-purpose image-regression system.
summary.tldr: Fixed latent offsets let a pretrained StyleGAN generate intrinsic property maps that compare well with regression methods and resist relighting effects.

title: StyleGAN knows Normal, Depth, Albedo, and More

abstract: Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) are fundamental to machine learning due to their flexibility as approximating densities. However, uncertainty quantification of GMMs remains a challenge as differential entropy lacks a closed form. This paper explores polynomial approximations, specifically Taylor and Legendre, to the GMM entropy from a theoretical and practical perspective. We provide new analysis of a widely used approach due to Huber et al.(2008) and show that the series diverges under simple conditions. Motivated by this divergence we provide a novel Taylor series that is provably convergent to the true entropy of any GMM. We demonstrate a method for selecting a center such that the series converges from below, providing a lower bound on GMM entropy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that orthogonal polynomial series result in more accurate polynomial approximations. Experimental validation supports our theoretical results while showing that our method is comparable in computation to Huber et al. We also show that in application, the use of these polynomial approximations, such as in Nonparametric Variational Inference by Gershamn et al. (2012), rely on the convergence of the methods in computing accurate approximations. This work contributes useful analysis to existing methods while introducing a novel approximation supported by firm theoretical guarantees.

Its contribution is therefore both corrective and constructive: it identifies a failure mode in an established method and supplies alternatives with explicit mathematical guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies divergence in an established Gaussian mixture entropy approximation and introduces a provably convergent alternative.

title: On Convergence of Polynomial Approximations to the Gaussian Mixture Entropy

abstract: Machine learning (ML) models have been widely used to make predictions. Instead of a predictive statement about future outcomes, in many situations we want to pursue a decision: what can we do to avoid the undesired future if an ML model predicts so? In this paper, we present a rehearsal learning framework, in which decisions that can persuasively avoid the happening of undesired outcomes can be found and recommended. Based on the influence relation, we characterize the generative process of variables with structural rehearsal models, consisting of a probabilistic graphical model called rehearsal graphs and structural equations, and find actionable decisions that can alter the outcome by reasoning under a Bayesian framework. Moreover, we present a probably approximately correct bound to quantify the associated risk of a decision. Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed rehearsal learning framework and the informativeness of the bound.

paragraphs: A prediction that an undesirable outcome is likely does not itself identify what someone can do about it. This paper introduces rehearsal learning to move from forecasting an outcome to recommending actionable decisions intended to avoid it. The central problem is to reason about how changes in available choices could alter what happens.

The framework represents the generation of variables through structural rehearsal models. These combine a probabilistic graphical structure, called a rehearsal graph, with structural equations based on influence relations. Bayesian reasoning then uses that model to identify decisions that can change the outcome. This links the recommendation to an explicit account of how variables influence one another.

The authors also provide a probably approximately correct bound to quantify the risk associated with a decision. That bound makes uncertainty part of the recommendation rather than treating a proposed action as an unconditional promise of success. Experiments support both the effectiveness of the framework and the informativeness of the bound, connecting decision recommendations with an assessment of their associated risk.
summary.tldr: Rehearsal learning uses structural models and Bayesian reasoning to recommend actions for avoiding unwanted outcomes while bounding decision risk.

title: Rehearsal Learning for Avoiding Undesired Future

abstract: Gesture synthesis is a vital realm of human-computer interaction, with wide-ranging applications across various fields like film, robotics, and virtual reality. Recent advancements have utilized the diffusion model to improve gesture synthesis. However, the high computational complexity of these techniques limits the application in reality. In this study, we explore the potential of state space models (SSMs).Direct application of SSMs in gesture synthesis encounters difficulties, which stem primarily from the diverse movement dynamics of various body parts. The generated gestures may also exhibit unnatural jittering issues.To address these, we implement a two-stage modeling strategy with discrete motion priors to enhance the quality of gestures.Built upon the selective scan mechanism, we introduce MambaTalk, which integrates hybrid fusion modules, local and global scans to refine latent space representations.Subjective and objective experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art models. Our project is publicly available at~\url{https://kkakkkka.github.io/MambaTalk/}.

paragraphs: Gesture synthesis must coordinate body parts whose movements have different dynamics. Although diffusion models have improved generated gestures, their computational demands can hinder practical use. This paper explores state space models as another approach, while recognizing that applying them directly creates difficulties, including unnatural jitter in the resulting movements.

MambaTalk addresses those difficulties through a two-stage modeling strategy with discrete motion priors. These priors provide structure for generating gestures rather than leaving all movement behavior to a direct state space model. The architecture builds on a selective scan mechanism and combines hybrid fusion modules with both local and global scans to refine its internal representations.

The local and global processing is part of the method's response to the need for coordinated motion across different body parts. Subjective assessments and objective experiments report performance beyond the state-of-the-art models considered in the study. The findings support the proposed combination of state space modeling and structured motion priors as a promising approach to holistic gesture synthesis, motivated by the computational burden of existing diffusion-based techniques.
summary.tldr: MambaTalk combines selective state space modeling with discrete motion priors to improve holistic gesture synthesis in subjective and objective evaluations.

title: MambaTalk: Efficient Holistic Gesture Synthesis with Selective State Space Models

abstract: Text-driven image synthesis has made significant advancements with the development of diffusion models, transforming how visual content is generated from text prompts. Despite these advances, text-driven image editing, a key area in computer graphics, faces unique challenges. A major challenge is making simultaneous edits across multiple objects or attributes. Applying these methods sequentially for multi-attribute edits increases computational demands and efficiency losses. In this paper, we address these challenges with significant contributions. Our main contribution is the development of ParallelEdits, a method that seamlessly manages simultaneous edits across multiple attributes. In contrast to previous approaches, ParallelEdits not only preserves the quality of single attribute edits but also significantly improves the performance of multitasking edits. This is achieved through innovative attention distribution mechanism and multi-branch design that operates across several processing heads. Additionally, we introduce the PIE-Bench++ dataset, an expansion of the original PIE-Bench dataset, to better support evaluating image-editing tasks involving multiple objects and attributes simultaneously. This dataset is a benchmark for evaluating text-driven image editing methods in multifaceted scenarios.

paragraphs: Editing an image from text becomes harder when the request involves several objects or attributes at once. Applying separate edits sequentially adds computational demands and reduces efficiency. ParallelEdits addresses this setting by designing a method that handles multiple requested changes simultaneously within its editing process.

The method combines an attention-distribution mechanism with a multi-branch design operating across several processing heads. These components organize the handling of multiple edits. The authors report that ParallelEdits preserves the quality of single-attribute editing while significantly improving performance when several editing tasks must be carried out together.

The paper also introduces PIE-Bench++, expanding the original PIE-Bench dataset to evaluate simultaneous edits involving multiple objects and attributes. This matters because single-edit evaluation does not directly capture the demands of managing several changes in one image. Together, the method and dataset make multi-aspect editing a distinct target for both system design and assessment. The stated findings support the effectiveness of simultaneous editing, while the expanded benchmark supplies material for evaluating that capability.
summary.tldr: ParallelEdits combines attention grouping and multiple processing branches to improve simultaneous image edits, alongside a benchmark expanded for that task.

title: ParallelEdits: Efficient Multi-Aspect Text-Driven Image Editing with Attention Grouping

abstract: Kernel methods are widely utilized in machine learning field to learn, from training data, a latent function in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. It is well known that the approximator thus obtained usually achieves a linear representation, which brings various computational benefits, while maintaining great representation power (i.e., universal approximation). However, when non-negativity constraints are imposed on the function's outputs, the literature usually takes the kernel method-based approximators as offering linear representations at the expense of limited model flexibility or good representation power by allowing for their nonlinear forms. The main contribution of this paper is to derive a sufficient condition for a positive definite kernel so that it may construct flexible and linear approximators of non-negative functions. We call a kernel function that offers these attributes an *inverse M-kernel*; it is reminiscent of the inverse M-matrix. Furthermore, we show that for a one-dimensional input space, universal exponential/Abel kernels are inverse M-kernels and construct linear universal approximators of non-negative functions. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first time that the existence of linear universal approximators of non-negative functions has been elucidated. We confirm the effectiveness of our results by experiments on the problems of non-negativity-constrained regression, density estimation, and intensity estimation. Finally, we discuss issues and perspectives on multi-dimensional input settings.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can represent learned functions linearly while retaining substantial expressive power. Requiring every output to be non-negative complicates that combination: existing approaches often retain linearity with limited flexibility or gain flexibility through nonlinear representations. This paper investigates whether linear representations and universal approximation can coexist with the non-negativity constraint.

The main result gives a sufficient condition on a positive definite kernel for constructing flexible linear approximators of non-negative functions. The authors call kernels with these properties inverse M-kernels. For one-dimensional inputs, they establish that universal exponential, or Abel, kernels satisfy the condition and yield linear universal approximators with non-negative outputs.

Experiments examine non-negativity-constrained regression, density estimation, and intensity estimation, supporting the usefulness of the theoretical results. The established universal construction is specifically for one-dimensional input spaces; the paper separately discusses issues and prospects for higher dimensions. The contribution is an existence result and a constructive route showing that non-negativity need not force the usual tradeoff between linear representation and approximation power in this setting.
summary.tldr: Inverse M-kernels provide sufficient conditions for flexible linear non-negative approximators, including universal constructions for one-dimensional inputs.

title: Inverse M-Kernels for Linear Universal Approximators of Non-Negative Functions

abstract: Physical models in the form of partial differential equations serve as important priors for many under-constrained problems. One such application is tumor treatment planning, which relies on accurately estimating the spatial distribution of tumor cells within a patient’s anatomy. While medical imaging can detect the bulk of a tumor, it cannot capture the full extent of its spread, as low-concentration tumor cells often remain undetectable, particularly in glioblastoma, the most common primary brain tumor. Machine learning approaches struggle to estimate the complete tumor cell distribution due to a lack of appropriate training data. Consequently, most existing methods rely on physics-based simulations to generate anatomically and physiologically plausible estimations. However, these approaches face challenges with complex and unknown initial conditions and are constrained by overly rigid physical models. In this work, we introduce a novel method that integrates data-driven and physics-based cost functions, akin to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). However, our approach parametrizes the solution directly on a dynamic discrete mesh, allowing for the effective modeling of complex biomechanical behaviors. Specifically, we propose a unique discretization scheme that quantifies how well the learned spatiotemporal distributions of tumor and brain tissues adhere to their respective growth and elasticity equations. This quantification acts as a regularization term, offering greater flexibility and improved integration of patient data compared to existing models. We demonstrate enhanced coverage of tumor recurrence areas using real-world data from a patient cohort, highlighting the potential of our method to improve model-driven treatment planning for glioblastoma in clinical practice.

Physics-based simulations provide plausible estimates, yet unknown initial conditions and rigid physical models make incorporating patient evidence difficult.

The stated outcome concerns localization and recurrence coverage, with improved clinical planning presented as a potential application.
summary.tldr: A mesh-based method combines patient imaging with growth and elasticity constraints to improve coverage of brain-tumor recurrence areas.

title: Physics-Regularized Multi-Modal Image Assimilation for Brain Tumor Localization

abstract: Adaptive methods are extremely popular in machine learning as they make learning rate tuning less expensive. This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm named KATE, which presents a scale-invariant adaptation of the well-known AdaGrad algorithm. We prove the scale-invariance of KATE for the case of Generalized Linear Models. Moreover, for general smooth non-convex problems, we establish a convergence rate of $O((\log T)/\sqrt{T})$ for KATE, matching the best-known ones for AdaGrad and Adam. We also compare KATE to other state-of-the-art adaptive algorithms Adam and AdaGrad in numerical experiments with different problems, including complex machine learning tasks like image classification and text classification on real data. The results indicate that KATE consistently outperforms AdaGrad and matches/surpasses the performance of Adam in all considered scenarios.

We also compare KATE to other state-of-the-art adaptive algorithms Adam and AdaGrad in numerical experiments with different problems, including complex machine learning tasks like image classification and text classification on real data. The results indicate that KATE consistently outperforms AdaGrad and matches/surpasses the performance of Adam in all considered scenarios.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimization methods are popular because they reduce the effort needed to tune learning rates. This paper introduces KATE, an adaptation of AdaGrad designed around scale invariance. It examines the algorithm through both mathematical guarantees and numerical comparisons with established adaptive optimizers.

The authors prove KATE's scale invariance for generalized linear models. Separately, for general smooth non-convex optimization problems, they establish a convergence rate of O((log T)/sqrt(T)). This matches the best-known rates stated for AdaGrad and Adam. The scope of the two results differs: the scale-invariance proof concerns generalized linear models, while the convergence result applies to the broader smooth non-convex setting.

Experiments compare KATE with AdaGrad and Adam on several problems, including image and text classification using real data. KATE consistently outperforms AdaGrad and matches or exceeds Adam in all scenarios considered. These findings combine competitive theoretical convergence with favorable empirical performance, providing support for the proposed AdaGrad variant across the tested optimization and machine-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: KATE adapts AdaGrad with proven scale invariance for generalized linear models and competitive convergence and empirical performance.

title: Remove that Square Root: A New Efficient Scale-Invariant Version of AdaGrad

abstract: Modeling the shape of garments has received much attention, but most existing approaches assume the garments to be worn by someone, which constrains the range of shapes they can assume. In this work, we address shape recovery when garments are being manipulated instead of worn, which gives rise to an even larger range of possible shapes. To this end, we leverage the implicit sewing patterns (ISP) model for garment modeling and extend it by adding a diffusion-based deformation prior to represent these shapes. To recover 3D garment shapes from incomplete 3D point clouds acquired when the garment is folded, we map the points to UV space, in which our priors are learned, to produce partial UV maps, and then fit the priors to recover complete UV maps and 2D to 3D mappings. Experimental results demonstrate the superior reconstruction accuracy of our method compared to previous ones, especially when dealing with large non-rigid deformations arising from the manipulations.
