paragraphs: Neurosymbolic models combine neural perception with symbolic reasoning, but satisfying logical constraints does not necessarily mean they learned the intended concepts. A model can instead exploit correlations that let incorrect internal concepts produce acceptable answers. This paper addresses that failure by grounding learned concepts in a small collection of labeled examples.

The proposed architectures use prototypical learning: similarity to labeled examples helps guide which concepts the model should recognize. Training jointly accounts for this similarity and satisfaction of background knowledge. The authors demonstrate that this combination can avoid reasoning shortcuts, connecting correct symbolic outputs to learning the correct basic concepts even when supervision is extremely scarce.

Evaluation uses the rsbench suite across multiple settings, including the synthetic MNIST-EvenOdd and Kand-Logic tasks and the real-world BDD-OIA task. The authors report significant improvements in learning the intended concepts. These findings support prototype grounding as an annotation-efficient strategy for more reliable neurosymbolic learning, with concept quality itself serving as a central outcome rather than logical constraint satisfaction alone.
summary.tldr: Grounding neurosymbolic concepts in a few labeled prototypes helps models avoid reasoning shortcuts and learn intended concepts under scarce supervision.

title: Right for the Right Reasons: Avoiding Reasoning Shortcuts via Prototypical Neurosymbolic AI

abstract: Discriminative latent-variable models are typically learned using EM or gradient-based optimization, which suffer from local optima. In this paper, we develop a new computationally efficient and provably consistent estimator for the mixture of linear regressions, a simple instance of discriminative latent-variable models. Our approach relies on a low-rank linear regression to recover a symmetric tensor, which can be factorized into the parameters using the tensor power method. We prove rates of convergence for our estimator and provide an empirical evaluation illustrating its strengths relative to local optimization (EM).
originalAbstract: Discriminative latent-variable models are typically learned using EM or gradient-based optimization, which suffer from local optima. In this paper, we develop a new computationally efficient and provably consistent estimator for the mixture of linear regressions, a simple instance of discriminative latent-variable models. Our approach relies on a low-rank linear regression to recover a symmetric tensor, which can be factorized into the parameters using the tensor power method. We prove rates of convergence for our estimator and provide an empirical evaluation illustrating its strengths relative to local optimization (EM).

paragraphs: Mixtures of linear regressions describe a relationship using multiple linear components whose identities are latent. Such discriminative latent-variable models are commonly fitted using expectation-maximization or gradient-based optimization, both of which can encounter local optima. This paper develops a computationally efficient, provably consistent estimator for the mixture-of-regressions setting.

The method first uses a low-rank linear regression to recover a symmetric tensor. It then applies the tensor power method to factor that tensor into the model parameters. This creates a staged estimation procedure in which recovering an intermediate mathematical object provides the route to identifying the regression components.

The authors prove convergence rates for the estimator and evaluate it empirically against expectation-maximization. The evaluation illustrates strengths relative to local optimization, while the consistency result supplies a theoretical foundation for estimation. Together, these contributions establish a tensor-based approach to learning this particular latent-variable model and connect its computational procedure to formal statistical guarantees.
summary.tldr: A tensor-based estimator efficiently learns mixtures of linear regressions with consistency and convergence guarantees.

title: Spectral Experts for Estimating Mixtures of Linear Regressions

abstract: A mean function in reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), or a kernel mean, is an important part of many algorithms ranging from kernel principal component analysis to Hilbert-space embedding of distributions. Given a finite sample, an empirical average is the standard estimate for the true kernel mean. We show that this estimator can be improved due to a well-known phenomenon in statistics called Stein phenomenon. After consideration, our theoretical analysis reveals the existence of a wide class of estimators that are better than the standard one. Focusing on a subset of this class, we propose efficient shrinkage estimators for the kernel mean. Empirical evaluations on several applications clearly demonstrate that the proposed estimators outperform the standard kernel mean estimator.

title: Kernel Mean Estimation and Stein Effect

abstract: Context Tree Weighting (CTW) is a powerful probabilistic sequence prediction technique that efficiently performs Bayesian model averaging over the class of all prediction suffix trees of bounded depth. In this paper we show how to generalize this technique to the class of K-skip prediction suffix trees. Contrary to regular prediction suffix trees, K-skip prediction suffix trees are permitted to ignore up to K contiguous portions of the context. This allows for significant improvements in predictive accuracy when irrelevant variables are present, a case which often occurs within record-aligned data and images. We provide a regret-based analysis of our approach, and empirically evaluate it on the Calgary corpus and a set of Atari 2600 screen prediction tasks.

This paper extends the approach to a richer family of trees that can ignore parts of the available context. The motivating issue is that some contextual variables may be irrelevant, so using a contiguous context can obscure information useful for prediction.

The proposed family consists of K-skip prediction suffix trees. Each tree may skip up to K contiguous portions of its context, allowing the prediction rule to use separated pieces of information. This flexibility can significantly improve predictive accuracy when irrelevant variables are present. The paper identifies record-aligned data and images as settings where such irrelevant context often occurs.

The authors provide a regret-based analysis and evaluate the method on the Calgary corpus and Atari 2600 screen prediction tasks. These evaluations examine the approach in both sequence and image-related settings. The central contribution is to expand the contexts over which prediction can be organized, giving the model a way to bypass unhelpful stretches while retaining relevant information.
summary.tldr: Skip context trees improve sequence modeling flexibility by allowing predictors to ignore up to K contiguous portions of irrelevant context.

title: Skip Context Tree Switching

abstract: Probabilitic Finite Automata (PFA) are generative graphical models that define distributions with latent variables over finite sequences of symbols, a.k.a. stochastic languages. Traditionally, unsupervised learning of PFA is performed through algorithms that iteratively improves the likelihood like the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. Recently, learning algorithms based on the so-called Method of Moments (MoM) have been proposed as a much faster alternative that comes with PAC-style guarantees. However, these algorithms do not ensure the learnt automata to model a proper distribution, limiting their applicability and preventing them to serve as an initialization to iterative algorithms. In this paper, we propose a new MoM-based algorithm with PAC-style guarantees that learns automata defining proper distributions. We assess its performances on synthetic problems from the PAutomaC challenge and real datasets extracted from Wikipedia against previous MoM-based algorithms and EM algorithm.

They are commonly learned through iterative likelihood-improvement methods such as expectation-maximization. Method-of-moments approaches offer a much faster alternative with PAC-style guarantees, but earlier versions have an important drawback: the learned automaton may fail to define a proper probability distribution.

This paper proposes a method-of-moments algorithm that retains PAC-style guarantees while producing automata that define proper distributions. The distinction matters because a statistical learning guarantee alone does not ensure that an output can be used as a valid probabilistic model. The abstract also identifies invalid distributions as an obstacle to initializing iterative learning algorithms.

The authors evaluate their method on synthetic problems from the PAutomaC challenge and real datasets drawn from Wikipedia. Comparisons include previous method-of-moments algorithms and expectation-maximization. The central stated contribution is the combination of probabilistically valid outputs with formal learning guarantees, addressing a concrete applicability problem in earlier moment-based approaches.
summary.tldr: A new method-of-moments algorithm learns probabilistic automata that define valid distributions while retaining PAC-style guarantees.

title: PAC learning of Probabilistic Automaton based on the Method of Moments

abstract: A search engine recommends to the user a list of web pages. The user examines this list, from the first page to the last, and clicks on all attractive pages until the user is satisfied. This behavior of the user can be described by the dependent click model (DCM). We propose DCM bandits, an online learning variant of the DCM where the goal is to maximize the probability of recommending satisfactory items, such as web pages. The main challenge of our learning problem is that we do not observe which attractive item is satisfactory. We propose a computationally-efficient learning algorithm for solving our problem, dcmKL-UCB; derive gap-dependent upper bounds on its regret under reasonable assumptions; and also prove a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. We evaluate our algorithm on synthetic and real-world problems, and show that it performs well even when our model is misspecified. This work presents the first practical and regret-optimal online algorithm for learning to rank with multiple clicks in a cascade-like click model.

paragraphs: The paper studies ranking when users can click several items before finding something satisfactory. In its dependent click model, a user examines a list in order, clicks attractive items, and stops when satisfied. The learning objective is to increase the probability of recommending satisfactory items, which is different from merely collecting clicks.

The central difficulty is that the learner does not observe which attractive item actually satisfied the user. The authors formulate an online learning problem around this incomplete feedback and propose dcmKL-UCB, a computationally efficient algorithm. They derive regret upper bounds that depend on performance gaps under stated reasonable assumptions, along with a lower bound matching up to logarithmic factors.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems show good performance, including cases where the assumed click model is misspecified. That robustness is an empirical finding rather than a guarantee for arbitrary user behavior. The work presents a practical, regret-optimal approach to learning rankings with multiple clicks within a cascade-like model, connecting a richer interaction model to learning guarantees.
summary.tldr: DCM bandits learn rankings from multiple clicks while accounting for the unobserved distinction between attractiveness and satisfaction.

title: DCM Bandits: Learning to Rank with Multiple Clicks

abstract: We introduce the Contextual Graph Markov Model, an approach combining ideas from generative models and neural networks for the processing of graph data. It founds on a constructive methodology to build a deep architecture comprising layers of probabilistic models that learn to encode the structured information in an incremental fashion. Context is diffused in an efficient and scalable way across the graph vertexes and edges. The resulting graph encoding is used in combination with discriminative models to address structure classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: The Contextual Graph Markov Model is an approach to representing graph data that combines generative modeling with ideas from neural networks. Its focus is structured information: a graph's representation must account for its vertices, edges, and the context carried through their connections. The paper develops a deep architecture for learning such encodings.

The architecture is built constructively from layers of probabilistic models. These layers learn to encode graph structure incrementally, so the representation develops through successive modeling stages. Context is propagated across vertices and edges using a procedure described as efficient and scalable. This propagation is the mechanism through which connected parts of the graph contribute to the learned encoding.

The resulting representation is combined with discriminative models for structure-classification benchmarks. This connects probabilistic representation learning to the task of assigning classes to graph structures. The contribution is a layered generative approach to graph processing, with context diffusion linking local graph elements to the encodings used for classification.
summary.tldr: The Contextual Graph Markov Model builds graph encodings through probabilistic layers that propagate context for subsequent classification.

title: Contextual Graph Markov Model: A Deep and Generative Approach to Graph Processing

abstract: We present a framework to compose artificial neural networks in cases where the data cannot be treated as independent events. Our particular motivation is star galaxy classification for ground based optical surveys. Due to a turbulent atmosphere and imperfect instruments, a single image of an astronomical object is not enough to definitively classify it as a star or galaxy. Instead the context of the surrounding objects imaged at the same time need to be considered in order to make an optimal classification. The model we present is divided into three distinct ANNs: one designed to capture local features about each object, the second to compare these features across all objects in an image, and the third to make a final prediction for each object based on the local and compared features. By exploiting the ability to replicate the weights of an ANN, the model can handle an arbitrary and variable number of individual objects embedded in a larger exposure. We train and test our model on simulations of a large up and coming ground based survey, the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST). We compare to the state of the art approach, showing improved overall performance as well as better performance for a specific class of objects that is important for the LSST.

An isolated image of an object may not settle its identity. Other objects captured in the same exposure supply relevant context because the classification problem involves observations that cannot simply be treated as independent.

The framework divides the task among three neural networks. One extracts features from each object, another compares features across the objects in an exposure, and a third combines local and comparative information to classify each object. Sharing network weights allows the same composition to accommodate exposures containing different, arbitrary numbers of objects.

The authors train and evaluate the framework using simulations for the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope. Compared with the stated leading approach, they report better overall performance and improvements for a particular object class important to the survey. These results support using exposure-level context alongside individual appearance in this simulated classification setting.
summary.tldr: ContextNet improves simulated star–galaxy classification by combining each object’s features with information from other objects in the same exposure.

title: ContextNet: Deep learning for Star Galaxy Classification

abstract: Statistical learning relies upon data sampled from a distribution, and we usually do not care what actually generated it in the first place. From the point of view of causal modeling, the structure of each distribution is induced by physical mechanisms that give rise to dependences between observables. Mechanisms, however, can be meaningful autonomous modules of generative models that make sense beyond a particular entailed data distribution, lending themselves to transfer between problems. We develop an algorithm to recover a set of independent (inverse) mechanisms from a set of transformed data points. The approach is unsupervised and based on a set of experts that compete for data generated by the mechanisms, driving specialization. We analyze the proposed method in a series of experiments on image data. Each expert learns to map a subset of the transformed data back to a reference distribution. The learned mechanisms generalize to novel domains. We discuss implications for transfer learning and links to recent trends in generative modeling.

paragraphs: A data distribution reflects the processes that generated its observations. This paper explores whether learning those processes as separate mechanisms can produce components that remain useful beyond one particular distribution. Its focus is on recovering inverse mechanisms from transformed data: operations that map examples back toward a reference distribution.

The proposed unsupervised algorithm uses multiple experts that compete for the transformed examples. Competition drives specialization, with each expert learning to reverse transformations for a subset of the data. This provides a way to divide the recovery problem among distinct learned mechanisms without requiring supervised assignments of examples to experts.

Experiments on image data show each expert learning a mapping back to the reference distribution, and the learned mechanisms generalize to novel domains. These findings support the idea that a transformation mechanism can be useful outside the particular data on which it was learned. The authors discuss how this modular view connects to transfer learning and generative modeling, where reusable components may help organize what a model learns.
summary.tldr: Competing unsupervised experts learn specialized inverse transformations that generalize to new image domains.

title: Learning Independent Causal Mechanisms

abstract: Adaptive regularization methods pre-multiply a descent direction by a preconditioning matrix. Due to the large number of parameters of machine learning problems, full-matrix preconditioning methods are prohibitively expensive. We show how to modify full-matrix adaptive regularization in order to make it practical and effective. We also provide a novel theoretical analysis for adaptive regularization in non-convex optimization settings. The core of our algorithm, termed GGT, consists of the efficient computation of the inverse square root of a low-rank matrix. Our preliminary experiments show improved iteration-wise convergence rates across synthetic tasks and standard deep learning benchmarks, and that the more carefully-preconditioned steps sometimes lead to a better solution.

paragraphs: Adaptive regularization changes an optimizer’s descent direction using a preconditioning matrix. A full matrix can adjust the direction jointly across parameters, but handling such a matrix becomes prohibitively expensive when a model has many parameters. This paper asks how to retain a useful form of full-matrix adaptation while making its computation practical.

The proposed algorithm, GGT, centers on efficiently computing the inverse square root of a low-rank matrix. That calculation provides the computational foundation for the modified adaptive regularization method. The paper also develops a theoretical analysis for nonconvex optimization, connecting the algorithmic design to the kind of objectives encountered in deep learning.

Preliminary experiments on synthetic tasks and standard deep learning benchmarks show faster convergence when measured by optimization iterations. The more carefully adjusted steps also sometimes produce a better final solution. These are qualified findings: better progress per iteration is the reported convergence benefit, and improved solution quality occurs in some cases. Together, they suggest that making richer preconditioning affordable can change both training progress and the solution reached.
summary.tldr: GGT makes full-matrix adaptive regularization practical through low-rank computation, with preliminary evidence of faster iteration-wise convergence and sometimes better solutions.

title: Efficient Full-Matrix Adaptive Regularization

abstract: In this paper, we study the prediction of a real-valued target, such as a risk score or recidivism rate, while guaranteeing a quantitative notion of fairness with respect to a protected attribute such as gender or race. We call this class of problems fair regression. We propose general schemes for fair regression under two notions of fairness: (1) statistical parity, which asks that the prediction be statistically independent of the protected attribute, and (2) bounded group loss, which asks that the prediction error restricted to any protected group remain below some pre-determined level. While we only study these two notions of fairness, our schemes are applicable to arbitrary Lipschitz-continuous losses, and so they encompass least-squares regression, logistic regression, quantile regression, and many other tasks. Our schemes only require access to standard risk minimization algorithms (such as standard classification or least-squares regression) while providing theoretical guarantees on the optimality and fairness of the obtained solutions. In addition to analyzing theoretical properties of our schemes, we empirically demonstrate their ability to uncover fairness–accuracy frontiers on several standard datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to predict numerical outcomes while satisfying quantitative fairness requirements concerning a protected attribute. Examples include risk scores and recidivism rates. The central problem is to make fairness an explicit constraint on learning, so that a solution can be assessed for both predictive performance and the chosen fairness criterion.

The authors consider two different criteria. Statistical parity requires predictions to be statistically independent of the protected attribute. Bounded group loss instead requires prediction error within each protected group to stay below a chosen threshold. These criteria address different properties of a predictor: one concerns the distribution of its outputs, while the other concerns errors within groups.

The proposed schemes use standard risk-minimization algorithms as components and provide theoretical guarantees for optimality and fairness. They support arbitrary Lipschitz-continuous losses, covering tasks such as least-squares, logistic, and quantile regression. Experiments on several standard datasets show that the schemes can trace fairness–accuracy frontiers. These frontiers expose the attainable tradeoffs under the specified fairness definition rather than reducing fairness to a single unqualified label.
summary.tldr: Reduction-based algorithms reuse standard learning methods to fit numerical predictors with guarantees under statistical parity or bounded group loss.

title: Fair Regression: Quantitative Definitions and Reduction-Based Algorithms

abstract: We show how to turn any classifier that classifies well under Gaussian noise into a new classifier that is certifiably robust to adversarial perturbations under the L2 norm. While this "randomized smoothing" technique has been proposed before in the literature, we are the first to provide a tight analysis, which establishes a close connection between L2 robustness and Gaussian noise. We use the technique to train an ImageNet classifier with e.g. a certified top-1 accuracy of 49% under adversarial perturbations with L2 norm less than 0.5 (=127/255). Smoothing is the only approach to certifiably robust classification which has been shown feasible on full-resolution ImageNet. On smaller-scale datasets where competing approaches to certified L2 robustness are viable, smoothing delivers higher certified accuracies. The empirical success of the approach suggests that provable methods based on randomization at prediction time are a promising direction for future research into adversarially robust classification.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness asks whether a classifier's predictions remain reliable when its input is deliberately perturbed. This paper studies randomized smoothing, which transforms a classifier that performs well under Gaussian noise into a classifier with provable robustness against perturbations measured by the L2 norm. The quality of the underlying classifier under noise is central to this construction.

The main theoretical contribution is a tight analysis of smoothing, establishing a close relationship between Gaussian noise and L2 robustness. This matters because a certificate provides a guarantee within a specified perturbation size, giving a stronger kind of evidence than performance against a particular collection of attacks.

The authors train an ImageNet classifier with a reported certified top-1 accuracy of 49% for perturbations with L2 norm below 0.5. They also report higher certified accuracies on smaller datasets where competing certification approaches are feasible. These results support prediction-time randomization as a promising route to scalable certified robustness, with the guarantees specifically tied to the stated perturbation norm and radius.
summary.tldr: A tight analysis of randomized smoothing turns Gaussian-noise classification performance into scalable certificates of L2 adversarial robustness.

title: Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing

abstract: Motivated by the repeated sale of online ads via auctions, optimal pricing in repeated auctions has attracted a large body of research. While dynamic mechanisms offer powerful techniques to improve on both revenue and efficiency by optimizing auctions across different items, their reliance on exact distributional information of buyers’ valuations (present and future) limits their use in practice. In this paper, we propose robust dynamic mechanism design. We develop a new framework to design dynamic mechanisms that are robust to both estimation errors in value distributions and strategic behavior. We apply the framework in learning environments, leading to the first policy that achieves provably low regret against the optimal dynamic mechanism in contextual auctions, where the dynamic benchmark has full and accurate distributional information.

paragraphs: Repeated auctions, such as those used to sell online advertisements, create opportunities to optimize decisions across multiple sales. Dynamic mechanisms can improve revenue and efficiency by coordinating auctions across items. Their practical usefulness is constrained, however, by reliance on exact information about the distributions of buyers' present and future valuations.

The paper proposes a framework for robust dynamic mechanism design that addresses both inaccurate distribution estimates and strategic buyer behavior. These are two sources of difficulty that a learning auction policy must handle together. The framework aims to preserve the benefits of dynamic design while accounting for uncertainty in the information used to construct the mechanism.

Applied to learning in contextual auctions, the framework yields what the authors identify as the first policy with provably low regret against the optimal dynamic mechanism. That benchmark has complete and accurate distributional information. The guarantee therefore compares a learning policy with an informed dynamic alternative, making the result stronger in scope than a comparison restricted to a simpler static auction benchmark.
summary.tldr: A robust dynamic-auction framework enables a learning policy with low regret against a fully informed optimal dynamic mechanism.

title: Robust Pricing in Dynamic Mechanism Design

abstract: Black-box variational inference tries to approximate a complex target distribution through a gradient-based optimization of the parameters of a simpler distribution. Provable convergence guarantees require structural properties of the objective. This paper shows that for location-scale family approximations, if the target is M-Lipschitz smooth, then so is the “energy” part of the variational objective. The key proof idea is to describe gradients in a certain inner-product space, thus permitting the use of Bessel’s inequality. This result gives bounds on the location of the optimal parameters, and is a key ingredient for convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Black-box variational inference approximates a difficult target distribution by adjusting the parameters of a simpler distribution through gradient-based optimization. To prove that this optimization converges, one needs structural information about its objective. This paper establishes a smoothness property for an important part of that objective.

The result applies to approximations from a location-scale family. If the target satisfies M-Lipschitz smoothness, the energy portion of the variational objective has the same smoothness constant. In practical terms, the result controls how sharply its gradient can change as the approximation parameters change. The guarantee is conditional on the target's smoothness and concerns the energy component specifically.

The proof represents gradients in a suitable inner-product space and applies Bessel's inequality. Beyond the smoothness statement, the analysis gives bounds on where optimal parameters can lie. These results supply a key ingredient for convergence guarantees, connecting a property of the target distribution to the optimization problem used to approximate it.
summary.tldr: For location-scale approximations, target smoothness transfers to the variational energy objective and helps support convergence analysis.

title: Provable Smoothness Guarantees for Black-Box Variational Inference

abstract: Recent advancements in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) enable the generation of highly realistic images, raising concerns about their misuse for malicious purposes. Detecting these GAN-generated images (GAN-images) becomes increasingly challenging due to the significant reduction of underlying artifacts and specific patterns. The absence of such traces can hinder detection algorithms from identifying GAN-images and transferring knowledge to identify other types of GAN-images as well. In this work, we present the Transferable GAN-images Detection framework T-GD, a robust transferable framework for an effective detection of GAN-images. T-GD is composed of a teacher and a student model that can iteratively teach and evaluate each other to improve the detection performance. First, we train the teacher model on the source dataset and use it as a starting point for learning the target dataset. To train the student model, we inject noise by mixing up the source and target datasets, while constraining the weight variation to preserve the starting point. Our approach is a self-training method, but distinguishes itself from prior approaches by focusing on improving the transferability of GAN-image detection. T-GD achieves high performance on the source dataset by overcoming catastrophic forgetting and effectively detecting state-of-the-art GAN-images with only a small volume of data without any metadata information.

paragraphs: As GAN-generated images become more realistic, the artifacts that help detectors recognize them become less obvious. A detector may also struggle to transfer what it learned about one kind of generated image to another. T-GD addresses this transfer problem through a teacher-and-student framework designed to improve detection while preserving earlier knowledge.

The teacher first learns from a source dataset and provides the starting point for learning on a target dataset. Student training introduces noise by mixing source and target data, while constraining changes in the weights to retain that starting point. Teacher and student then iteratively teach and evaluate one another within a self-training process.

The authors report strong performance on the source data while overcoming catastrophic forgetting, together with effective detection of state-of-the-art GAN images using a small amount of data and no metadata. The method’s distinguishing focus is transferring detection knowledge. Its training design connects adaptation to new generated images with preservation of the detector’s ability on the source dataset.
summary.tldr: T-GD uses teacher-student self-training to transfer GAN-image detection to new data while preserving performance on the source dataset.

title: T-GD: Transferable GAN-generated Images Detection Framework

abstract: Bias in machine learning has manifested injustice in several areas, such as medicine, hiring, and criminal justice. In response, computer scientists have developed myriad definitions of fairness to correct this bias in fielded algorithms. While some definitions are based on established legal and ethical norms, others are largely mathematical. It is unclear whether the general public agrees with these fairness definitions, and perhaps more importantly, whether they understand these definitions. We take initial steps toward bridging this gap between ML researchers and the public, by addressing the question: does a lay audience understand a basic definition of ML fairness? We develop a metric to measure comprehension of three such definitions–demographic parity, equal opportunity, and equalized odds. We evaluate this metric using an online survey, and investigate the relationship between comprehension and sentiment, demographics, and the definition itself.

Some definitions draw on legal or ethical ideas, while others are primarily mathematical. This paper asks whether people outside the field understand basic fairness definitions.

The authors develop a metric for measuring comprehension of three definitions: demographic parity, equal opportunity, and equalized odds. They evaluate that metric through an online survey. They also investigate how comprehension relates to respondents’ sentiment, their demographics, and the particular fairness definition being presented.

The contribution is a way to study understanding as a distinct part of the relationship between technical fairness research and the public. Agreement with a definition and comprehension of it are different questions, and the study examines factors associated with comprehension. The abstract presents this as an initial step toward connecting researchers and non-experts; it does not report which definition was best understood or which demographic groups performed differently. Its stated contribution centers on measurement and the survey investigation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates a survey-based measure of non-experts’ understanding of three machine learning fairness definitions.

title: Measuring Non-Expert Comprehension of Machine Learning Fairness Metrics

abstract: To scale up data analysis, distributed and parallel computing approaches are increasingly needed. Here we study a fundamental problem in this area: How to do ridge regression in a distributed computing environment? We study one-shot methods constructing weighted combinations of ridge regression estimators computed on each machine. By analyzing the mean squared error in a high dimensional model where each predictor has a small effect, we discover several new phenomena including that the efficiency depends strongly on the signal strength, but does not degrade with many workers, the risk decouples over machines, and the unexpected consequence that the optimal weights do not sum to unity. We also propose a new optimally weighted one-shot ridge regression algorithm. Our results are supported by simulations and real data analysis.

We also propose a new optimally weighted one-shot ridge regression algorithm. Our results are supported by simulations and real data analysis.

paragraphs: Distributed ridge regression allows separate machines to fit estimators on their data and then combine the results. This paper studies one-shot methods that form a weighted combination of those local estimators. The question is how to choose the combination well when the data are high-dimensional, so that distributing the computation remains statistically effective.

The analysis examines mean squared error in a model where each predictor has a small effect. Within that setting, efficiency depends strongly on signal strength but does not deteriorate with many workers, and the risk separates across machines. Another finding is that the optimal combination weights do not sum to one, so the best combination is not a conventional weighted average.

Using these results, the authors propose an optimally weighted one-shot ridge regression algorithm. Simulations and real-data analysis support their findings. The contribution shows that aggregation deserves its own statistical design: local estimators can be combined more effectively by accounting for signal strength and the structure of the high-dimensional risk.
summary.tldr: High-dimensional risk analysis yields an optimally weighted distributed ridge estimator whose weights need not sum to one.

title: One-shot Distributed Ridge Regression in High Dimensions

abstract: Stochastic linear bandits are a natural and well-studied model for structured exploration/exploitation problems and are widely used in applications such as on-line marketing and recommendation. One of the main challenges faced by practitioners hoping to apply existing algorithms is that usually the feedback is randomly delayed and delays are only partially observable. For example, while a purchase is usually observable some time after the display, the decision of not buying is never explicitly sent to the system. In other words, the learner only observes delayed positive events. We formalize this problem as a novel stochastic delayed linear bandit and propose OTFLinUCB and OTFLinTS, two computationally efficient algorithms able to integrate new information as it becomes available and to deal with the permanently censored feedback. We prove optimal O(d\sqrt{T}) bounds on the regret of the first algorithm and study the dependency on delay-dependent parameters. Our model, assumptions and results are validated by experiments on simulated and real data.

paragraphs: In recommendation and online marketing, feedback may arrive long after an action, and some outcomes never produce an explicit signal. A purchase might eventually be recorded, while a decision not to buy remains unreported. This paper models that combination of random delay and permanently missing negative feedback using stochastic linear bandits.

The authors introduce OTFLinUCB and OTFLinTS, two computationally efficient algorithms that incorporate information as it arrives. Their design addresses the fact that an absent event can mean either that feedback is still delayed or that no positive event will occur. This makes partially observable delays central to the learning problem.

For OTFLinUCB, the paper proves an optimal regret bound of order d times the square root of T, with d representing dimension and T the time horizon, and examines dependence on delay-related parameters. Experiments with simulated and real data support the model, assumptions, and results. The contribution brings structured exploration to a feedback pattern that ordinary immediate-observation formulations do not capture.
summary.tldr: Two efficient linear-bandit algorithms handle randomly delayed positive feedback and permanently censored outcomes, with an optimal regret bound for OTFLinUCB.

title: Linear bandits with Stochastic Delayed Feedback

abstract: We propose a new algorithmic framework for learning autoencoders of data distributions. In this framework, we minimize the discrepancy between the model distribution and the target one, with relational regularization on learnable latent prior. This regularization penalizes the fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) distance between the latent prior and its corresponding posterior, which allows us to learn a structured prior distribution associated with the generative model in a flexible way. Moreover, it helps us co-train multiple autoencoders even if they are with heterogeneous architectures and incomparable latent spaces. We implement the framework with two scalable algorithms, making it applicable for both probabilistic and deterministic autoencoders. Our relational regularized autoencoder (RAE) outperforms existing methods, e.g., variational autoencoder, Wasserstein autoencoder, and their variants, on generating images. Additionally, our relational co-training strategy of autoencoders achieves encouraging results in both synthesis and real-world multi-view learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops an autoencoder framework that learns a structured latent prior alongside a generative model. Training aims to reduce the discrepancy between the generated distribution and the target data distribution, while also regularizing the relationship between the latent prior and its corresponding posterior.

The regularizer penalizes fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance between those latent distributions. This relational formulation provides flexibility in learning the prior and supports joint training of multiple autoencoders, even when their architectures differ and their latent spaces are not directly comparable. The authors implement the framework through two scalable algorithms covering both probabilistic and deterministic autoencoders.

For image generation, the relationally regularized autoencoder outperforms variational autoencoders, Wasserstein autoencoders, and variants in the reported experiments. The co-training strategy also produces encouraging results on synthetic and real-world multi-view learning tasks. Together, these findings support two uses of the same framework: improving an individual generative model and coordinating models whose internal representations do not share a directly comparable space.
summary.tldr: Relational regularization learns structured latent priors and enables co-training of autoencoders with different architectures and incomparable latent spaces.

title: Learning Autoencoders with Relational Regularization

abstract: We study problems where a learner aims to learn the valuations of an agent by observing which goods he buys under varying price vectors. More specifically, we consider the case of a $k$-demand agent, whose valuation over the goods is additive when receiving up to $k$ goods, but who has no interest in receiving more than $k$ goods. We settle the query complexity for the active-learning (preference elicitation) version, where the learner chooses the prices to post, by giving a \emph{biased binary search} algorithm, generalizing the classical binary search procedure. We complement our query complexity upper bounds by lower bounds that match up to lower-order terms. We also study the passive-learning version in which the learner does not control the prices, and instead they are sampled from some distribution. We show that in the PAC model for passive learning, any \emph{empirical risk minimizer} has a sample complexity that is optimal up to a factor of $\widetilde{O}(k)$.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer a buyer’s valuations by observing purchases under different prices. The buyer is a k-demand agent: values add across goods when receiving at most k items, but the buyer has no interest in additional items beyond that limit. This restriction gives the learning problem a specific structure.

In the active-learning version, the learner chooses the prices and observes the resulting purchases. The authors introduce a biased binary search algorithm that generalizes ordinary binary search to this preference-elicitation problem. They establish upper bounds on the number of queries and complementary lower bounds that match up to lower-order terms, settling the query complexity at that precision.

The passive version removes control over prices, which instead come from a distribution. In the probably approximately correct learning model, the authors show that any empirical risk minimizer has sample complexity within a factor of approximately k, allowing logarithmic factors, of optimal. The results distinguish what can be learned through deliberate price experiments from what can be learned through observation.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes near-matching learning bounds for inferring a k-demand buyer’s valuations from actively chosen or passively observed prices.

title: Learning the Valuations of a $k$-demand Agent

abstract: Transfer in reinforcement learning is usually achieved through generalisation across tasks. Whilst many studies have investigated transferring knowledge when the reward function changes, they have assumed that the dynamics of the environments remain consistent. Many real-world RL problems require transfer among environments with different dynamics. To address this problem, we propose an approach based on successor features in which we model successor feature functions with Gaussian Processes permitting the source successor features to be treated as noisy measurements of the target successor feature function. Our theoretical analysis proves the convergence of this approach as well as the bounded error on modelling successor feature functions with Gaussian Processes in environments with both different dynamics and rewards. We demonstrate our method on benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms current baselines.

Our theoretical analysis proves the convergence of this approach as well as the bounded error on modelling successor feature functions with Gaussian Processes in environments with both different dynamics and rewards. We demonstrate our method on benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms current baselines.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning transfer often considers a new reward function while keeping the environment's dynamics unchanged. Many practical transfer problems also change how actions affect the environment. This paper develops a successor-feature approach for that broader situation, aiming to reuse information even when both dynamics and rewards differ between source and target environments.

The authors model successor feature functions with Gaussian processes. The central move is to treat source successor features as noisy measurements of the target function. This gives transferred information a role without treating it as an exact description of the new environment. The representation explicitly accommodates the mismatch that makes transfer across different dynamics difficult.

The theoretical analysis establishes convergence and bounds the error of the Gaussian process modeling approach in environments with different dynamics and rewards. Benchmark experiments also report performance above current baselines. These contributions address complementary questions: the analysis supports the method's mathematical behavior, while the experiments demonstrate its usefulness on the evaluated tasks. The stated advance is transfer beyond the shared-dynamics setting considered by much earlier work.
summary.tldr: Gaussian process modeling treats source successor features as noisy target information, enabling reinforcement learning transfer across changes in both dynamics and rewards.

title: A New Representation of Successor Features for Transfer across Dissimilar Environments

abstract: Online advertisements are primarily sold via repeated auctions with reserve prices. In this paper, we study how to set reserves to boost revenue based on the historical bids of strategic buyers, while controlling the impact of such a policy on the incentive compatibility of the repeated auctions. Adopting an incentive compatibility metric which quantifies the incentives to shade bids, we propose a novel class of reserve pricing policies and provide analytical tradeoffs between their revenue performance and bid-shading incentives. The policies are inspired by the exponential mechanism from the literature on differential privacy, but our study uncovers mechanisms with significantly better revenue-incentive tradeoffs than the exponential mechanism in practice. We further empirically evaluate the tradeoffs on synthetic data as well as real ad auction data from a major ad exchange to verify and support our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Repeated advertising auctions can adjust reserve prices using past bids to improve revenue. Strategic buyers, however, may have incentives to shade their bids when those bids influence future pricing. This paper studies how a reserve-price policy can balance revenue gains against the incentive effects it creates across repeated auctions.

The authors adopt a metric that quantifies incentives to shade bids and propose a class of reserve-pricing policies. They derive analytical tradeoffs between revenue performance and that incentive measure. The policies take inspiration from the exponential mechanism in differential privacy, using it as a starting point for designing pricing rules.

The study identifies mechanisms with substantially better practical revenue-incentive tradeoffs than the exponential mechanism itself. Experiments use both synthetic data and real advertising-auction data from a major exchange to support the theoretical findings. The contribution makes the tension between revenue and strategic response explicit, providing policies whose behavior can be assessed along both dimensions instead of evaluating revenue alone.
summary.tldr: New dynamic reserve-price policies offer analytically characterized tradeoffs between auction revenue and buyers’ incentives to shade bids.

title: Revenue-Incentive Tradeoffs in Dynamic Reserve Pricing

abstract: Recent exploration methods have proven to be a recipe for improving sample-efficiency in deep reinforcement learning (RL). However, efficient exploration in high-dimensional observation spaces still remains a challenge. This paper presents Random Encoders for Efficient Exploration (RE3), an exploration method that utilizes state entropy as an intrinsic reward. In order to estimate state entropy in environments with high-dimensional observations, we utilize a k-nearest neighbor entropy estimator in the low-dimensional representation space of a convolutional encoder. In particular, we find that the state entropy can be estimated in a stable and compute-efficient manner by utilizing a randomly initialized encoder, which is fixed throughout training. Our experiments show that RE3 significantly improves the sample-efficiency of both model-free and model-based RL methods on locomotion and navigation tasks from DeepMind Control Suite and MiniGrid benchmarks. We also show that RE3 allows learning diverse behaviors without extrinsic rewards, effectively improving sample-efficiency in downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Exploration in reinforcement learning becomes difficult when observations are high dimensional. RE3 encourages broader exploration by using state entropy as an intrinsic reward: the learner receives an internal incentive related to the diversity of states it visits. The challenge is estimating that diversity efficiently from complex observations.

The method maps observations into a lower-dimensional space using a convolutional encoder and applies a nearest-neighbor entropy estimator there. Its distinctive choice is to initialize the encoder randomly and keep it fixed throughout training. The authors find that this provides stable, computationally efficient entropy estimates, so the exploration signal does not require learning and continually updating the encoder.

Experiments show significant improvements in sample efficiency for both model-free and model-based reinforcement learning on locomotion and navigation tasks from DeepMind Control Suite and MiniGrid. RE3 also learns diverse behaviors without external rewards, which improves sample efficiency on downstream tasks. The findings demonstrate that a fixed random representation can be useful for driving exploration in the evaluated environments.
summary.tldr: RE3 estimates state diversity with a fixed random encoder and uses it as an intrinsic reward to improve exploration efficiency.

title: State Entropy Maximization with Random Encoders for Efficient Exploration

abstract: In fully cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) settings, the environments are highly stochastic due to the partial observability of each agent and the continuously changing policies of the other agents. To address the above issues, we integrate distributional RL and value function factorization methods by proposing a Distributional Value Function Factorization (DFAC) framework to generalize expected value function factorization methods to their distributional variants. DFAC extends the individual utility functions from deterministic variables to random variables, and models the quantile function of the total return as a quantile mixture. To validate DFAC, we demonstrate DFAC’s ability to factorize a simple two-step matrix game with stochastic rewards and perform experiments on all Super Hard tasks of StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge, showing that DFAC is able to outperform expected value function factorization baselines.

To address the above issues, we integrate distributional RL and value function factorization methods by proposing a Distributional Value Function Factorization (DFAC) framework to generalize expected value function factorization methods to their distributional variants. DFAC extends the individual utility functions from deterministic variables to random variables, and models the quantile function of the total return as a quantile mixture. paragraphs: In fully cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents work toward a shared outcome while each sees only part of the environment. Their policies also change during learning, adding uncertainty to the outcomes each agent experiences. This paper addresses that uncertainty by combining distributional reinforcement learning with methods that factor a team value function into individual utilities.

The Distributional Value Function Factorization framework, or DFAC, extends individual utilities from single deterministic values to random variables. It represents the quantile function of the team’s total return through a mixture of quantiles. This provides a way to extend factorization methods based on expected returns so that they can model distributions of returns.

The authors demonstrate the framework on a two-step matrix game with stochastic rewards and evaluate it on every Super Hard task in the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge. They report better performance than expected-value factorization baselines. The results support the usefulness of incorporating return distributions into cooperative value factorization when agents face uncertain outcomes and incomplete observations.
summary.tldr: DFAC extends cooperative multi-agent value factorization to return distributions using a quantile mixture.

title: DFAC Framework: Factorizing the Value Function via Quantile Mixture for Multi-Agent Distributional Q-Learning

abstract: We introduce repriorisation, a data-dependent reparameterisation which transforms a Bayesian neural network (BNN) posterior to a distribution whose KL divergence to the BNN prior vanishes as layer widths grow. The repriorisation map acts directly on parameters, and its analytic simplicity complements the known neural network Gaussian process (NNGP) behaviour of wide BNNs in function space. Exploiting the repriorisation, we develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) posterior sampling algorithm which mixes faster the wider the BNN. This contrasts with the typically poor performance of MCMC in high dimensions. We observe up to 50x higher effective sample size relative to no reparametrisation for both fully-connected and residual networks. Improvements are achieved at all widths, with the margin between reparametrised and standard BNNs growing with layer width.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty through distributions over their weights, but sampling from the posterior can be difficult. This paper introduces repriorisation, a data-dependent change of parameter coordinates. In the transformed representation, the posterior’s KL divergence from the network prior tends to zero as layer widths grow, giving a simple description of the wide-network limit in parameter space.

This result complements the known Gaussian-process description of wide networks in function space. The authors use the parameter transformation to develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling algorithm. Its mixing improves as the network becomes wider, an unusual outcome given the difficulties MCMC commonly faces as dimensionality increases.

Experiments with fully connected and residual networks show up to 50 times higher effective sample size than sampling without reparameterization. Improvements occur at every width tested, and the advantage grows with layer width. The asymptotic theoretical result and the finite-network experiments jointly support changing parameter coordinates as a practical route to more effective Bayesian posterior sampling.
summary.tldr: Repriorisation simplifies wide Bayesian neural-network posteriors in transformed coordinates and accelerates MCMC sampling, with gains increasing with width.

title: Wide Bayesian neural networks have a simple weight posterior: theory and accelerated sampling

abstract: Data poisoning attacks aim at manipulating model behaviors through distorting training data. Previously, an aggregation-based certified defense, Deep Partition Aggregation (DPA), was proposed to mitigate this threat. DPA predicts through an aggregation of base classifiers trained on disjoint subsets of data, thus restricting its sensitivity to dataset distortions. In this work, we propose an improved certified defense against general poisoning attacks, namely Finite Aggregation. In contrast to DPA, which directly splits the training set into disjoint subsets, our method first splits the training set into smaller disjoint subsets and then combines duplicates of them to build larger (but not disjoint) subsets for training base classifiers. This reduces the worst-case impacts of poison samples and thus improves certified robustness bounds. In addition, we offer an alternative view of our method, bridging the designs of deterministic and stochastic aggregation-based certified defenses. Empirically, our proposed Finite Aggregation consistently improves certificates on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and GTSRB, boosting certified fractions by up to 3.05%, 3.87% and 4.77%, respectively, while keeping the same clean accuracies as DPA’s, effectively establishing a new state of the art in (pointwise) certified robustness against data poisoning.

In this work, we propose an improved certified defense against general poisoning attacks, namely Finite Aggregation. Empirically, our proposed Finite Aggregation consistently improves certificates on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and GTSRB, boosting certified fractions by up to 3.05%, 3.87% and 4.77%, respectively, while keeping the same clean accuracies as DPA’s, effectively establishing a new state of the art in (pointwise) certified robustness against data poisoning.

paragraphs: Data poisoning changes training data to influence a model’s behavior. Deep Partition Aggregation addresses this threat by training separate classifiers on disjoint data subsets and combining their predictions. Partitioning restricts how dataset distortions can affect the ensemble, allowing robustness guarantees for individual predictions.

The proposed Finite Aggregation changes how those training subsets are constructed. It first divides the data into smaller disjoint pieces, then combines duplicates of these pieces into larger, overlapping subsets for the base classifiers. This construction reduces the worst-case impact of poisoned examples and strengthens the certified robustness bounds. The authors also connect the method to both deterministic and stochastic aggregation defenses.

On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and GTSRB, the method consistently improves certificates while maintaining DPA’s clean accuracies. The reported increases in certified fractions reach 3.05%, 3.87%, and 4.77%, respectively. These gains concern provable protection at the individual-prediction level, showing that reorganizing the ensemble’s training data can strengthen guarantees without sacrificing the reported clean-data accuracy.
summary.tldr: Finite Aggregation strengthens certified defenses against data poisoning by constructing overlapping classifier training sets from smaller disjoint data partitions.

title: Improved Certified Defenses against Data Poisoning with (Deterministic) Finite Aggregation

abstract: We study the autonomous exploration (AX) problem proposed by Lim & Auer (2012). In this setting, the objective is to discover a set of $\epsilon$-optimal policies reaching a set $\mathcal{S}_L^{\rightarrow}$ of incrementally $L$-controllable states. We introduce a novel layered decomposition of the set of incrementally $L$-controllable states that is based on the iterative application of a state-expansion operator. We leverage these results to design Layered Autonomous Exploration (LAE), a novel algorithm for AX that attains a sample complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(LS^{\rightarrow}_{L(1+\epsilon)}\Gamma_{L(1+\epsilon)} A \ln^{12}(S^{\rightarrow}_{L(1+\epsilon)})/\epsilon^2)$, where $S^{\rightarrow}_{L(1+\epsilon)}$ is the number of states that are incrementally $L(1+\epsilon)$-controllable, $A$ is the number of actions, and $\Gamma_{L(1+\epsilon)}$ is the branching factor of the transitions over such states. LAE improves over the algorithm of Tarbouriech et al. (2020a) by a factor of $L^2$ and it is the first algorithm for AX that works in a countably-infinite state space. Moreover, we show that, under a certain identifiability assumption, LAE achieves minimax-optimal sample complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(LS^{\rightarrow}_{L}A\ln^{12}(S^{\rightarrow}_{L})/\epsilon^2)$, outperforming existing algorithms and matching for the first time the lower bound proved by Cai et al. (2022) up to logarithmic factors.

We leverage these results to design Layered Autonomous Exploration (LAE), a novel algorithm for AX that attains a sample complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(LS^{\rightarrow}_{L(1+\epsilon)}\Gamma_{L(1+\epsilon)} A \ln^{12}(S^{\rightarrow}_{L(1+\epsilon)})/\epsilon^2)$, where $S^{\rightarrow}_{L(1+\epsilon)}$ is the number of states that are incrementally $L(1+\epsilon)$-controllable, $A$ is the number of actions, and $\Gamma_{L(1+\epsilon)}$ is the branching factor of the transitions over such states. LAE improves over the algorithm of Tarbouriech et al. (2020a) by a factor of $L^2$ and it is the first algorithm for AX that works in a countably-infinite state space. Moreover, we show that, under a certain identifiability assumption, LAE achieves minimax-optimal sample complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(LS^{\rightarrow}_{L}A\ln^{12}(S^{\rightarrow}_{L})/\epsilon^2)$, outperforming existing algorithms and matching for the first time the lower bound proved by Cai et al. (2022) up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Autonomous exploration here means discovering policies that reach incrementally controllable states with a specified accuracy. The paper organizes those states into layers through repeated application of a state-expansion operator. This decomposition provides the structure for Layered Autonomous Exploration, or LAE, linking incremental discovery to a provable sample-complexity bound.

The general bound depends on the reachability parameter L, the number of relevant controllable states, the number of actions, the transition branching factor, and the inverse square of the accuracy tolerance, along with logarithmic factors. LAE improves the compared algorithm's bound by a factor of L squared. It is also presented as the first algorithm for this exploration problem that supports countably infinite state spaces.

Under an additional identifiability assumption, the authors establish a stronger bound that is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. This conditional result matches an existing lower bound and removes the branching factor from the displayed expression. The layered formulation thus supports both broader state-space coverage and sharper guarantees about the samples required for exploration.
summary.tldr: LAE uses layered state discovery to improve autonomous exploration bounds, with near-optimal sample complexity under an identifiability assumption.

title: Layered State Discovery for Incremental Autonomous Exploration

abstract: We study a $K$-armed bandit with delayed feedback and intermediate observations. We consider a model, where intermediate observations have a form of a finite state, which is observed immediately after taking an action, whereas the loss is observed after an adversarially chosen delay. We show that the regime of the mapping of states to losses determines the complexity of the problem, irrespective of whether the mapping of actions to states is stochastic or adversarial. If the mapping of states to losses is adversarial, then the regret rate is of order $\sqrt{(K+d)T}$ (within log factors), where $T$ is the time horizon and $d$ is a fixed delay. This matches the regret rate of a $K$-armed bandit with delayed feedback and without intermediate observations, implying that intermediate observations are not helpful. However, if the mapping of states to losses is stochastic, we show that the regret grows at a rate of $\sqrt{\bigl(K+\min\{|\mathcal{S}|,d\}\bigr)T}$ (within log factors), implying that if the number $|\mathcal{S}|$ of states is smaller than the delay, then intermediate observations help. We also provide refined high-probability regret upper bounds for non-uniform delays, together with experimental validation of our algorithms.

paragraphs: In a delayed bandit problem, a learner chooses among K actions but learns the resulting loss only later. This paper adds an immediate observation: a state from a finite collection. It asks whether that early signal can improve decisions while the final feedback remains delayed.

The answer depends on how states relate to losses, regardless of whether actions lead to states stochastically or adversarially. With adversarial state-to-loss relationships and fixed delay d, regret scales as the square root of (K + d)T, up to logarithmic factors. This matches the rate without intermediate observations, so those observations do not improve the regret rate in this regime.

When state-to-loss relationships are stochastic, the rate instead involves the smaller of the number of states and the delay. Intermediate observations therefore help when there are fewer states than delay steps. The paper also gives refined high-probability upper bounds for varying delays and experimentally validates its algorithms. The distinction identifies when immediate information has enough statistical structure to reduce the cost of waiting.
summary.tldr: Intermediate observations improve delayed-bandit regret rates when state-to-loss relationships are stochastic and the state count is smaller than the delay.

title: Delayed Bandits: When Do Intermediate Observations Help?

abstract: Large deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance across various natural language processing (NLP) tasks and demonstrated remarkable few-shot learning performance. However, training them is often challenging and resource-intensive. In this paper, we study an efficient approach to train language models using few-shot learners. We show that, by leveraging the fast learning nature of few-shot learners, one can train language models efficiently in a stagewise manner. Our main insight is that stacking a good few-shot learner on a good small language model provides a good initializer for a larger language model. Using this insight and building upon progressive stacking approaches, we develop novel approaches for training such networks in a stagewise manner. Furthermore, we also provide a theoretical framework and accompanying empirical studies to support our insights, thereby creating a theoretical foundation for progressive stacking. Finally, we provide empirical results to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reducing the training time of few-shot learners.

paragraphs: Large language models can learn effectively from few examples, yet training the models themselves is expensive. This paper investigates whether the fast-learning behavior of few-shot learners can help with that training cost. Its approach builds larger models in stages, using components that already provide a useful starting point for the next stage.

The central insight is that stacking a good few-shot learner on top of a good small language model can produce a good initialization for a larger language model. The authors use this idea to develop training methods based on progressive stacking. The quality of the smaller model and the added learner matters to the stated insight: the construction builds on capabilities already acquired by those components.

A theoretical framework and empirical studies support this view of initialization, giving progressive stacking a theoretical foundation. Further experiments demonstrate reduced training time for few-shot learners. The contribution therefore links a model’s ability to learn quickly with a strategy for constructing and training larger networks, making staged growth an explicit part of the training approach.
summary.tldr: The paper uses few-shot learners to initialize progressively larger language models, supporting staged training with theory and reported training-time reductions.

title: Efficient Training of Language Models using Few-Shot Learning

abstract: In this paper, we focus on mean-field variational Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) and explore the representation capacity of such BNNs by investigating which types of concepts are less likely to be encoded by the BNN. It has been observed and studied that a relatively small set of interactive concepts usually emerge in the knowledge representation of a sufficiently-trained neural network, and such concepts can faithfully explain the network output. Based on this, our study proves that compared to standard deep neural networks (DNNs), it is less likely for BNNs to encode complex concepts. Experiments verify our theoretical proofs. Note that the tendency to encode less complex concepts does not necessarily imply weak representation power, considering that complex concepts exhibit low generalization power and high adversarial vulnerability. The code is available at https://github.com/sjtu-xai-lab/BNN-concepts.

paragraphs: Neural networks can represent interactions among input features as concepts that help explain their outputs. This paper asks whether mean-field variational Bayesian neural networks favor different kinds of such concepts than standard deep networks. The focus is on what the representation tends to encode, rather than only its predictive accuracy.

Building on an interaction-based account of network representations, the authors prove that the Bayesian models are less likely to encode complex concepts. Experiments verify the theoretical findings. The analysis therefore identifies a representational preference associated with the particular Bayesian approximation being studied.

The authors argue that avoiding some complex concepts need not mean weak representation power, since these concepts can generalize poorly and be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. This makes the preference potentially useful rather than merely restrictive. The conclusion is specific to mean-field variational BNNs and the paper’s concept framework; it does not establish that every Bayesian model learns simpler or more robust representations in all settings.
summary.tldr: Mean-field variational Bayesian networks are less likely to encode complex interaction concepts than the compared standard networks.

title: Bayesian Neural Networks Avoid Encoding Complex and Perturbation-Sensitive Concepts

abstract: The size of deep neural networks has grown exponentially in recent years. Unfortunately, hardware devices have not kept pace with the rapidly increasing memory requirements. To cope with this, researchers have proposed various techniques including spilling, rematerialization, reduced precision training, model pruning, and so on. However, these approaches suffer from various limitations, such as increasing training time, affecting model accuracy, or requiring extensive manual modifications to the neural networks. We present MODeL, an algorithm that optimizes the lifetime and memory location of the tensors used to train neural networks. Our method automatically reduces the memory usage of existing neural networks without any of the drawbacks of other techniques. We formulate the problem as a joint integer linear program (ILP). We present several techniques to simplify the encoding of the problem, and enable our approach to scale to the size of state-of-the-art neural networks using an off-the-shelf ILP solver. We experimentally demonstrate that MODeL only takes seconds to allow the training of neural networks using 30% less memory on average.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks requires managing many tensors within limited device memory. Existing approaches can reduce memory demand through techniques such as spilling, recomputation, reduced precision, or pruning, but may add training time, affect accuracy, or require substantial manual changes. MODeL focuses on optimizing tensor lifetimes and memory locations automatically.

The method formulates these decisions jointly as an integer linear program. Treating them together allows the optimization to consider how tensor storage requirements interact during training. The authors introduce simplifications to the mathematical encoding so that an off-the-shelf solver can handle problems at the scale of state-of-the-art neural networks.

Experiments show that MODeL takes only seconds to enable training with 30% less memory on average. The authors report these savings without the drawbacks they identify in the alternative techniques. The stated reduction is an experimental average, rather than a guaranteed saving for each network. The contribution is a tractable joint optimization of memory use that can be applied to existing models automatically.
summary.tldr: MODeL jointly optimizes tensor lifetimes and storage locations, enabling training with 30% less memory on average in the reported experiments.

title: MODeL: Memory Optimizations for Deep Learning

abstract: We propose new techniques for reducing communication in private federated learning without the need for setting or tuning compression rates. Our on-the-fly methods automatically adjust the compression rate based on the error induced during training, while maintaining provable privacy guarantees through the use of secure aggregation and differential privacy. Our techniques are provably instance-optimal for mean estimation, meaning that they can adapt to the “hardness of the problem” with minimal interactivity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on real-world datasets by achieving favorable compression rates without the need for tuning.
