paragraphs: A model learning successive tasks can accumulate damage from poisoned data, potentially diverging or suffering large prediction errors. This paper analyzes attacks and defenses specifically for regularization-based continual learning. It models the interaction as an online zero-sum game, giving a formal setting for asking when successful defense is possible.

The first result establishes an impossibility boundary: no defense succeeds in this setting when an adversary poisons a linear proportion of tasks with unbounded noise or pattern shifts. The authors then examine two more restricted regimes that may admit defenses. These separate limited attack frequency from limited attack magnitude, clarifying which constraint makes a proposed defense relevant.

For infrequent attacks, a task-to-task verification mechanism detects poisoning and reduces accumulated bias to support convergence. For bounded noise per attack, a robust defense reduces sensitivity to poisoned features and provably accelerates convergence. Experiments on realistic tasks support the theory. summary.tldr: The paper establishes poisoning limits for regularization-based continual learning and develops defenses for infrequent attacks or bounded attack noise.

title: Theory of Continual Learning Against Data Poisoning Attacks

abstract: Linear Attention (LA) offers a promising paradigm for scaling large language models (LLMs) to long sequences by avoiding the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Recent LA models such as Mamba2 and GDN interpret linear recurrences as closed-form online stochastic gradient descent (SGD), but naive SGD updates suffer from rapid information decay and suboptimal convergence in optimization. While momentum-based optimizers provide a natural remedy, they pose challenges in simultaneously achieving training efficiency and effectiveness. To address this, we develop a chunkwise parallel algorithm for LA with a stepwise momentum rule by geometrically reordering the update coefficients. Further, from a dynamical systems perspective, we analyze the momentum-based recurrence as a second-order system that introduces complex conjugate eigenvalues. This analysis guides the design of stable gating constraints. The resulting model, Momentum DeltaNet (MDN), leverages Triton kernels to achieve comparable training throughput with competitive linear models such as Mamba2 and KDA. Extensive experiments on the 400M and 1.3B parameter models demonstrate consistent performance improvements over strong baselines, including Transformers, Mamba2 and GDN, across diverse downstream evaluation benchmarks. Code: https://github.com/HuuYuLong/MomentumDeltaNet.

title: MDN: Parallelizing Stepwise Momentum for Delta Linear Attention

abstract: In this paper, we provide a comprehensive convergence analysis for the Lion optimizer. First, we establish that the original Lion achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(d^{1/2}T^{-1/4})$, where $d$ denotes the problem dimension and $T$ is the iteration number. To improve this rate, we propose a variance reduction variant of Lion, which attains an enhanced rate of $\mathcal{O}(d^{1/2}T^{-1/3})$ with the average smoothness assumption. Then, we extend our analysis to distributed settings. We demonstrate that the distributed Lion optimizer and its variance reduction counterpart achieve linear speedup with respect to the number of nodes $n$, yielding convergence rates of $\mathcal{O}(d^{1/2}(nT)^{-1/4})$ and $\mathcal{O}(d^{1/2}(nT)^{-1/3})$, respectively. Additionally, we investigate a communication-efficient distributed Lion variant that utilizes sign compression for bidirectional communication. By employing unbiased sign operations, this variant achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O} \left( \max { \frac{d^{1/4}}{T^{1/4}}, \frac{d^{1/10}}{n^{1/5}T^{1/5}} } \right)$, and its variance-reduced counterpart can further improve the rate to $\mathcal{O}\left( \frac{d^{1/4}}{T^{1/4}} \right)$. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: This paper supplies convergence guarantees for Lion and several variants, explaining how their theoretical rates depend on problem dimension, iteration count, and distributed resources. For the original optimizer, the rate is O(d^(1/2) T^(-1/4)), where d is dimension and T is the number of iterations.

A variance-reduced variant improves the iteration dependence to T^(-1/3), retaining the same dimensional factor under an average smoothness assumption. The analysis then extends both methods to distributed training. With n nodes, their rates replace T with nT, establishing the stated linear speedup with respect to node count in these convergence bounds.

The authors also analyze a communication-efficient version that sends sign-compressed information in both directions. Using unbiased sign operations yields a bound with separate dependencies on dimension, iterations, and node count; variance reduction improves it to O(d^(1/4) T^(-1/4)). Numerical experiments support the proposed methods. Together, the results clarify how variance reduction, parallel computation, and compressed communication affect Lion’s optimization guarantees, with the stronger variance-reduced result explicitly tied to its additional smoothness assumption.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes convergence rates for Lion and shows how variance reduction, distributed computation, and sign compression change those guarantees.

title: Convergence Analysis of the Lion Optimizer in Centralized and Distributed Settings

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are regarded as the third generation of neural networks, offering energy-efficient computing for neuromorphic devices. Despite this benefit, hardware-implemented SNNs are vulnerable to hardware faults, which severely degrade their performance. Previous approaches have required direct access to internal SNN circuits to modify weights or monitor internal states, limiting their practicality. Improving robustness to hardware faults without such access remains challenging. To overcome this challenge, we propose a fault-tolerant mechanism that operates only through input data control. Hardware faults reduce the usable learning capacity of SNNs, resulting in a mismatch between the instantaneous input load and the degraded network dynamics. Our mechanism mitigates this mismatch by dividing each input sample into multiple fragments, redistributing the input load via a learnable fragmentation strategy. The strategy learns two key fragmentation components: 1) division boundaries and 2) the number of fragments. To our knowledge, this is the first mechanism to improve the fault tolerance of SNNs without accessing the internal circuits. Experimental results demonstrate that our mechanism consistently outperforms previous methods in various SNN models, achieving these gains without direct access to internal circuits. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness on SNNs implemented with a physical FPGA platform, confirming its practicality.

This paper develops a mechanism that operates entirely by controlling the input data, addressing situations where that internal access is unavailable.

summary.tldr: Learned input fragmentation improves spiking-network fault tolerance without accessing internal circuits, including on a physical FPGA platform.

title: Practical Mechanism for Fault-Tolerant Spiking Neural Networks via Simple Input Control Based on Learnable Fragmentation

abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow natural language instructions in partially observed 3D environments, motivating map representations that aggregate spatial context beyond local perception. However, most existing approaches rely on hand-crafted maps constructed independently of the navigation policy. We argue that maps should instead be learned representations shaped directly by navigation objectives rather than exhaustive reconstructions. Based on this insight, we propose MapDream, a map-in-the-loop framework that formulates map construction as autoregressive bird’s-eye-view (BEV) image synthesis. The framework jointly learns map generation and action prediction, distilling environmental context into a compact three-channel BEV map that preserves only navigation-critical affordances. Supervised pre-training bootstraps a reliable mapping-to-control interface, while the autoregressive design enables end-to-end joint optimization through reinforcement fine-tuning. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE achieve state-of-the-art monocular performance, validating task-driven generative map learning.

paragraphs: An agent following spoken or written directions needs spatial context beyond its current view. Many navigation systems supply that context through manually designed maps built separately from the navigation policy. MapDream instead learns a map whose contents are shaped by what the agent needs to navigate successfully.

The framework generates bird's-eye-view maps autoregressively and learns map generation jointly with action prediction. Its compact, three-channel map retains navigation-critical affordances rather than attempting an exhaustive reconstruction of the environment. Supervised pretraining first establishes a reliable connection between mapping and control, giving the system a starting point for learning how its maps support actions.

Reinforcement fine-tuning then jointly optimizes the map and navigation policy end to end. This places map construction inside the learning process, so the representation can develop around navigation objectives. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE report state-of-the-art monocular performance. The results support the central proposal that a generated map can be useful because it preserves task-relevant spatial information, even when it is deliberately compact.
summary.tldr: MapDream jointly learns compact bird's-eye-view maps and navigation actions, reporting state-of-the-art monocular results on two navigation benchmarks.

title: MapDream: Task-Driven Map Learning for Vision-Language Navigation

abstract: While diffusion models enable new approaches for estimating Local Intrinsic Dimension (LID), existing methods fail in high-dimensional spaces where noise from vast normal directions overwhelms the tangent signal. We propose Local Hessian Spectral Dimension (LHSD), which resolves this by applying spectral filtering to the log-density Hessian, explicitly cutting off large eigenvalues associated with normal directions to count zero-curvature tangent directions. Implemented using Stochastic Lanczos Quadrature (SLQ), LHSD avoids full Hessian construction, achieving linear scalability with dimension $D$. Experiments on synthetic and real data confirm LHSD’s superior robustness and its utility in detecting memorization in large-scale diffusion models.

paragraphs: Local intrinsic dimension measures how many directions describe the meaningful variation near a data point. Diffusion-based estimators can struggle in high-dimensional spaces because numerous directions normal to the data manifold overwhelm the tangent signal. This paper estimates dimension by filtering the local curvature spectrum instead.

Local Hessian Spectral Dimension applies spectral filtering to the log-density Hessian. Large eigenvalues associated with normal directions are removed, leaving near-zero-curvature tangent directions to count. Stochastic Lanczos Quadrature implements the calculation without constructing the full Hessian, giving linear scaling with ambient dimension under the proposed computation.

Synthetic and real-data experiments show improved robustness and demonstrate usefulness for detecting memorization in large diffusion models. The contribution is a scalable spectral estimator and an application of it. The abstract does not claim that intrinsic dimension alone is a definitive memorization test or provide exact recovery for every noisy data manifold.
summary.tldr: LHSD filters the log-density Hessian spectrum to estimate local dimension robustly without forming a full high-dimensional Hessian.

title: Local Hessian Spectral Filtering for Robust Intrinsic Dimension Estimation

abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models enable streaming generation, opening the door to long-form synthesis, video world models, and interactive neural game engines. However, their core attention layers become a major bottleneck at inference time: as generation progresses, the KV cache grows, causing both increasing latency and escalating GPU memory, which in turn restricts usable temporal context and harms long-range consistency. In this work, we study redundancy in autoregressive video diffusion and identify three persistent sources: near-duplicate cached keys across frames, slowly evolving (largely semantic) queries/keys that make many attention computations redundant, and cross-attention over long prompts where only a small subset of tokens matters per frame. Building on these observations, we propose a unified, training-free attention framework (FAST-AR) for FAST-AutoRegressive diffusion, consisting of three components: TempCache compresses the KV cache via temporal correspondence to bound cache growth; AnnCA accelerates cross-attention by selecting frame-relevant prompt tokens using fast approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) matching; and AnnSA sparsifies self-attention by restricting each query to semantically matched keys, also using a lightweight ANN. Together, these modules reduce attention, compute, and memory and are compatible with existing autoregressive diffusion backbones and world models. Experiments demonstrate up to x5–x10 end-to-end speedups while preserving near-identical visual quality and, crucially, maintaining stable throughput and nearly constant peak GPU memory usage over long rollouts, where prior methods progressively slow down and suffer from increasing memory usage.

This increases latency and GPU memory use, limiting the temporal context available for consistent long videos. FAST-AR targets three observed redundancies: similar cached keys across frames, slowly changing semantic attention information, and long prompts with only a few relevant tokens for each frame.

The findings make sustained generation efficiency a central result alongside faster individual computations.
summary.tldr: FAST-AR combines temporal cache compression and sparse attention to accelerate video diffusion while stabilizing memory use and throughput during long generation.

title: FAST-AR: Fast Autoregressive Video Diffusion and World Models with Temporal Cache Compression and Sparse Attention

abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. Both track context-induced uncertainty over the latent parts, but the factored representation sacrifices fidelity when factors are not conditionally independent. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. When factors are conditionally independent, models learn factored representations; when noise or dependencies break this structure, models gradually expand their effective dimensionality over training to recover fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

The first strategy requires a space that grows exponentially with the number of parts; the second uses orthogonal subspaces whose total dimension grows linearly. This paper formalizes those two representational possibilities.

Both representations can track uncertainty about hidden factors given the current context. However, separating factors loses fidelity when they are not conditionally independent. The authors derive distinct geometric predictions for the two hypotheses, including how many subspaces should appear, their dimensions, and how context representations should be arranged within them.

Tests use Transformers trained on synthetic processes with known hidden structure. With conditionally independent factors, the models learn factored representations. When noise or dependencies disrupt that structure, their effective dimensionality gradually grows during training to recover fidelity. These results explain factorization in the studied setting and suggest that interpretable low-dimensional structure may also persist in models trained on more complex data.
summary.tldr: Synthetic-process experiments show Transformers separating independent latent factors into orthogonal subspaces and expanding dimensionality when dependencies demand richer representations.

title: Transformers learn factored representations

abstract: Recent advancements in Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) have demonstrated impressive results, yet existing approaches handle either temporal or spatial dimension in isolation, struggling in the analysis of complex events that require spatial-temporal integration. To bridge this gap, we propose VideoLoom, a unified Video LLM for joint spatial-temporal understanding. To facilitate the development of fine-grained spatial and temporal localization capabilities, we curate LoomData-8.7k, a character-centric video dataset with temporally grounded and spatially localized captions. With this, VideoLoom achieves the state-of-the-art performance across a variety of spatial and temporal benchmarks. In addition, we introduce LoomBench, a benchmark consisting of temporal, spatial, and compositional video–question pairs, with a novel metric $J$&$F_{bi-fore}$, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs from diverse aspects. Collectively, these contributions offer a universal and effective suite for joint spatial-temporal video understanding, setting a new standard in multimodal intelligence.

paragraphs: Understanding a complex video event requires connecting what happens over time with where it happens in the image. VideoLoom targets this joint spatial and temporal problem. The paper argues that approaches treating the two dimensions separately struggle with events whose interpretation depends on their integration.

To develop fine-grained localization, the authors curate LoomData-8.7k, a character-centered video dataset whose captions are tied to both temporal intervals and spatial locations. This gives the model training material connecting descriptions with when and where their content occurs. The contribution spans a model, training data, and evaluation infrastructure, placing joint localization at the center of both learning and assessment rather than measuring the two dimensions only in isolation.
summary.tldr: VideoLoom combines spatial and temporal video understanding with a localized-caption dataset and a benchmark for evaluating both dimensions together.

title: VideoLoom: A Video Large Language Model for Joint Spatial-Temporal Understanding

abstract: Reasoning in knowledge-intensive domains remains challenging as intermediate steps are often not locally verifiable: unlike math or code, evaluating step correctness may require synthesizing clues across large external knowledge sources. As a result, subtle errors can propagate through reasoning traces, potentially never to be detected. Prior work has proposed process reward models (PRMs), including retrieval-augmented variants, but these methods operate post hoc, scoring completed trajectories, which prevents their integration into dynamic inference procedures. Here, we introduce Process Reward Agents (PRA), an inference-time method for providing domain-grounded, online, step-wise rewards to a frozen policy. In contrast to prior retrieval-augmented PRMs, PRA enables search-based decoding to rank and prune candidate trajectories at every generation step. Experiments on multiple medical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PRA consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving 81.9% accuracy on MedQA with Qwen3-4B, a new state of the art at the 4B scale. Importantly, PRA generalizes to unseen frozen policy models ranging from 0.5B to 8B parameters, improving their accuracy by up to 25.7% without any policy model updates. More broadly, PRA suggests a paradigm in which frozen reasoners are decoupled from domain-specific reward modules, allowing the deployment of new backbones in complex domains without retraining. All code and data are publicly available at https://process-reward-agents.github.io/.

paragraphs: Checking a reasoning step in a knowledge-intensive domain may require combining evidence from large external sources. An error can therefore pass unnoticed and influence later steps. This paper introduces Process Reward Agents, or PRA, to provide domain-grounded feedback while a frozen reasoning model is generating its answer.

PRA supplies online rewards for individual steps, allowing search-based decoding to rank and prune candidate reasoning paths throughout generation. This differs from the post hoc trajectory scoring described for earlier process reward methods. The separation is useful because the policy model keeps its existing parameters while a domain-specific reward component guides which reasoning paths continue.

It also transfers to previously unseen frozen policies from 0.5B to 8B parameters, improving accuracy by up to 25.7% without policy updates. summary.tldr: Process Reward Agents guide frozen models with online, domain-grounded step rewards, improving medical reasoning across several model sizes.

title: Process Reward Agents for Steering Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning

abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) integrate both visual understanding and generation within a single framework. Their ultimate aspiration is to create a cycle where understanding and generation mutually reinforce each other. While recent post-training methods have successfully leveraged understanding to enhance generation, the reverse direction of utilizing generation to improve understanding remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose UniMRG (Unified Multi-Representation Generation), a simple yet effective architecture-agnostic post-training method. UniMRG enhances the understanding capabilities of UMMs by incorporating auxiliary generation tasks. Specifically, we train UMMs to generate multiple intrinsic representations of input images, namely pixel (reconstruction), depth (geometry), and segmentation (structure), alongside standard visual understanding objectives. By synthesizing these diverse representations, UMMs capture rich complementary information regarding appearance, spatial relations, and structural layout. Consequently, UMMs develop a deeper and more comprehensive understanding of visual inputs. Extensive experiments across diverse UMM architectures demonstrate that our method notably enhances fine-grained perception, reduces hallucinations, and improves spatial understanding, while simultaneously boosting generation capabilities.

paragraphs: Unified multimodal models combine visual understanding and image generation, creating an opportunity for the two capabilities to improve each other. Previous post-training work has used understanding to strengthen generation. UniMRG investigates the reverse direction by making auxiliary generation tasks part of training for better visual understanding.

The method trains a model to generate three representations of an input image alongside its usual understanding objectives. Pixel reconstruction emphasizes appearance, depth represents geometry, and segmentation captures structure. Producing these complementary views encourages the model to learn information about visual details, spatial relationships, and how a scene is organized. The post-training method is designed to work across model architectures.

Experiments across diverse unified multimodal architectures report improved fine-grained perception, fewer hallucinations, and stronger spatial understanding. Generation capabilities also improve. These results suggest that generating alternative representations of an image can supply useful learning signals for understanding that image, supporting a more mutually beneficial relationship between the two capabilities within a shared model.
summary.tldr: UniMRG improves visual understanding by training unified multimodal models to generate pixel, depth, and segmentation representations of input images.

title: Generation Enhances Understanding in Unified Multimodal Models via Multi-Representation Generation

abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained diffusion and flow models to optimize downstream utilities is central to real-world deployment. Existing entropy-regularized methods primarily maximize expected reward, providing no mechanism to shape tail behavior. However, tail control is often essential: the lower tail determines reliability by limiting low-reward failures, while the upper tail enables discovery by prioritizing rare, high-reward outcomes. In this work, we present Tail-aware Flow Fine-Tuning (TFFT), a principled and efficient distributional fine-tuning algorithm based on the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). We address two distinct tail-shaping goals: right-CVaR for seeking novel samples in the high-reward tail and left-CVaR for controlling worst-case samples in the low-reward tail. Unlike prior approaches that rely on non-linear optimization, we leverage the variational dual formulation of CVaR to decompose it into a decoupled two-stage procedure: a lightweight one-dimensional threshold optimization step, and a single entropy-regularized fine-tuning process via a specific pseudo-reward. This decomposition achieves CVaR fine-tuning efficiently with computational cost comparable to standard expected fine-tuning methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TFFT across illustrative experiments, high-dimensional text-to-image generation, and molecular design.

paragraphs: Improving a generator’s average reward does not directly control its unusually poor or unusually good outputs. These extremes serve different purposes: reducing low-reward outcomes supports reliability, while emphasizing rare high-reward outcomes supports discovery. Tail-aware Flow Fine-Tuning gives these two objectives an explicit role in adapting pretrained flow models.

This decomposition makes tail-directed fine-tuning computationally comparable to standard methods focused on expected reward. The authors demonstrate effectiveness in illustrative experiments, high-dimensional text-to-image generation, and molecular design. The contribution is a practical mechanism for choosing which part of the outcome distribution to improve, rather than expecting an increase in average reward to shape the extremes appropriately.
summary.tldr: TFFT efficiently fine-tunes flow models to favor exceptional outputs or reduce poor ones by explicitly optimizing reward-distribution tails.

title: Efficient Tail-Aware Generative Optimization via Flow Model Fine-Tuning

abstract: The scalability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to long contexts is fundamentally constrained by the quadratic complexity of standard attention, motivating the adoption of linear attention mechanisms with sub-quadratic cost. To improve representation capacity under long contexts, recent approaches organize memory in a multi-state manner. However, existing multi-state linear attention methods rely on fixed state merging policies that cannot adapt to dynamically varying token importance, irreversibly obscuring critical tokens and causing severe error accumulation over long sequences. To address this limitation, we propose DLA, a dynamic memory modeling framework for multi-state linear attention. DLA introduces (i) Information-Aware Dynamic State Merging, which adaptively determines state boundaries based on token-level information variation, preserving high-resolution representations around semantic transitions while aggressively summarizing stable regions, and (ii) Capacity-Bounded Memory Modeling, which maintains a fixed-size, chronologically ordered state cache by selectively merging adjacent low-information states to control memory growth with minimal information loss. We pre-train DLA on two different linear attention models and evaluate on 10 datasets from three different aspects. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of DLA over state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Linear attention offers a less costly alternative to standard attention for long contexts. Some approaches retain several memory states to improve representation, but fixed rules for combining those states can obscure important tokens. Dynamic Linear Attention addresses this problem by adapting how memory is summarized as the information in a sequence changes.

Its first mechanism chooses state boundaries using token-level information variation. It preserves more detail near semantic transitions and compresses relatively stable stretches more aggressively. Its second mechanism keeps the state cache at a fixed size and in chronological order. When space must be managed, it selectively combines adjacent states with low information content.

Together, these mechanisms connect the allocation of memory detail to the sequence itself while bounding cache growth. The authors pre-train the framework on two different linear attention models and evaluate it on ten datasets across three aspects. They report improvements over state-of-the-art approaches, supporting adaptive state merging as a way to improve the evaluated models’ handling of long contexts.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Linear Attention preserves detail around meaningful changes while selectively merging memory states to keep storage bounded.

title: Dynamic Linear Attention

abstract: Post-training quantization at the 2-bit level enables low-cost deployment and inference acceleration for large language models (LLMs). Scalar quantization (SQ) and vector quantization (VQ) are two primary quantization methods, however, the former suffers from significant performance degradation, and the latter incurs computational and storage overhead. We propose UniSVQ, a unified 2-bit quantization framework that bridges scalar and vector quantization by parameterizing codewords as an affine transform of integer lattices. This structure preserves compatibility with optimized integer kernels while retaining much of VQ’s flexibility. We further introduce a data-driven block-wise fine-tuning strategy to directly minimize quantization reconstruction error. Extensive experiments across multiple LLM families and zero-shot benchmarks demonstrate that UniSVQ consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SQ methods and achieves performance comparable to advanced VQ methods, while providing higher inference throughput.

paragraphs: Compressing language-model weights to two bits can reduce deployment cost and accelerate inference, but the choice of representation creates trade-offs. Scalar quantization handles values individually and can lose substantial model quality at this precision. Vector quantization represents groups of values more flexibly, but brings additional computation and storage overhead. UniSVQ seeks a useful middle ground between these approaches.

The framework represents codewords through an affine transformation of integer lattices. This structured representation retains much of vector quantization’s flexibility while remaining compatible with optimized integer computation kernels. A data-driven, block-wise fine-tuning procedure directly minimizes reconstruction error caused by quantization, adapting the compressed representation to better preserve the model’s behavior.

Experiments across multiple language-model families and zero-shot benchmarks show consistently better performance than the compared state-of-the-art scalar methods. UniSVQ also achieves quality comparable to advanced vector methods while offering higher inference throughput. These findings suggest that carefully structured codewords can combine strong compression quality with efficient execution, reducing the practical tension between flexible representations and hardware-friendly arithmetic.
summary.tldr: UniSVQ combines integer-compatible structure with vector-style flexibility to deliver accurate two-bit language-model compression and higher inference throughput.

title: UniSVQ: 2-bit Unified Scalar-Vector Quantization

abstract: Reconstructing complete yet compact 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from sparse-view monocular videos remains a significant challenge. While hierarchical training with Video Frame Interpolation (VFI) improves coverage, its correlated pseudo-views and repeated merging accumulate structured, non-i.i.d. redundancy, violating the implicit independence assumptions of standard pruning methods and rendering global thresholding ineffectual. We propose CoverPruneGS, a coverage-preserving structured pruning framework specifically designed for hierarchical 3DGS. Our approach implements a coarse-to-fine pruning pipeline using voxel-based local diversity selection and ground-truth-guided lazy refinement via randomized dropout rendering. To ensure reliable refinement, we introduce a footprint-aware CUDA attribution mechanism. By aggregating ground-truth-aligned error degradation across Gaussian-influenced pixels, we generate faithful importance scores that enable precise, quantile-based "rescue" of essential primitives. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that CoverPruneGS substantially reduces Gaussian counts by 56.8% and significantly accelerates inference speeds, all while enhancing or maintaining the quality of novel view synthesis.

paragraphs: Building a 3D scene from a monocular video with few viewpoints creates a tension between covering the scene and keeping its representation compact. Hierarchical training with interpolated frames improves coverage, but repeated merging and correlated artificial viewpoints introduce structured duplication. According to the paper, this redundancy undermines the independence assumptions behind standard pruning and makes global thresholds ineffective.

CoverPruneGS removes redundant Gaussian primitives through a coarse-to-fine process. It first selects locally diverse primitives within voxels. It then refines those choices using randomized dropout rendering and comparisons against ground-truth images, allowing the method to assess which removals damage the reconstruction.

A CUDA attribution mechanism accounts for each Gaussian’s image footprint and aggregates error increases over affected pixels. These importance scores support quantile-based rescue of essential primitives, helping preserve coverage during compression. Across multiple datasets, the method reports a 56.8% reduction in Gaussian count and faster inference while maintaining or improving novel-view synthesis quality. The results connect compactness to preserving useful scene coverage.
summary.tldr: CoverPruneGS removes structured redundancy from 3D Gaussian scenes while rescuing primitives needed to preserve reconstruction quality.

title: CoverPruneGS: Coverage-Preserving Structured Pruning for Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting from Sparse-View Monocular Videos

abstract: Identifying temporal causal structure is fundamental to understanding complex systems. Neural Granger causality has emerged as a powerful paradigm for this task, leveraging the expressiveness of neural networks to model intricate nonlinear dynamics. Although complex architectures excel at predictive modeling, existing methods typically rely on simple local measures for causal discovery, which extract only partial information from the learned model and may miss global dependencies. To address this issue, we reformulate Granger causality as a feature attribution problem and propose the Information-Theoretic Shapley value (Info-Shap) to measure global feature importance. We first establish the theoretical equivalence between zero Info-Shap and Granger non-causality. On top of this, we construct two novel regularizers to suppress spurious relationships and mitigate overfitting. These regularizers are model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into the training of any differentiable neural network. Through extensive experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets, we demonstrate that our method robustly recovers the underlying causal relationships, providing a flexible tool for causal discovery in high-dimensional nonlinear time series.

Although the networks can capture nonlinear dynamics, causal discovery often relies on simple local measures extracted from them. This paper argues that such measures can overlook global dependencies already represented by the learned model.

summary.tldr: Info-Shap connects global feature attribution to Granger non-causality and supports regularizers that improve temporal structure recovery.

title: Shapley Regularized Neural Granger Causality

abstract: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is increasingly expected to provide reusable spatial representations for downstream perception. However, existing approaches often struggle with scale-consistency and producing maps that lack the geometric fidelity required for reliable perception. We propose UniMapping, a unified SLAM framework that constructs a persistent neural-descriptor map from multimodal observations. We introduce a Spatial-Aware Deformable Transformer that injects explicit geometric inductive bias to ensure scale-invariant feature extraction, alongside a Spatial Fusion strategy that decouples feature aggregation from temporal sequences. Extensive experiments on both indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate competitive SLAM performance. Notably, our method significantly enhances downstream tasks (mAP +3.1% and mIoU +7.1%) by leveraging accumulated multi-view context.

paragraphs: UniMapping treats simultaneous localization and mapping as a way to build a reusable representation for later perception tasks. A map must support more than tracking position: its features need consistent scale behavior and sufficient geometric fidelity to remain useful across observations. The framework constructs a persistent map of learned descriptors from multimodal input.

A Spatial-Aware Deformable Transformer introduces explicit geometric structure into feature extraction to ensure scale invariance. A separate Spatial Fusion strategy decouples feature aggregation from temporal sequences. Together, these components support accumulating information from multiple views in the map, making that accumulated context available for downstream perception rather than relying only on an individual observation.

Indoor and outdoor benchmark experiments show competitive SLAM performance. Downstream tasks also improve, with reported gains of 3.1% in mAP and 7.1% in mIoU. These findings support the framework's map-centered goal: maintaining a persistent representation can benefit later visual understanding as well as localization and mapping. The stated downstream gains are attributed to the accumulated multi-view context.
summary.tldr: UniMapping builds persistent neural-descriptor maps that combine multi-view context to support competitive SLAM and improved downstream perception.

title: UniMapping: Unified SLAM Framework for Map-Centric Embodied Perception

abstract: The development of high-quality text embeddings is increasingly drifting toward an exclusionary future, defined by three critical barriers: prohibitive computational costs, a narrow linguistic focus that neglects most of the world’s languages, and a lack of transparency from closed-source or open-weight models that stifles research. To dismantle these barriers, we introduce ML-Embed, a suite of inclusive and efficient models built upon a new framework: 3-Dimensional Matryoshka Learning (3D-ML). Our framework addresses the computational challenge with comprehensive efficiency across the entire model lifecycle. Beyond the storage benefits of Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) and flexible inference-time depth provided by Matryoshka Layer Learning (MLL), we introduce Matryoshka Embedding Learning (MEL) for enhanced parameter efficiency. To address the linguistic challenge, we curate a massively multilingual dataset and train a suite of models ranging from 140M to 8B parameters. In a direct commitment to transparency, we release all models, data, and code. Extensive evaluation on 430 tasks demonstrates that our models set new records on 9 of 17 evaluated MTEB benchmarks, with particularly strong results in low-resource languages, providing a reproducible blueprint for building globally equitable and computationally efficient AI systems.

paragraphs: ML-Embed addresses three barriers in text embedding development: computational expense, limited language coverage, and insufficient transparency. The authors propose a family of multilingual embedding models and a training framework intended to make efficiency extend across the model lifecycle. Their goal connects practical resource use with broader linguistic access and reproducibility.

The framework, called 3-Dimensional Matryoshka Learning, combines three forms of efficiency. Matryoshka Representation Learning provides storage benefits, while Matryoshka Layer Learning allows flexible inference depth. The new Matryoshka Embedding Learning component targets parameter efficiency. summary.tldr: ML-Embed combines three forms of model efficiency with multilingual training and open releases, setting records on 9 of 17 evaluated MTEB benchmarks.

title: ML-Embed: Inclusive and Efficient Embeddings for a Multilingual World

abstract: Foundation models are increasingly trained on synthetic data generated by prior model iterations rather than exclusively on real data. This self-consuming training paradigm can lead to model collapse, divergence, or bias amplification. Recent work (Ferbach et al., 2024) shows that incorporating human curation into the loop can steer a self-consuming model toward human-aligned behavior, but these analyses focus on a single, isolated model that solely consumes its own outputs. In practice, however, models often interact and train on input output pairs produced by other models. This paper studies self-consuming training in the multi-model regime. We first formalize a framework for interacting self-consuming models and characterize when the resulting dynamical system converges to a stable point. We then examine how human curation of one model affects its own alignment (self-influence) and how such effects propagate to other models (cross-influence). Unlike isolated settings where human curation always enhances model alignment, we show that cross-model interactions can dampen or even invert this effect, ultimately degrading long-term alignment.

paragraphs: Models increasingly train on synthetic examples produced by earlier models, creating feedback loops that can amplify bias or destabilize learning. Prior analysis of a single model consuming its own outputs found that human curation could steer alignment. This paper examines what happens when several models instead learn from one another’s generated input-output pairs.

The authors formalize interacting self-consuming models as a dynamical system and characterize when it converges to a stable point. They distinguish the effect of curating a model’s data on that model’s alignment from the effects that propagate to other models. This separates direct influence from the changes transmitted through the wider training loop.

The analysis shows that interactions can weaken or even reverse the alignment benefits of human curation, potentially worsening long-term alignment. The claim is conditional on cross-model dynamics, rather than a claim that curation generally fails. Its significance is that a locally beneficial intervention may behave differently inside an interconnected training system, making the relationships among models relevant to understanding the eventual outcome.
summary.tldr: In interacting synthetic-data training loops, cross-model feedback can weaken or reverse the alignment benefits of human curation.

title: When and How Human Curation Backfires: Preference Alignment under Multi-Model Self-Consuming Loop

abstract: The transition from single-turn models to Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) promises enhanced problem-solving capabilities, yet the centralized orchestration topology remains a critical point of fragility. To analyze this, we propose a Mean-Field Entropy Dynamics framework, modeling the orchestration process as a system governed by the competing forces of task resolution and cumulative context loading. To facilitate high-resolution validation, we introduce Inverse Workflow Generation (IWG), a multi-agent pipeline that synthesizes process-verifiable, high-complexity benchmarks with dense intermediate checkpoints. We demonstrate that our entropy dynamics model fits empirical trajectories, providing physically interpretable parameters that quantify system stability and performance collapse. Crucially, our analysis uncovers a “Reasoning Trap": while reasoning-heavy models excel in isolated tasks, they frequently fail as orchestrators due to context squeezing. By elucidating the physical mechanisms underlying the Orchestrator and quantifying systemic uncertainty, our findings offer insights for the architectural design development of Multi-Agent Systems in prospective research.

paragraphs: A multi-agent system depends on an orchestrator to coordinate work, making centralized coordination a potential source of failure. This paper models orchestration through two competing processes: resolving parts of the task and accumulating context. Its Mean-Field Entropy Dynamics framework aims to explain how that balance affects stability and eventual performance collapse.

To examine the process in detail, the authors introduce Inverse Workflow Generation. This multi-agent pipeline creates complex benchmarks whose intermediate steps can be checked, with dense checkpoints throughout the workflow. Those checkpoints support analysis of evolving system behavior rather than relying solely on whether the final output succeeds. The proposed dynamics model fits the observed empirical trajectories.

The analysis identifies a Reasoning Trap: models that perform well on isolated reasoning tasks frequently fail as orchestrators because of context squeezing. Interpretable parameters in the framework quantify stability and collapse, connecting this behavior to cumulative context loading. The findings suggest that isolated task-solving strength is insufficient for assessing orchestration suitability and offer a framework for studying the design of coordinated multi-agent systems.
summary.tldr: An entropy-dynamics model links orchestration failures to accumulating context and explains why strong reasoners can struggle as multi-agent coordinators.

title: Recognize Your Orchestrator: An Entropy Dynamics Perspective for LLM Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models sparsely activate only a subset of experts per token, reducing activated computation while maintaining high model capacity. However, in memory-constrained inference scenarios, only a small set of experts can be cached. Experts not in the cache must be fetched from slow external storage (e.g., UFS), leading to frequent evictions and substantial I/O overhead. We propose ReMoE, a router fine-tuning framework designed to boost token-wise expert reuse. ReMoE biases the router toward recently selected experts, producing temporally stable routing that better matches cache locality constraints. By increasing short-horizon expert reuse, ReMoE reduces expert fetches from storage without adding inference-time computation. Experiments on DeepSeek and Qwen models show that ReMoE improves expert reuse by 26% while maintaining downstream task performance. Real-system evaluations further confirm these benefits, improving output throughput by 8.4% under vLLM GPU–CPU expert offloading and reducing TPOT by 43.6-49.8% under llama.cpp on Jetson Orin NX, corresponding to a 1.77-1.99$\times$ decode speedup across diverse workloads. Checkpoints and usage instructions are available at https://github.com/BUAA-OSCAR/ReMoE.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models save computation by activating only a few experts for each token. However, when memory can hold only a small expert cache, changing experts frequently requires costly transfers from external storage. ReMoE addresses this data-movement bottleneck by changing routing behavior through fine-tuning.

The framework biases the router toward experts selected recently. This makes consecutive routing decisions more stable and increases the chance that needed experts are already cached. By encouraging short-horizon reuse, it reduces storage fetches without introducing additional computation at inference time. The intervention aligns model routing with the practical constraints of limited memory.

Experiments on DeepSeek and Qwen models report 26% higher expert reuse while maintaining downstream task performance. System evaluations show 8.4% higher output throughput with vLLM GPU–CPU expert offloading. On Jetson Orin NX using llama.cpp, time per output token falls by 43.6–49.8%, corresponding to 1.77–1.99-fold decoding speedups. These results illustrate that reducing expert movement can translate into substantial speed gains, with the magnitude depending on the evaluated deployment.
summary.tldr: ReMoE fine-tunes expert routing to favor recent experts, reducing memory-transfer overhead and accelerating constrained MoE inference.

title: ReMoE: Boosting Expert Reuse through Router Fine-Tuning in Memory-Constrained MoE LLM Inference

abstract: Online feature selection (OFS) provides an efficient way to sort through a large space of features, particularly in a scenario where the feature space is large and features take a significant amount of memory to store. Image processing operators, and especially combinations of image processing operators, provide a rich space of potential features for use in machine learning for image processing tasks but they are expensive to generate and store. In this paper we apply OFS to the problem of edge detection in grayscale imagery. We use a standard data set and compare our results to those obtained with traditional edge detectors, as well as with results obtained more recently using “statistical edge detection.” We compare several different OFS approaches, including hill climbing, best first search, and grafting.

paragraphs: Image-processing operators can generate many potential features for a learning system, especially when the operators are combined. That richness creates a practical problem: generating and storing the features can be expensive. This paper applies online feature selection to edge detection in grayscale images as a way to explore this large feature space efficiently.

The study considers several approaches to selecting features, including hill climbing, best-first search, and grafting. These offer different ways to search among the available image-derived features. The central question is how feature selection can make a rich collection of candidate operators usable when retaining all their outputs would demand substantial memory.

The authors evaluate the approaches on a standard dataset and compare their results with traditional edge detectors and statistical edge-detection methods. This places learned feature selection in the context of existing ways to solve the same image-processing task. The abstract establishes the application and comparison framework, emphasizing efficient feature exploration without reporting a particular winning search method or a quantified performance gain.
summary.tldr: The paper evaluates online feature-selection strategies for grayscale edge detection when candidate image features are costly to generate and store.

title: Online feature selection for pixel classification

abstract: Finding a good representation of text documents is crucial in document retrieval and classification systems. Nowadays, the most popular representation is simply based on a vector of counts storing the number of occurrences of each word in the document. This representation falls short in describing the dependence existing between similar words, and it cannot disambiguate phenomena like synonymy and polysemy of words. In this paper, we propose an algorithm to learn text document representations based on the recent advances in training deep networks. This technique can efficiently produce a very compact and informative representation of a document. Our experiments compare favorably this algorithm against similar algorithms but producing sparse and binary representations. Unlike other models, this method is trained by taking into account both an unsupervised and a supervised objective. We show that it is very advantageous to exploit even a few labeled samples during training, and that we can learn extremely compact representations by using deep and non-linear models.

paragraphs: Representing documents as word-count vectors is straightforward, but it poorly captures relationships between similar words and ambiguities in word meaning. This paper uses deep networks to learn compact document representations for retrieval and classification. The aim is to retain informative properties of a document within a much smaller representation.

Training combines an unsupervised objective with a supervised objective. This lets the representation learning process use both document information and available labels. The authors report that even a small number of labeled examples is very advantageous during training, making the supervised component useful when labels are limited.

Experiments compare favorably with related methods that produce sparse and binary representations. The paper also shows that deep, nonlinear models can produce extremely compact representations efficiently. Together, these findings support learning document encodings through combined objectives: the representation can be small while remaining informative, and limited supervision can improve the learning process in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Deep networks trained with supervised and unsupervised objectives learn compact document representations, benefiting substantially from even a few labeled examples.

title: Semi-supervised learning of compact document representations with deep networks

abstract: In game theory, a Correlated Equilibrium (CE) is an equilibrium concept that generalizes the more well-known Nash Equilibrium. If the game is represented as a graphical game, the computational complexity of computing an optimum CE is exponential in the tree-width of the graph. In settings where this exact computation is not feasible, it is desirable to approximate the properties of the CE, such as its expected social utility and marginal probabilities. We study outer relaxations of this problem that yield approximate marginal strategies for the players under a variety of utility functions. Results on simulated games and in a real problem involving drug design indicate that our approximations can be highly accurate and can be successfully used when exact computation of CE is infeasible.

paragraphs: A correlated equilibrium is a game-theoretic equilibrium concept that generalizes Nash equilibrium. For games represented by graphs, finding an optimal correlated equilibrium has computational complexity exponential in the graph's treewidth. The paper addresses settings where this makes exact computation infeasible but useful information about the equilibrium is still needed.

The authors study outer relaxations of the optimization problem. These provide approximations through an enlarged mathematical description of the feasible possibilities. The target quantities include players' marginal strategy probabilities and expected social utility. By focusing on these properties, the approach seeks useful equilibrium information without requiring the original exact computation.

The relaxations accommodate a variety of utility functions. Tests on simulated games and a drug-design problem indicate that the resulting approximations can be highly accurate and useful when exact methods are infeasible. This is an empirical statement about the studied applications: it supports approximation as a practical route to equilibrium properties without asserting exactness for every game.
summary.tldr: Outer relaxations approximate correlated-equilibrium properties and can remain highly accurate when exact computation is infeasible.

title: Approximating Correlated Equilibria using Relaxations on the Marginal Polytope

abstract: In unknown or partially unknown environments exploration is necessary to learn how to perform well. Existing reinforcement learning algorithms provide strong exploration guarantees, but they tend to rely on an ergodicity assumption. While ergodicity is a more generally applicable property, it is simplest to state for discrete state spaces, and its essence is that any state is reachable from any other state within some finite amount of time with non-zero probability by following a suitable policy. This assumption allows for exploration algorithms that operate by favoring visiting previously unvisited (or rarely visited) states. For most physical systems this assumption is completely impractical as the systems would break before any reasonable exploration has taken place, i.e., most physical systems don't satisfy the ergodicity assumption. In this paper we address the need for safe exploration methods in Markov decision processes. We first propose a general formulation of safety that can be thought of as forcing ergodicity. We show that imposing the safety constraint exactly is NP-hard. We present an efficient approximation algorithm for guaranteed safe, but potentially suboptimal, exploration. At the core of our approach is an optimization formulation in which the constraints restrict attention to guaranteed safe policies. The objective favors exploration policies. Our framework is compatible with the majority of previously proposed exploration methods, which rely on an exploration bonus, which we can replicate in the objective. Our experiments show that our method is able to safely explore state-spaces in which classical exploration methods get stuck.

paragraphs: Exploration helps an agent learn an unknown environment, but visiting unfamiliar states can be dangerous in physical systems. Many exploration methods rely on ergodicity: suitable actions give a nonzero chance of reaching any state from any other in finite time. Physical damage can make that assumption unrealistic.

The paper proposes a safety formulation that can be understood as enforcing this kind of reachability. Imposing the constraint exactly is NP-hard, so the authors develop an efficient approximation. Its optimization constraints restrict the search to guaranteed safe policies, while its objective encourages exploration. The safety guarantee comes with the possibility of suboptimal exploration.

The framework can incorporate exploration bonuses used by most previously proposed exploration methods by placing them in the objective. Experiments show safe exploration in state spaces where classical methods become stuck. The contribution is a way to pursue informative behavior within a guaranteed safe policy set, while explicitly acknowledging the computational difficulty of enforcing the original constraint exactly.
summary.tldr: An efficient approximation restricts exploration to guaranteed safe policies, potentially sacrificing optimality while avoiding failures seen with classical exploration.

title: Safe Exploration in Markov Decision Processes
